speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT ON CONCLUSION OF MEETINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a short report to the house on the dominion-provincial conference. The premiers of all the provinces, together with a number of their ministers and advisers, met at the invitation of the government, as hon. members know, to commence discussions which are requisite in preparation for the revision of the financial arrangements with the provinces, which expire in March of 1962.
This meeting was a most active one at which many proposals were put forward by the various provinces, and an opportunity was afforded for the discussion of these proposals in camera. Now they will be studied by my colleagues and myself during the next several months in preparation for subsequent discussions. Most of the meetings took place in public, and the press has given a most full and comprehensive report as to what transpired in these meetings. I shall not, therefore, endeavour to summarize the many suggestions and points of view that were put forward by the ten premiers. I do, however, wish to table copies, in English and in French, of the preliminary verbatim report of the public proceedings of the conference. I would point out, too, that these reports still have to be corrected before they are issued in final printed form. When the copies have been revised the documents will be made available to all hon. members.
The financial proposals that were advanced covered a wide range of subjects and involved very large sums. Indeed, if parliament were to act upon even the more modest of them, it would involve far-reaching changes in the budget and tax system. There were two central problems; one, the nature and extent of the net payments to be made to provinces based upon some measure of
their fiscal need, which payments include the equalization payments, which this government insists shall be continued, and such other payments as the Atlantic adjustment grants, the special grants to Newfoundland and other comparable payments. The second central problem considered was the sharing of the direct tax fields. Not unnaturally, some of the provincial governments would prefer to have the federal government reduce the federal corporation and personal income taxes and estate taxes. It would be necessary to give careful study to the various provincial suggestions and thereafter, as was the case in 1955, make preparations for the agreements such as were ultimately entered into in 1957; that is, a further conference or conferences will have to take place. It has been agreed that the present conference will resume on October 26, at which time a period of three days will be devoted to it.
The conference, though called to discuss fiscal matters, provided an opportunity for discovering that there was now a wider measure of agreement on the desirability and possibility of having two fundamental improvements made in the constitution. It was concluded that we should proceed at once to seek agreement on a means of amending Canada's constitution in Canada rather than by petition to Her Majesty the Queen to request the parliament at Westminster to make amendments which have to do with the distribution of powers as between the federal parliament and the provincial legislatures.
There was discussion also respecting a bill of rights. I hope that in consequence of the meeting which has been arranged for the latter part of September or the early part of October, to be convened by the Minister of Justice and attended by him and the various attorneys general, we may possibly look forward to the day when the constitution will be brought home, so to speak, and that consideration will then be given to making arrangements by agreement to incorporate, following the return of the constitutional powers to Canada, all the guarantees of those fundamental rights for Canadian citizens.
I think I need say no more at this time than to give this general report; for, as hon. members know, the discussions that took place in Canada are not revealed at this time in accordance with the tradition that has been built up through the years.

Dominion-Provincial Conference
Questions have been asked with regard to the agenda. I might summarize the questions that were on the agenda following the determination by the conference on Tuesday. The first had to do with tax arrangements, a discussion of the possible arrangements after March 31, 1962, under the following headings: (a) arrangements with respect to personal income tax, corporation income tax and succession duties; (b) equalization and fiscal need payments, the principles underlying equalization and fiscal need payments and an examination of possible formulas; and (c) stabilization payments; indirect provincial retail sales tax; a matter such as uniform rules for allocation of corporate profits and the income of individuals to provinces; taxation of natural resource industries; sharing of the federal income tax collected from corporations whose main business is the distribution or generation for distribution to the public of electrical energy, gas or steam. Then some time was taken on the question of action respecting the application of the sales tax to crown agencies. In addition to those I have mentioned were such matters as economic development and employment and capital financing. Constitutional questions also received attention, as did the important field of conditional grants and shared-cost programs.
That is a resume of those things that received consideration, and I feel it is only fair to say that it was most careful consideration having regard to the time available. All the deliberations took place in a spirit of frankness and with every regard being had by all to assure that the federal and provincial governments are not separate one from another when questions such as the welfare of Canada as a whole are being considered.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT ON CONCLUSION OF MEETINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has just told us that the conference which has just concluded was an active one. The record of the proceedings and the Prime Minister's own statement show that it was indeed an active conference. Part of that activity, so far as one can judge from the record, seems to have been the reaction of the provincial premiers to the statement of the Minister of Finance interpreting in statistical terms the requests made of the federal government by those provincial premiers who spoke on this matter, an interpretation which was challenged, as indeed the procedure adopted in the minister's speech was also challenged, by the premier of Ontario as repeating a controversial procedure in the conference of 1957.
On the side of more constructive activity one must mention the proposal taken on the initiative of the premier of Quebec that a

conference should be called in the autumn to consider ways and means by which Canadians can amend their own constitution. That was a proposal made by the premier of Quebec which was supported by other premiers, including the new premier of New Brunswick. The proposal also dealt with the possibility of a national bill of rights at a time when we have before us only a limited bill of rights. This activity at the conference, Mr. Speaker, was indeed constructive.
Perhaps less productive of a reaction was the request made by certain provinces that there should also be a discussion at this time of the unemployment problem. So far as the financial proposals are concerned, it would appear that after a long series of conferences, study groups, seminars and examinations by the federal government and federal officials, after nearly three years' consideration of this matter the federal government at this conference had no proposals to make to the provincial premiers. It appears that their attitude on this matter was negative and passive. This, Mr. Speaker, is a far cry from the new deal that was promised to the provinces in the electoral period of 1957 and 1958.

Before the Leader of the Opposition proceeds I want to remind him that in these statements which are made on routine proceedings there is an opportunity for comment which I think the good sense of every hon. member will dictate should be of a constructive, non-provocative and noncontroversial character. Otherwise we are doing that which is not permissible, namely entering upon a debate without opportunity for reply, and that was demonstrated the other day.
So in giving this word of caution my suggestion to all hon. members who take part in such discussions is that they must bear in mind that it is not really a discussion but merely an opportunity for brief comment. I particularly felt that the Leader of the Opposition, in entering into political controversy of this kind which he was approaching, was perhaps getting beyond the proper scope of this kind of discussion.
Hon. members will realize that there are no fixed rules. There is no subject before the house. Comment by a spokesman for each party has been customary; it has usually been brief, and it has usually been constructive. I am sure the house does not want to limit any hon. member to concurrence or approval only, but I think some restraint is in order at this time.

Dominion-Provincial Conference

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT ON CONCLUSION OF MEETINGS
speechtext:
I find myself in a somewhat difficult position. I want to obey your admonition, Mr. Speaker, and I intend to. At the same time I hate to sit out any partisan political controversy that may be going on in this house. There is an overall rule which says we are equal here, although some of us think there are some who are more equal than others.
I want to thank the Prime Minister for having taken this opportunity to report to the house on the federal-provincial conference, because that does give opposition spokesmen a chance to make some brief comment. As has been the custom in the recent past, the federal government approached this conference, I will not say in a negative and passive manner but with a blank sheet of paper. The government was not showing its hand at this conference, except that the Minister of Finance did add up all the proposals which the provincial premiers had made and then got into a controversy as to whether the total was $2 billion or some other figure.
A very definite theme was enunciated by the premiers as they rose one after another, and that was that the revenues of the provinces, as well as of the federal government, depend to a very large extent on the state of our economy. There was great concern at this conference about the weak and unhealthy state of the economy, and it was emphasized that everything should be done to make our economy more buoyant and therefore by that means to increase the revenues of all the provinces.
I was glad that the Prime Minister underlined today this belief in the principle of equalization grants. I think equalization grants are a part of our economic structure in this country today which must be maintained. I feel that in the future greater emphasis needs to be laid on the fiscal needs of the provinces. I would think that before the coming conference this fall there are two general economic areas that should be considered. First of all, there is need to embark upon programs on a co-operative basis which will strengthen our economy. Second, I submit there is need to make a broad attack in the field of welfare measures, and now is the time to go forth.
The Prime Minister has said, and very properly so, that if the many proposals that were made were acceded to by the federal government it would mean far-reaching tax changes. Undoubtedly that is true. I feel that as a parliament, or as a nation, we should not shy away from increased taxes where they appear to be necessary to provide improvements in essential services or to contribute to

Inquiries of the Ministry an expanding economy. Between now and the conference this fall I hope the federal government will consider economic proposals and will bring in something in the nature of those contained in the green book proposals of 1945, because I think once again our country is at the economic crossroads.
The Prime Minister has said there was greater acceptance among the provinces of the idea of bringing our constitution to this country, having it domiciled here, and there was greater support for embedding in our constitution a bill of rights. I hope the Prime Minister will proceed with all energy to endeavour to get agreement from the provinces so we can bring our constitution to this country and so we can have a bill of rights embedded in it which will provide for a strengthening of human rights and fundamental freedoms in this country.
I have expressed in another place the position of our group; that pending this conference there should be a postponement of further procedure on the bill of rights. I do not intend, Mr. Speaker, to make any further comment on that matter. I merely say the Prime Minister should consider now every practical means of speeding the day when we may have a bill of rights embedded in our constitution.

Mr. Speaker, that is a very interesting question because, if the hon. gentleman will recall 1955, when a similar conference was convened, the federal government at the initial conference made no proposals nor did it indicate its attitude regarding the agreements that might be entered into. The first meeting, as I remember, was held in the month of April; then there was a later meeting in October. We have arranged, as I mentioned, for a meeting to be convened in October, at which time the federal government, in keeping with the experience of 1955, will submit its views, having secured from the provinces the benefit of their suggestions.

The present conference was to be entirely a fiscal conference. During the course of representations, naturally, matters dealing with the economy as a whole were brought forward. My answer still stands; that any replies or views expressed were, it was clearly understood by all present, not to be made public. Indeed, the only statement that came out of the conference was the one that I had cleared with the members of the conference, indicating that there would be a further conference after the preliminary one, in October, and that a meeting of the provincial attorneys general would be held with the Minister of Justice.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. speechtext:

speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with great reluctance on a question of privilege. My question of privilege arises out of a press report in the Ottawa Citizen of yesterday evening with respect to a certain statement made by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Tardif) at a board of control meeting recently. In order to get the point correctly I just wish to read briefly, as follows:
At one point in the meeting the discussion produced reference to the facilities sought by "M.P.'s" when they are sick. "I understand they do not always stay in the best of places, observed Mayor Nelms." Countered Con. Paul Tardif, who is M.P.

for Russell: "There are M.P.'s who are not accustomed to anything .. . There are five rows of them in front of me in the house."
My question of privilege is this, Mr. Speaker, and I rise more from a feeling of hurt than from a sense of anger. While members of this group are members of the working class and consequently are able to make only modest expenditures on food, dress and habitation, I consider it most unfair and ungentlemanly of a colleague in this house or any colleague who enjoys better financial circumstances to ridicule our humble circumstances.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Flynn in the chair.
66. Departmental administration, $8,323,356.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. House in committee of supply, Department of Defence Production, item No. 66. This item is to be found on page 16 of the blue book, the details on page 153.

speakeroldname: Hon. Raymond O'Hurley (Minister of Defence Production):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the estimates of the Department of Defence Production have been the subject of consideration by the special committee on defence expenditures; accordingly I do not propose to make a lengthy statement at this time. First of all, however, I would like to express my appreciation and thanks to the members of the special committee for the work they have performed and also for the action that has been taken in approving my departmental estimates and commending them to this committee. I would like in particular to express my appreciation to the hon. member for London, who carried out his duties as chairman of the special committee in such a splendid manner.
I would now like to refer to the content of the departmental estimates, and in this connection I propose to follow the order of the votes, Nos. 66 to 74 and votes 508 and 509 in the supplementary estimates.
Vote 66 shows an increase of $774,000 over last year's estimate. The largest individual item which contributes to this increase is salaries. In this regard I would like to point out that for the first time in eight years we have found it necessary to ask for an increase in staff. This increase amounts to an addition of 74 new positions, of which 42 are required for the intensified activities in connection with the Canada-United States joint production sharing program.
Supply-Defence Production
Vote 67 and supplementary vote 508, for the care, maintenance and custody of standby defence plants, buildings, machine tools and production tooling, provides some $90,000 less than the total provision made last year, but about $450,000 more than was actually spent in 1959-1960. The provision under this vote is contingent to a great degree upon decisions which must be taken during the course of the fiscal year, and requirements therefore cannot be forecast with any close accuracy.
Vote 68 provides for capital assistance to industry and for the underwriting of certain tooling preproduction costs involved in bids submitted by Canadian industry for United States orders under the production sharing program. There is also a substantial contingent element in this vote, as it is not possible to anticipate the opportunities for bidding which are going to be open to Canadian industry nor the degree of success which they will enjoy. The total provision made this year is slightly less than that of 1959-1960, owing to a reduction in the forecast requirements for capital assistance.
The plants covered by vote 69 have been acquired by the crown under the capital assistance programs of previous years and are operated by private contractors on the same basis as industrial plants. The grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes are computed on the normal assessment evaluation by the municipality, taking account of the services rendered, and are estimated to equal the taxes which would otherwise be payable.
The provision made in vote 70 to establish qualified sources of supply of component parts and materials is identical with that made in 1959-1960. This is a selective program in which we must weigh each case in the light of the quantities of components likely to be required and existing manufacturing capabilities on which we can build. While it is intended primarily to establish sources of components which will be needed for future Canadian military requirements, the likelihood of United States defence requirements is also taken into account.
Vote 71 continues the provision which was made for the first time last year to support select defence development programs as part of our Canada-United States production sharing program. It is becoming increasingly clear that as a result of the rapid pace of change in military equipment, the future success of Canadian industry under the production sharing program requires that Canadian engineering capacity be maintained and advanced to the greatest extent practical.
Votes 72, 73, 74 and supplementary vote 509 relate to crown companies. Vote 72 provides for the expenses incurred by Defence Construction (1951) Limited in procuring the

Supply-Defence Production construction and defence projects on behalf of the Department of National Defence. During the past few days it has been possible to obtain a firmer estimate of the construction work required during the current fiscal year and it will be possible to reduce the vote requirement for the current fiscal year by $250,000 to a revised figure of $3,626,117. I propose to ask one of my colleagues to move an amendment in this connection when we reach the vote in question.
Vote 73 and supplementary vote 509 provide for an increase in the provision made for administrative expenses of Canadian Arsenals Limited. As I explained in my statement on the estimates for 1959-60 the decline in the sales of this company has made it necessary to revert to the practice of appropriating funds to cover a part of its administrative costs. At the time the main estimates for the current year were prepared it was thought that this financial requirement could be reduced by accelerating the production of ammunition needed by the navy in future years. Subsequently it has been found impractical to do this and the additional funds must therefore be sought under the supplementary estimates.
As regards vote 74 I would point out that the provision for the cost of construction improvements and new equipment for Canadian Arsenals Limited has been substantially reduced. This vote covers capital costs of a general nature and excludes any sums attributable to specific programs which would be covered by vote 68. The reduction is, of course, a reflection of the reduced volume of operations at Canadian Arsenals.
As I have already pointed out to the special committee on defence expenditures, there is an important new function reflected in these estimates. An emergency supply planning branch has been established within the Department of Defence Production to undertake the planning and organization necessary to permit a war supplies agency to come into existence immediately should a nuclear attack be made on this country. As the Prime Minister explained when advising this house of the government's decision to assign this planning task to the Department of Defence Production, the war suplies agency would be charged with responsibility and authority for all aspects of control over the production, distribution and pricing of supplies, both civil and military, during at least the early period of a nuclear war, other than production on the farm and the catching and landing of fish. Such a war supplies agency would combine the responsibilities carried out in the last war by the department of munitions and supply and the wartime prices and trade board.


I wish to emphasize that this new branch is a planning agency and should not be confused with the war supplies agency itself. Broadly speaking, the functions of the emergency supply planning branch with respect to supply planning are analogous to those of the emergency measures organization in the field of civil emergency planning generally. In addition to being responsible for the preparation of a basic plan for the creation of a war supplies agency, it will thus also have responsibility for co-ordinating those aspects of emergency supply planning that are properly the responsibility of other branches of the Department of Defence Production or of other departments and agencies of the federal government, particularly planning in the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Fisheries.
The initial staff of the emergency supply planning branch is small. In the future it is intended to establish a number of regional offices of the emergency supply planning branch across the country, similar to those already established by the emergency measures organization of the privy council office.
At this time I would like to deal with certain matters which arose in the course of the consideration of these estimates by the special committee. The hon. member for Trinity inquired as to the status of Iroquois engine tooling. In this connection. I can report that from the early development stages of the Iroquois engine, many groups engaged in aircraft production have expressed interest in using this power plant in various types of aircraft. My department and Orenda Engines Limited have received inquiries from governmental agencies and private interests in North America and Europe.
Officers of Orenda and of my department are co-operating in discussions with all groups who may be in a position to complete the development and put the Iroquois into production. The future use of the engine is now under serious consideration by one aircraft manufacturer in the United States. Proposals have been submitted to the manufacturer, and these are presently undergoing technical and economic evaluation. I regret that I cannot reveal the name of the manufacturer or any of the details at this time, because a premature announcement would not be conducive to the successful completion of negotiations.
Interest in the Iroquois for the purpose of furthering the "state of art" has been shown by a company in the United Kingdom. This company has requested the use of one engine and we have agreed, in principle, to make one or more engines available in the event that

the engines are not required for the production program which is now under consideration.
In the meantime 13 completed prototypes, components sufficient to complete an additional seven engines, and all essential tooling are stored in the crown-owned high altitude test facility at Malton. This facility is not in current operation but is being retained for future use. The storage costs are therefore negligible.
The hon. member for Renfrew North stated that invitations to tender are submitted to both wholesale and retail stores in Pembroke. My departmental officials have investigated this matter and I have been advised that the invitations to tender by my department, which relate to food requirements in the Pembroke area, are not directed in the manner suggested by the hon. member. The cases he has in mind may concern small local purchases which are made direct from the trade by service officers in connection with the requirements of various messes and canteens.
The hon. member for Renfrew North also suggested the inclusion of a clause dealing with the employment of local labour in contracts covering the construction of housing units at Camp Petawawa. As the chief engineer of Defence Construction (1951) Limited pointed out to the special committee, the construction of these units is a responsibility of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The comments of the hon. member have been brought to the attention of that corporation. As regards the firm price construction contracts which are placed by Defence Construction (1951) Limited, I would like to point out that the general conditions covering such contracts provide as follows:
To the full extent to which they are procurable, consistent with proper economy and the expeditious carrying out of the work, the contractor shall use Canadian labour and material in the work and shall employ labour from the locality of the work and reasonable proportions of men who have served on active service with the armed forces of Canada and been honourably discharged therefrom.
I am not going to make any further comments at this time. However, I shall be most pleased to deal with any questions that may arise as we proceed with the consideration of the estimates.

As the minister has stated, his estimates were considered by the special committee which examined governmental expenditure, and since we went into this subject at length it is not our purpose to ask a lot of questions in committee of supply today.
However, there are a few questions we should like to put to the minister, and the
Supply-Defence Production first is this. Some time ago there was newspaper speculation about the possibility of obtaining for Canada a very large order for picket planes, long range radar aircraft. I wonder if the minister could tell us what happened in that case; whether the order has been let by the United States government and, if not, whether there is still a possibility of obtaining it for Canadian manufacturers.
I am advised that the United States did not continue with the purchase of these planes. As far as we know they have not purchased the planes in question.
Can I take it from that reply that as far as the minister knows there are no current negotiations which may lead to a Canadian order in this respect.
Not at this time.

I should like to ask the minister a question. I realize there is difficulty in obtaining an accurate statistical analysis because of the very nature of the operation, but is it fair to say that the volume of procurement for the armed services is down? The estimates of the department would tend to indicate that, and I wonder if the minister would go as far as is practicable in giving us information as to the volume of procurement this year as related to the last few years.
In my report to the committee I dealt with this subject. I should just like to repeat that part of the brief I read.
Would you give me the page reference?

Page 5 of my report. I might sum up by giving a few figures which are particularly relevant. We spent for supplies and services, on behalf of the Department of National Defence, $654 million. This was about 12 per cent lower than the level of expenditure in 1958-59 and continued a decline in defence production expenditures which has been going on for some years. Out of the total spending last year, $593 million went directly to contractors in Canada. To put it in another way, expenditures by our department going to foreign contractors represented 9.3 per cent of the total payments during 1959-60.
Does that answer the question asked by the hon. member?

It does in part. As I say, I recognize the difficulty of giving precise information. Perhaps we could approach the subject from another direction. Can the minister tell the house in general terms the total number of staff in his department this year as compared with the last three years,
7114	HOUSE OF
Supply*-Defence Production or over a shorter period if the figures for the last three years are not available at the moment.

There was no increase in the staff of the department for eight years; there were even considerable reductions. In 1959-GO the total number of staff was 1,510. We went into the production sharing program, and there has been an increase this year for the first time in eight years. For 1960-61 we plan on having a staff of 1,584, which is an increase of 74. These are positions available; the actual number of staff is somewhat less.
That is the establishment?

Yes the establishment.
The actual staff on March 31, 1959 amounted to 1,441. On March 31, 1960, it was 1,476 and on June 30, 1960, 1,483.

I think the point I wanted to make can be made from the figures given by the minister. The staff of this department has been decreasing for some seven or eight years. This year, for the first time, the establishment is increased. This raises a point which should be watched, namely that there is an increase of staff and administrative costs in a department which is facing less procurement responsibilities at a time when there is less material to procure.
Perhaps the point can be dealt with better when the estimates of the Department of National Defence are before us and we shall be dealing with the actual procurement for defence purposes in this country, but I wanted to put that general warning on record'; that there is a problem here which will require to be watched, and watched carefully, because at the very time we are reducing our procurement program for the defence department, as we have been doing for the last couple of years, we are increasing the administrative organization of the department which is charged with the responsibility of procuring those supplies, materials, equipment and so on. This is something that I think should be drawn to the attention of the committee for checking and watching in the future.

Mr. Chairman, it looks as though government departments have to be on guard at all times with respect to Parkinson's law, that staff increases to fill the time available. The minister will keep this in mind as he considers his establishment from year to year.
Can the minister tell us the present state of negotiations with respect to the proposed United States purchase of CL-44 aircraft from Canadair Limited? As the minister knows, there were reports in the newspapers which indicated first of all that there was a possible order of some $900 million for those
IMr. Mcllraith.]

aircraft. Later reports indicated that the figure was reduced to something of the order of $150 million or $160 million. Can the minister bring us up to date on the matter?

Mr. Chairman, in reply to the request of the hon. member for Trinity, I should like very much to be able to give full information to the hon. member at this time. If Canada is to have an interceptor, it will have to be a military requirement; it will also have to be the policy of the government. With respect to the question of the exchange of the CL-44, on the one hand and the F-101 from the United States on the other, this matter is under active discussion at the present time with the government. I should like to be able to make a declaration, but no decision has been made up to this date.

The minister is stating, then, that the purchase by the United States air force of the CL-44 cargo carrier is dependent on the purchase by the Canadian government of a certain number of interceptors to be supplied to our air defence squadrons? Is that correct?

The position of the government and of the Department of Defence Production has been and is still today that we would wish the United States to purchase from us the CL-44, and the other question can be discussed at another time. It is fair to say that one of the conditions that is being discussed is the exchange of the two planes.

Mr. Chairman, the figures that have been given on the increase in staff are interesting. The minister has indicated that it is due to increased work, and I do not quarrel with that statement at all. I know how hard working the members of this department are, but it is nevertheless interesting to relate this increase to the reduced work of the department in so far as production is concerned for the armed forces.
But that is not really what I rose to speak about, Mr. Chairman. The minister has told us that this question of the possible exchange of the CL-44 air freighter for United States interceptors for our continental defence squadrons is now under consideration; indeed it has been under consideration for some time. It would be a very unfortunate thing indeed if this principle of defence sharing were applied, not only in this connection but in any other connection, in a way which brought about the result that "if you wish the U.S.A. to purchase certain material from Canada, which it may need and which it can get in Canada, we must in return purchase certain defence material in the United States to offset against that".

I am not suggesting that any such principle is being applied in that hard and fast way, but there have been indications that this is the situation in regard to this particular proposal. It would be most unfair for the United States to take that stand. For one thing, it would be pressure brought to bear on a Canadian government to do something which it might not otherwise feel necessary or desirable to do.
If this principle of defence sharing means anything at all, and it certainly should mean something, it means sharing-and not in the way I have suggested-in defence production generally, and it means sharing in the production of defence materials. The United States has certainly shown no awareness of the application of that principle in connection with such an essential defence material, for instance, as uranium. That has nothing to do with the minister's department, and I am only bringing it up as an illustration of the general argument I am making.
In connection with the CL-44 proposal- and I know how important this would be for the aircraft industry in Canada if it could be followed through, and I know the minister's department is doing its very best in this regard-I should like to ask the minister this question. Perhaps I should know this, and if I am ignorant on the matter I hope he will accept my apology. Has the bill which was submitted to the United States congress some months ago by Senator Mon-roney, which would have had the effect of compelling the United States federal government to underwrite 75 per cent of the cost of constructing air freighters built in the United States, made any progress? Has it been passed or not? If it has been passed, of course, it would have an effect on this whole problem. It is interesting to note that this bill was submitted to congress, I think last February, by Senator Monroney, who is a very great friend of Canada and who has been quoted in this house by the Secretary of State for External Affairs as having given some resounding utterance about continental co-operation in continental defence. This is the kind of bill which, if it were to prevent Canadian competition in the defence field, would hardly be a reflection of that kind of defence co-operation and defence sharing that I would like to see brought about.
Also, it is difficult, at least difficult for me, to get the facts and statistics regarding the defence sharing program. be facilitated, and of course we hoped to our advantage, in the defence sharing agreements about which we have heard so much. First of all may I say to the Leader of the Opposition that the Monroney bill, which was discussed at length and whose introduction came as a surprise to Canada, was finally quashed and was never passed. It was shelved. With respect to purchase of the CL-44 by the United States air force, my information is that there is no impediment whatsoever and that the United States could purchase these planes from Canada.
The Leader of the Opposition spoke about our intensified efforts to get into the field of production sharing with the United States. I want to be quite frank with the Leader of the Opposition. I am not enthusiastic about the results to date myself. I think it is a long range program. In my view we have to start now to get into this field, which involves engineering because there is a complete change-over in armaments. If Canada wants to produce in this field we have to start now and probably the first results will not be very satisfactory.
Last year was the first year that we really kept records, and we did not have the staff to do the work. We did it with our ordinary

Supply-Defence Production office staff which we had to spread out fairly thin. One reason we have had to increase our staff is that we were sending too many of the boys to the hospital. Production sharing is a very difficult matter. A lot of credit has to be given for keeping the program alive. Many Canadian companies have shown their interest by writing us or visiting the department and they are quite pleased with the results, but of course not all companies are happy about it. There are companies that are not pleased and where the results have not been good.
So far as the long range program is concerned involving production sharing by Canada and the United States, I give my frank view to the Leader of the Opposition that we have to keep harping on the subject, working on the matter and putting forth all our efforts to reach an understanding. I wish to say that I think the United States officials on the secretarial level and the heads of departments in the Pentagon realize the usefulness of the program and have really made quite an effort to help. But in the United States so much of their defence program is concerned with the missile field, and there are many contracts that are allocated. My goal was that the United States should spend at least an equal amount on defence production in Canada as we spend in the United States. At least it would have been something if we could have equalized our purchases in the United States. This year we will not do so on account of the expensive purchasing for the CF-104 program, involving licensing and so on.
We will certainly not achieve that result unless we are fortunate enough to have something unexpected happen before the end of the year. Several projects are being studied. I want to give credit to the secretaries in Washington and the heads of their departments for their real interest in doing something about production sharing. However, I still make the statement that the situation could be much better and that the present state of affairs is no fault of the department. We are doing everything we can with respect to production sharing under these different programs in the years to come.

I do not wish to minimize the importance of the program, its difficulties or the efforts that are being made by the officials of the minister's department to realize it. I think one aspect of this difficulty may well be that a defence production sharing program of this kind inevitably becomes linked with co-operation in defence strategy and defence generally. There is an interrelationship between defence production and defence generally which can operate to our


advantage, but when we are dealing with such a powerful nation can also operate to our disadvantage. I am sure the minister is much more aware of this than I am. For instance, on page 25 of the report of the minister's department there is the following:
At the beginning of 1959, production sharing arrangements were based mainly upon four projects of mutual Canadian-United States interest: the Bomarc anti-aircraft missile, the semi-automatic ground environment (SAGE) control system, heavy radars and gap fillers for the radar lines.
These are four projects which, though it is an arguable matter, in our view may well be of much greater interest to the United States than to us. Indeed our position is that we should not be participating in at least one of these projects at all. I mention that just to illustrate the interrelationship I have talked about and which undoubtedly will have a bearing on the minister's laudable desire to increase United States purchasing in Canada and bring it to a basis at least of equality with our own purchases from the United States. These as he has mentioned, have increased during the years because of the CF-104 contract and presumably the necessity of remodelling the earlier version to make it suitable for the purpose which the government has in mind of equipping our squadrons in Europe with it. I have just been reminded that no doubt this is another major worry in the minds of the minister and his officials as to how this can be done and at what cost.
I should like to ask the minister one other question, and again I refer to page 25 of the 1959 departmental report, where there is reference to the arrangements which were made for exemption from the buy American act through a revision of the buy American regulations in order, presumably, to make it a little easier for our manufacturers to get contracts in the United States. Is the minister satisfied that these amendments to the regulations are working satisfactorily from our point of view and that our people are indeed given a fair opportunity to compete with United States manufacturers for these defence contracts?
In reply to the last remarks of the Leader of the Opposition, I honestly think that the changes in the buy American act regulations are really fair to Canadian manufacturers.

Well, Mr. Chairman, we certainly had hopes that the Iroquois engine would have a future. We have been working for some months with the United Kingdom in relation to the future development of this engine, and we are working with the United States in connection with the future development and use of the Iroquois engine. We are certainly following this situation very closely. We have some hopes that this Iroquois might be developed in the future in collaboration with some other countries, and that the engine might be brought to the point where it is supposed to be as a new power plant.
However, at the moment I cannot give any assurance to the committee that this project is going to really be a success. We are hoping it will be. We are hoping that the Canadian engineers who have worked on the Iroquois engine will have made a contribution to the future. The Canadian government has great faith in Canadian manufacturers, Canadian engineers and Canadian developers, and given the opportunity Canadians will be out in front with new developments and will make their mark in the world.

The government had the opportunity to assist in the completion of the development work on this engine. The government showed a complete lack of faith in the potential of the engine when it laid it aside in moth balls for this period of two years, thus allowing it to drop further behind in this very competitive field. Surely the government is demonstrating a lack of faith in its own salesmanship, because if it had any confidence in its own ability to make production sharing arrangements really work it would have gone ahead with this project, developed the engine to the place where it was pre-eminent in its field, and then proceeded to make a swap with other countries for the military equipment that Canada needed. Obviously the government has no faith in Canadian industry, and no faith in itself. We feel that the whole policy of the government in the last two years has been timorous and lacking in imagination, and this has been evidenced by the contracts we have received and the lack of results achieved.

As to the matter of production sharing, does it not come to this situation, namely that there is a long term continuing problem of great magnitude facing this country because of the rapid development of new and extremely complicated and expensive equipment as a defence requirement, and that by the very nature of things, notwithstanding the competence of our engineers and our industry-about which I agree wholeheartedly with the minister-there is the problem of development as opposed to production? Our problem in this country is in securing the participation of Canadians in development at a sufficiently early stage so that when it comes to the point of production they will be in a position to share in it.
I think that is the nub of the problem, and I think the term "production sharing", while I am not quarrelling with its practice, is sometimes an unhappy phrase to use. It seems to me too simple an expression to describe the problem. What I for my part would like to encourage the department to do is to seek to get Canadian participation at the earliest possible stage in the development of new weapons. Then we can follow up with getting all the production sharing we can at the production stage. It is really the participation at the development stage which creates the problem, because in many instances there is

Supply-Defence Production such abnormally high cost in relation to the ability of the taxpayers of this country to bear it, and that cost seems to be increasing as the nature of the weapons becomes more complicated.

In reply to the hon. member for Ottawa West, we have in fact changed the name of our defence production sharing program and now we call it defence production and development sharing. I realized at the outset that we wanted to get in on the ground floor of the development of these projects, and I think our engineers and our companies are wide enough awake. We have been much encouraged and are now really working on the development of any new missiles or weapons which come up, especially in the electronics field. It is very complicated, but we are really getting in on the ground floor on any new project coming up.

I agree with the minister's remarks about the engineers in Canadian industry, and so on, but the point I wish to make is that the term "sharing" and the use of that word rather indicates that there is participation by both Canada and the United States, and that we are trying to increase our participation in something already there.
What I am trying to focus attention on is this. It is a very real problem, and I am not trying in any way to minimize the difficulties before the minister; I am trying to encourage him to be very assiduous in the job of trying to protect our interests in this regard.

I was interested when the minister told us that his staff had increased, and I should like to put forward a suggestion which, incidentally, is not mine, which I think will enable the minister to effect a considerable saving and probably a reduction of staff.
This suggestion concerns the disposal of surplus equipment up to the value of $1,000. We know that government departments have responsible officials in charge, and these officials could, I think, be classed as sufficiently responsible to handle such matters as the disposal of assets in this category without the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation being involved. I should like to give an example of one instance which I think will clearly indicate the circumstances I refer to. It concerns a building which was leased by the crown over a period of years. Then a building owned by the crown was constructed. The usual procedure will be to remove the heating unit and equipment to storage where it will take up valuable storage space, or to dispose of it through the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. There is one other method; to declare it obsolete and beyond economic repair and of no economic value, and write it off.
Returning the equipment to store would cost a minimum for crating of $15. Cartage would amount to $6. Storage at $1.80 per square foot for five years would amount to $45 and time and effort would amount to $50 or a total expenditure of $116 to preserve an article which would be declared surplus after five years and disposed of. The value of this particular item at the time of putting it into storage would perhaps be $20. I suggest that the disposal could be handled by a responsible official of the department concerned, and the money remitted to the crown by the department. This would mean a very considerable saving to the department and would perhaps eliminate some of the large staff in crown assets.

I should like to make a little further reference to crown assets, based on my own experience. I spent four years in the army in Whitehorse, and annually there was a collection of equipment that was no longer usable and no longer required. A tremendous expense was involved in having an annual sale, because at a point like Whitehorse very expensive travel is involved to bring people there for the disposal sale. It also involved very considerable expense to the prospective buyers of this equipment who, therefore, bid very low.
I suggest to the minister that this could be a method of saving time, money and people. He should cut down on these sales and allow the disposal to be done through the responsible officials of the department who are on site, who know the material and who could dispose of it perhaps at a slight profit to the government instead of, as in most cases, a very substantial loss.

I have had many representations on this matter. It is of great concern to my own industry. These machines, which the United States government will not allow to come back into their own business channels, are appearing on our scene in ever increasing numbers and in ever expanding areas. Can the minister make a statement on this problem? Can he tell us whether there are any taxes on these machines, and how the valuation is arrived at? In other words, what is the government's policy at the present time in regard to this matter?

I was interested in the
remarks of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, and they will certainly be brought to the attention of the officials. I think we have two sales, one on the Alaska highway and one at Whitehorse, each year. I will take up the matter with crown assets, and I shall speak to the hon. member about it.
With respect to the question of the hon. member for Regina City respecting the sale of United States equipment by crown assets, we have had a lot of correspondence on the matter; pressure has been put on the government, and memoranda have been submitted to me and to other ministers of the government concerning the sale of this surplus equipment, especially in Newfoundland. This question has been looked into by crown assets and myself, and we have taken note of it.
This information we think has been put out by equipment suppliers, by some Canadian

manufacturers and by the Canadian contractors association. On the other hand we have small municipalities and small dealers in local communities who wish the sale of this equipment to be continued. They repair it and sell it on guarantee. Two briefs have been prepared and will be submitted to the government right after the session closes. The government will study this situation and its decision will be made known shortly.
I wish to tell the hon. member for Regina City and any other hon. members who have written to me about the disposal of United States equipment that the matter is receiving the attention of the government, and a decision will be arrived at shortly.
The hon. member for Trinity spoke to me about Polymer. Polymer is a very successful crown company which is going to have a very good year in the sale of its synthetic rubber and even in its specialty rubber, which is something new. As hon. members know, Polymer is in a competitive field. It is the duty of the minister to have, as former ministers did, a review once in a while to see what is the situation of a crown company. This review is going on at the present time and the results will be submitted to the government shortly.
I have no views as far as the future of Polymer is concerned. The company has been very successful; it is under very good management; the sales of rubber this year have been very good. Even during the difficult time of the strike last year the customers in Europe remained with Polymer after having been deprived of their rubber for some time. But the government will look into the future development and the capital expenditures and any other questions that might pertain to Polymer.
Mr. Chairman, I take it from the minister's answer that the government has not yet decided whether Polymer is to be sold?
No.

I will not, therefore,
elaborate on that phase of the matter other than to say I am somewhat surprised to hear the minister say he has no views on the matter. I would hope that as the responsible minister he would have a great many views on the matter. I might think they were wrong, or I might not agree with him, but I still hope he will not persist in having no views on the matter but that he will acquire some and assert them to his colleagues successfully.
In any event, the point I want to make is that if Polymer is to be sold I hope the government will bear in mind the fact that this
Supply-Defence Production country is facing a problem of balance of payments that is quite severe. The adverse balance of payments last year, as the minister will well know, was of the order of some $1,400 million. Polymer Corporation has been a good earner of money; it has a very good record as a crown company, and I would hope that in any sale the minister and the government would make sure that it is not sold in such a way that the earnings of the company are drained off to another country and our balance of payments situation is further worsened by the sale of this company.
There is perhaps no purpose in elaborating a view on it unduly at this stage. I did want to draw that to the attention of the government because I think it is a matter of major importance, and because I hope that in any decision they take, if they decide to sell it, the company will be sold only to interests whereby the earnings of the company will be retained in Canada for the development of Canada. The history of the company so far has been outstanding; it is a very good story. I hope that in the years that lie ahead it will continue to be a very good Canadian story.
I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa West. Mr. Chairman, my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce will move an amendment to item 72.

The minister mentioned production sharing. Can he say whether Canadian Arsenals have obtained any production sharing contracts to date?

speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member for Laurier would allow me to make a statement.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I was going to ask His Honour if he intended to make a statement at this stage. Perhaps the chairman would recognize me afterwards.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Thank you. I feel very strange in this position, and I hope that the chairman will not declare me out of order immediately.
We find it strange to see you there.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to say only one thing as we commence consideration of the legislation estimates, and that is to express the appreciation which I feel, and which I am sure all hon. members feel, for the staff of the House of Commons which suffers with us through these rather arduous days when we are trying to complete the work of the session. It puts no small strain upon all the officers of the house and particularly upon those who must be with us throughout the entire hours of our sittings. I do not want to mention names, but I include in my remarks the Clerk, who is responsible generally for the administration of the House of Commons staff, his assistants, the reporting staff and all the other employees of the House of Commons who serve us so well. They look forward, of course, to the compensating benefits that come from service with the House of Commons, which are real and, if they are not too long deferred, do help to compensate for the extra hours which service of this chamber calls for.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think all of us will realize that it has been the custom and tradition over a long period of time not to consider the estimates of Mr. Speaker as contentious in any way, and certainly it is not my desire to so consider them at this time. There are, however, a few brief remarks I should like to make on behalf of those who sit on this side of the house.
First of all I wish to extend to His Honour the Speaker our thanks and our gratitude for the consideration he has given to the many representations we on this side of the house have made with respect to secretarial assistance. I should also like to let him know that even if His Honour has not always been able to meet all our requests and demands they were always received with such courtesy and such sympathetic consideration

that we could not in any way feel otherwise than grateful to him for the manner in which these representations were received.
Before I go farther I should like to join with Mr. Speaker in the tribute he has paid to his officers, the officers of the House of Commons, the staff and all who are associated with our work in parliament not only during the whole of the session but more particularly toward the end. I join with him in the laudatory words he has expressed with respect to them. We know that their task is a difficult one, particularly at this stage of the session, and I personally should like to add to the list of those mentioned the bureau of translation. The translators, as Mr. Speaker knows, comprise a new group which has become a part of the staff arising out of the simultaneous translation system. Frankly, it is amazing to many of us how well and efficiently they perform their tasks.
Your Honour will remember that last year when there was a discussion of the matters that I should now like to take up, namely assistance, secretarial and otherwise, which members of parliament as a whole have, Your Honour replied that he had asked the civil service commission to prepare a report, and that they had reported at the time. Your Honour at that time put on record a paragraph from that report which I should like to quote because it is by way of preface, I assure you, to the brief remarks I intend to make. This paragraph will be found on page 6336 of Hansard for July 18, 1959:
It is dated June, 1959, and I am reading from the summary of conclusions on page 37, as follows:
"That the plan to provide supervised, small groups of stenographers in offices located close to the members served, and restricted to individual political parties, would be the most effective secretarial system for the House of Commons, and that such a service should include provision for telephone answering, dictation equipment and allied services."
This, of course, is an extremely important conclusion which was arrived at as a result of the survey. I was wondering whether it was not possible for Your Honour, before we dispose of the item, to give a further report on that matter. I am sure it is the wish, not only of Mr. Speaker but of all of us, that some day there will be a secretary assigned to each member of parliament, together with the additional assistance which is referred to in the report.
There is also the question of the secretaries who are without work during the period when the house is not in session. I did bring this matter to Your Honour's attention toward the close of the session last year. While it was not possible for Your Honour to meet all our requests, I again say that they were met with fairness and, I am
Supply-Legislation
happy to state, on the whole there was not too much hardship, although there was some during the intersessional period.
I said earlier we were happy about the arrangements which were made for the secretarial assistance during the period after the session had prorogued. However, there are still a number of young ladies and others, whose names of course I cannot assign to the record, who have had in one case 10 years service, in another case 10 years service, in a third case nine years service, in the fourth case eight years service, and in the last case three years service, and I am sure Your Honour agrees with me that those secretaries who have had years of experience and who have attained an age-I say this with deference-where it is not always easy during the intersessional period to find employment, should be given special consideration. I wonder whether Your Honour would not take the request which I make now in the spirit in which it is made.
Then there is the very important question, which I know is in Your Honour's mind, not only of secretarial assistance but of technical and research assistance as well. I need hardly remind the committee that when the house met in 1957, under the present administration, the Prime Minister had it in mind then to give some additional assistance to those of us who sit on this side of the house. He had that in mind in the light of the difficulties, the plight, and the extra work which the Prime Minister and his associates had when they sat on this side of the house.
Well, as you know, Mr. Speaker, it has not been found possible to grant this additional technical assistance. I wonder whether it is not a matter to be considered by either Mr. Speaker himself or by the commissioners of internal economy. My friend the hon. member for Ottawa West says, while it is known as the committee for internal economy, it is eternal economy which they practise. I am not going to comment on that interjection, other than to say that I know that particular committee of the house have given to this subject, and to many others, very careful consideration.
I know, too, what the views of Mr. Speaker are with reference to additional rooms for members, and I at once commend him and those who are responsible with him for the establishment of these additional rooms. I do hope the day is not far away when it will be possible to assign to each member a room, with his own secretarial assistance. I know that must be in the mind of His Honour the Speaker and those who sit on the committee that is responsible for the decisions taken with reference to the proceedings of the house.

Supply-Legislation
I have no more to say, sir, other than to ask you once again to give consideration to those several cases that have already been brought to your attention, and with which I am sure you will once again deal fairly.

I should like to join with the previous speaker in utilizing this opportunity to thank the Speaker for the co-operation he has always extended to us in connection with any problems we have taken up with him. We fully realize that he has not been able to accomplish all he himself desires, but we do hope he may be able to give us this afternoon some intimation as to still greater progress that he has in mind. I am not going to repeat what has already been said by the previous speaker, but will just add my words to his hope that in the not too distant future provision is going to be made for greater secretarial and research help.
I should like to add just a new thought on the subject of secretarial help. I should like to inquire why it is not possible for the secretaries, who sometimes have to work overtime because of the responsibilities of their members, either to get paid for the overtime or allowed time off for it. I think it is rather unfair that secretaries have to be placed in the position where they either do the overtime work on a voluntary basis or the member must pay out of his own pocket. I do hope something can be arranged in that connection.
While we are mentioning the staff, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I hope Your Honour can give us some information as to whether action is going to be taken on a matter that has been raised every year for a number of years. I refer to the supplying of new and adequate accommodation for the security staff. I know Your Honour has gone into the matter several times, but the accommodation provided is a disgrace to this house as employers of the security staff. This one room has to accommodate, I think it is, 52 men. They have to change their clothes there, spend their time off there and keep their clothes there. It is where they eat. The time is long past due for them to have received adequate accommodation. I hope that with the changes the Speaker is making now, he can inform us that there will be something better for those men in the near future. I am not going to say anything more at the present time, Mr. Chairman, because I can say the other things I have in mind under the various items.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps I should say what I can briefly on the subject which has been raised so considerately by the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Vancouver East.

The report to which the hon. member referred and which we discussed at this time last year was circulated in due course and was put in the hands of all hon. members, as was agreed at that time. Its relevance or the possibility of its implementation I think improves considerably now with the prospect we have for more accommodation for hon. members. Some have already been accommodated in the west block. I think it is no secret that plans are going forward which will, I hope, within the term of this parliament or in any event before long give us the objective which certainly has been mine and which I know has been that of many hon. members, namely one office for each member and the facilities which will permit each member to have one stenographer. To my mind that is a minimum service for members of this house and it has been my objective since I have put it forward and which I intend to continue to put forward in the expectation that we are nearing the point now where we can achieve that objective.
As to the stenographic staff of the house -I refer to the temporary staff or the sessional staff-it is true, as the hon. member says, it perhaps does not get compensation for the extra hours which many of them put in voluntarily and quite agreeably. I know there is no compensation for that. Those who are continuous, of course-and this consideration applies to all staffs of the house-receive holidays with pay beyond those which are the rule in the civil service and they have the advantage of shorter hours in the recess period.
But the point which was made by the hon. member for Laurier about those who have over the years given good service to this house as stenographers is one which gives me a great deal of concern and has done so as the problem arises each session. There are two considerations that must be taken into account. First, there is the service of the members during the recess and that is a basic consideration. The personnel who are selected by the whips of the parties to fill the recess quotas are selected on the basis of their usefulness to thef members whom they will be serving and, as all hon. members will agree, that is a prior consideration. The other factor is the circumstances of the stenographers themselves-and seniority is one of those important circumstances as well as the personal considerations which apply in certain cases-* which make it important that continuous work should be available.
As I have done in the past, I shall do everything I can to meet to the fullest degree the problem of those who have claims on the basis of seniority but are not required on

the other basis which I have mentioned. A problem is created not only for the whips but for the Speaker and the Clerk in making the choice which has to be made to keep within the limit of the vote. Hon. members will note that the vote provided for only 38 stenographers, 33 actually in the category of continuous temporaries and five who are in the permanent category and therefore have status which is not subject to termination. That is a total of 38 and the division of those among the parties is one which is made by arrangement and the choice is necessarily limited by the amount of the vote. Each session we have gone beyond the authorized amount with the concurrence of the commissioners of internal economy in order to meet the kind of problem mentioned by the hon. member for Laurier. I only regret that we cannot meet all the problems and that is due to the fact that the introduction of new staff is from time to time made on all sides of the house in order to meet the problem of the special service that is required during the recess.
The other matter mentioned by the hon. member for Laurier is a larger one and I think I shall not attempt to discuss it, namely that of technical assistance for the opposition parties. The staff which is available for the Leader of the Opposition I believe compares favourably with that available in any period in the past and it is perhaps larger now than it was previously. I have not made an exact comparison but I realize that a problem exists. However, I feel it is a matter which is really beyond my jurisdiction or scope.
I have mentioned the expectation of better accommodation for the members and that consideration also applies to all of the staff. The renovation and reconstruction of the accommodation in the west block will give us an opportunity to deal with such problems as the accommodation of security staff mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I am sure that with those changes we shall meet some of the things that we have been unable to do in this building because of the severe limitations that exist here on our space. I think I have dealt with all of the matters that have been raised.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask this question of His Honour, Mr. Chairman? His Honour said that the vote provides for 38 stenographers only, 35 of a permanent nature and three of a non-permanent nature, I believe. I think he said that was an improvement on last year.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
No. We went beyond the vote last year and the year before. Actually we began the recess with 44 or 45 last year in order to meet some of the problems to which the hon. member referred. But the vote has
Supply-Legislation
been for 38 in total for some years. This is larger actually than it was in the time of my predecessor although prior to that time there was a period when the sessional staff was larger. I think it was because of the fact that it included secretaries who served the parliamentary assistants of that time. But the estimates which are now coming before parliament for stenographers is not what had been asked for. The number is not as large as I had put forward. I asked for more. As a matter of fact, I asked for one stenographer for each member but in the circumstances it was not felt possible to accede to that vote. I also attempted to rearrange the recess staff so that the more or less permanent secretaries would be separate from the recess staff proper for service of private members which could be looked at as one unit and considered as such.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I thank the Speaker for his explanation but I had not completed saying what I had in mind. What I had in mind was this. While I was under the impression that there had been more, apparently it was an erroneous impression. As His Honour knows there are in the list of persons who are going to be without employment quite a number who will be in difficult circumstances through the non-sessional period notwithstanding their priority and their years of service.
What I am coming to is this. I was going to ask His Honour whether it was not possible to increase this vote. I realize that that is what happened last year and perhaps this year the expenditure will go beyond the vote, which is all to the good. Of course, I am not inviting by the statement I make a reply to the effect that perhaps we did less when we were over there; but the point now is that there is a realization that we should be doing perhaps a bit more. I wonder if before the vote which will be coming forward next session it would not be possible to find sufficient funds to look after those secretaries who, because of their years of service, eight, nine or ten years of service, will find themselves in some hardship.
I remember one case which I brought to Your Honour's attention last year where there was real hardship and Your Honour fortunately was able to do something in that case. Again the matter repeats itself this year. It is impossible to put names on the record but Your Honour knows who they are, and I again simply bring them to his attention in the hope that it will be possible to go beyond the vote sufficiently to look after the requirements of those who will find themselves in these difficult circumstances.
