Mr. Chairman, I just wanted to draw to the attention of Mr. Speaker a couple of items of interest to me on the administrative aspect.
My first point is that I am wondering if Mr. Speaker could give consideration-and I am not too sure whether this comes under his jurisdiction-to having a loose leaf edition of Beauchesne where it would be possible to add at the appropriate place the frequent rulings which are made? From my own brief experience in the house I notice that one of the basic difficulties is that the majority of members do not seem to know what the rules are or what the previous rulings have been, and I thought it might be of some assistance to the house if we had an up to date loose leaf edition. Because even with a book such as Beauchesne it is extremely difficult to find the correct citation very quickly. Since it was published in 1958 there have been quite a number of decisions which Mr. Speaker has made which I think would be of considerable value to the house if they were available by this loose leaf method.
The other suggestion which I have made previously is that I would be interested in seeing an electronic roll call machine installed at the earliest opportunity to speed up the processes of the house. I realize that perhaps this discussion would have been more appropriate before the special committee on rules, but since their hearings are in camera I thought perhaps I would be permitted to put my suggestion forward at this time.

I have a grievance I would like to raise at this time. I am not too sure if I am on the right item of the estimates, but it has to do with the condition of the typewriters supplied to members. I share an office with my colleague from Northum-berland-Miramichi and we have been complaining at least ten or twelve times since the opening of the session that our machine is only good to be thrown on the scrap pile. We have not been able to get any results and I hope that before next session we will be supplied with a decent typewriter which we can use if we need it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps I might reply to those comments now.
The idea of a loose leaf edition is interesting. With changes in the rules revision would be necessary. I can say this much, with all respect to the late and learned author of Beauchesne, that I myself have found difficulty with the index and have in course of preparation an index which could be supplied to all members and which I think would be helpful in finding much good material which is there.

The typewriter question has been solved and all hon. members will have new typewriters at the beginning of next session. And I may say, at every session thereafter.

Mr. Chairman, I wanted to bring something to the attention of Mr. Speaker and the committee that we have had general comment on at various times and some views expressed. It concerns the problem of the development of more research help for members of parliament, and particularly for members of the opposition. I should raise this point just in connection with the office of the Leader of the Opposition, because I know the Leader of the Opposition is hardly in a position to raise it himself and perhaps members of his party feel the same way. But I do know that the more assistance one has, whether in a formal or informal way by people with certain expert knowledge, the better is the performance possible, not only in a party sense but in an individual sense.
Mr. Chairman, I have sat in some amusement, as I am sure other members have, and have watched the little corps of assistants in the Leader of the Opposition's gallery grow in the past two years and I know they now have a small corps of people. I do not know whether some of them are covered under this particular vote, but I do know that others are being paid through other arrangements.
I would like to suggest at this time that we make greater provision for assistance of officers such as the Leader of the Opposition. It seems to me that the opposition is undermanned in relation to the expertise which is available to cabinet ministers, and the essence of our parliamentary system is that of the opposition against the minister rather than the opposition being against the ordinary members on the government side.
So far as ordinary members on the government side are concerned, I think they are to a degree in the same position as members in the opposition. I know, whether the general public knows or not, that they have no greater access to governmental expertise than we have. Or if they have it is in a limited way. I feel that both the official opposition and also the average member of parliament are short of the kind of research assistance which we need.
I would not like to try to mark off any suggestions as to how this could be done. Two years ago I said that I felt the library of parliament as a reference service was completely inadequate, especially compared with what is available in other countries. The British handle this somewhat differently than the United States. The British library is no more effective than ours in terms of

resources, but the party organizations in Great Britain are much more so. Our parties have not got that tradition. But from what I can see they show very few indications that they will ever get to it. In the United States system each congressman as a congressman and each senator as a senator is given much greater provision in order to do the job as an individual representing his constituency, his region and his nation.
It seems to me that they are the two areas in which this committee should consider providing more extra knowledge and assistance in order that members can do a good job. First of all, help should be given to the offices or position of the official opposition, if you want to put it that way; second, there should be some means of helping the general membership, the ordinary membership of the House of Commons whatever the party.
It may be a poor thing to say, but what I have seen of the general framework of the library, or the committee of the house dealing with the library, has not given me much hope of our getting help from that direction, and if I may make the point bluntly as to why, it is because there is an influence on that committee by the other place, which is so traditional and, I may say, out of date, that we are not going to get from any such group a modern and up-to-date way of looking at this problem.
I think the research facilities and the assistance available to members of this house in the light of what the cabinet ministers have is very slight and I have a great deal of sympathy for every member of this house in his task of looking after his constituency responsibilities and the larger and more national one in the light of the resources he has. It is just pitiful when you think of us as having one full-time secretary with so very limited time available during which the ordinary member tries to do the best job he can. There comes a stage when diminishing returns reach such a point that he can scarcely do his task. This is much more pronounced with what is happening in this parliament with more committees meeting, and the onus of attendance in this house. If you do your duty in attending even, say, half the committees and attend the proceedings in the house for half the time, at least, you have no time to keep up with correspondence or to see that letters are framed to go after research that needs to be done not only in connection with the responsibilities of this house but also with regard to questions raised by constituents.
I think we are a living example of a cultural lag. We are in the mid-twentieth century and we are still acting in the House of Commons with regard to ourselves as if we were
Supply-Legislation
living in the mid-nineteenth century. One of the reasons we have this cultural lag is because the House of Commons tends to be dominated-this has nothing to do with party -by a relatively small number of people and I should like the small number of people who do dominate the house, whether they are cabinet ministers or stars of the opposition, to stop and look at the situation. Members of the Canadian parliament come from a tremendously disparate background. In the main you do not have the kind of person focussing into it as in some other parliaments. Congressmen and senators in the United States are much more educated to a full time political career. It is much more a matter of choice than it is in Canada. Similarly, in Britain there is a common educational background, and aspiration that we do not have in this country. This, to me, not only explains our cultural lag and our unwillingness to live in the mid-twentieth century in legislative terms but it underlines the extra difficulties that we have.
I have said before I have no wisdom in making great suggestions but I do feel that if the parliament of Canada is really going to adjust and be the forum which I and most other members think it should be, we are going to have to do something in this particular area and it is more than a question of just better typing facilities or better copying facilities or getting a few extra books from the Library or putting a few extra librarians on. It seems to me we need a new approach, and I think that approach should be made by a committee of this house with no association with the other place to study this whole question. I should like to see senior people and some junior people from all the parties get into some kind of group and go and see how other parts of the world are doing things.
I know it is not popular to go around complaining that an institution is senile, though I hold this view strongly. This is not a commentary on the government, but I think it is senile. I would judge from talking to a number of other hon. members that this is not a strange or odd view. I remember one businessman told me not long ago that we are not worth a heck of a lot as politicians as far as he was concerned if business was run the way parliament is run, business would go broke in a hurry. I do not buy that criticism completely but I certainly know that in the way we individually as members are geared to face the problems of the nation we should be going broke, as I believe we are.
I welcome this opportunity to express this point of view and I hope that the Speaker,

who is primarily concerned with the situation, will at least give it some attention and consideration. Any small improvements that he can make-and I can definitely say he has made them and this is very much appreciated by every member-are all to the good, but I do think there is a latent crisis here which needs to be met by much greater action than this, and one of the things that must be the goal or end in sight is raising and elevating the position and prestige of the individual member of parliament whatever his party and giving him some status, some real authority in the role he could play, a role I do not think he can play at the present time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is much which has been said by the hon. member for Port Arthur with which I agree, as I indicated earlier in my reference to additional technical assistance and research help. His Honour did, however, reply that this was a matter outside his jurisdiction.
The hon. member for Port Arthur now presents this matter in another light and it may be it can be considered in that context. However, I rise to say to the hon. member that he is wrong in his assumption with reference to the Leader of the Opposition. While it is true that in the gallery which is used by those who assist the Leader of the Opposition there are more people who have joined it of late-within the last year -I should like to reassure him and tell him, so that he will know what the position is, that these are people who are assigned to those of us other than the Leader of the Opposition who sit on this side of the house, and that they are paid exclusively by members of the official opposition themselves and their salaries do not form a part of this vote or of any other vote that has to do with the Leader of the Opposition. I am sure the hon. member was not aware of that.

I was aware of that, but I did not feel I was the one who should be bringing it out. But I did not want to leave the inference that these people were all paid under this vote. I believe I know the people who are paid under the vote and those who are not. It is all to the good. I would like to see a larger corps up there because the greater the number the better the government, in a sense.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Anyway there is no difference of opinion on this matter between what I have said and what the hon. member has added. It certainly was not clear from what the hon. member said. Although he may have been advised what the position was, the hon. member may have left an

impression that the Leader of the Opposition was adding and adding to his staff. Such is not the case. There are three additional members who have been added during the last 12 months or, perhaps, two sessions, whose services are being paid for exclusively by those of us who sit on this side of the house.

I wish to make a few brief remarks on this interesting item, an item which could be the cause of considerable debate, if we had plenty of time and opportunity. I fully appreciate the feelings of the hon. member for Port Arthur with regard to the situation in which members of parliament find themselves, although I do not take quite such a dim view with regard to the senility of this institution. I take an interest in this subject and I have been reading the proceedings of the committees which have been set up by the United Kingdom parliament to study procedure.
I find that this institution was becoming senile in Great Britain in 1860; frequent references were made to the disabilities that the institution suffers from and predictions were made as to how long it would function, and so on. But we must remember that parliament is an evolving institution which has to change its practices and its procedures to meet the changing circumstances in the country which are reflected in the work of the house. I remember reading some minutes of committees on procedure in which Mr. Campbell Bannerman expressed his views, and Mr. Asquith, later Lord Oxford, gave his views; Mr. Baldwin gave his views, and prominent members of the labour party gave their views. Mr. Chamberlain gave his views; Mr. Churchill gave his views, and Mr. Attlee and Mr. Bevin gave their views. All through the years of British history we find this recurrent concern over the efficient functioning of parliament, and rightly so, because from time to time changes have to be made to meet the circumstances under which parliament is functioning.
The criticism that we in this group have primarily is of those who refuse to make the changes which are required for parliament to operate efficiently under circumstances that change almost from day to day. As a matter of fact, in reading the history of the debates and of the committees in the British house particularly, one for which I have a particular affection-I think one rather finds inspiration than disappointment. One realizes that 50 years, 60 years, 75 years or 100 years ago parliament suffered the same concern and the same type of problem that we suffer from today, facing rapidly changing conditions. But the main point is this: with all the impact upon parliament because of the

entirely changed society today from that which existed when parliamentary institutions were first established as far as British countries are concerned, parliament is stronger than ever, and that is the test. That is all I wish to say with respect to general remarks on the parliamentary situation.
I do wish to say a word or two, while I have the opportunity, about the staff, because the staff functions here day after day, week after week and month after month, with possibly a good many people failing to realize that this whole process would come to a halt without the co-operation of a considerable number of persons who perform their duties responsibly from day to day. I think of the protective staff and the work they undertake day by day in assisting in the efficient operation of our parliament; the elevator staff, the public works staff around the building generally; the messengers, some of them quite on in years, whose duties on occasion take them many blocks around the city of Ottawa, meeting the requirements of members and so on; the page boys and the staff in general.
I also wish to make a reference to the Hansard staff who work under a particular strain during these lengthened hours. Speaking of the Hansard reporters and of the ladies -I always refer to them as the Hansard angels-who are required to work long hours and stay a considerable time after the house adjourns in the evening, sometimes until after midnight and later, in order to make certain that they have all the quotations and things of that sort that certain members have used in making speeches, I do trust, Mr. Chairman, that the members of the staff I have referred to, including the secretaries and all who are connected with this house, receive the increases in salaries that they are entitled to in relation to the increases received by other sections of the government service.
Now, again with respect to the Hansard staff, the reporters and the ladies in question, I feel that when one works the hours they work and at the salaries they receive at the present time one must realize they are underpaid, greatly underpaid, and I do suggest there should be some arrangement made to compensate those faithful people in a financial way for the unduly long hours they have had to endure in recent weeks and for the valuable service they have rendered by making it possible for parliament to continue to function for such long hours. Just imagine if they all fell ill what a state of affairs we would be in in so far as the operation of this house is concerned.

In conclusion I come back to the theme that has been repeated over and over again by members of this group, and simply say that this state of affairs will not be remedied until we are willing to make changes to meet the changing circumstances of our lives and society today and so organize our sessions that we come here in January and continue until possibly the 15th of June, or the end of June, and then recess until the 1st of October and accept some planning. I see the hon. member for Greenwood shakes his head as though he were in disagreement with me; if so, I should like him to rise and give his reasons. I have given my views; I wish he would give his reasons and other hon. members would do the same who are opposed to a recess in the summer. We in this group believe it would make it possible for the staff and members of parliament to carry on more efficiently, and also it would represent some fair consideration for the members of the staff whose holidays with their children in many instances are completely upset at the present time by our unorganized and unplanned parliamentary habits.

Mr. Chairman the reason for my rising today is one of gratitude which I should like to express for the service I have received. In doing so, I refer to the page boys. Their service has been given with a smile. They are to be commended for their forbearance in being sent here, there and everywhere, for a drink of water when you want it, for your mail when you want it, and so on. This sense of gratitude has caused me some concern also for their education. I have been told that these children or young boys have in the main about three half days education during the week when we sit at eleven o'clock in the morning. I should like to ask the Speaker to consider whether it would not be possible in the future to see that these children are given the same advantages through a tutor or a professor as those who are fortunate enough to be able to attend public school. I think we would be rendering a service to these children that would be most beneficial. Since I am the father of children myself I realize fully the importance of education. Therefore, I do not hesitate at this time to make this appeal on behalf of those who have rendered, and always render, this service with a smile.

Very often in rising one says he had not intended to speak, and I do not suppose that in 1 per cent of the cases it is believed, but possibly I shall be believed at this time, and particularly by the hon. member who interpreted the movement of my head in a way to suit him. It is quite

Supply-Legislation
true that I have been strongly against the proposal for two sessions a year, and for one very simple reason. To me it is clear- indeed, I believe this is admitted by those who advocate it-that it really means that to all intents and purposes we become professionals. At any rate, I was discussing this proposal the other day with some people who advocate it and they agreed. I think that can be taken as true and I take it as true.
I simply wish to say that would cut at the very root of the idea of parliamentary government. My idea of parliament is that it should be composed of people who have achieved some position in the community-
I do not necessarily mean in a money way- people who have done some service of some kind in business or otherwise and who therefore have something to contribute when they come to this house. If members of parliament become sheer professionals I believe we will lose a lot and parliament will be composed more and more of people who come here to make a living.
As another enthusiastic amateur like the hon. member for Greenwood, I should like to echo and endorse what he has just said.
May I say it is worth while to have spoken when my words are greeted with such an endorsement.

To reply briefly to the hon. gentleman, with whom I am often in such complete agreement on matters of principles related to parliament, I cannot understand why a person becomes a professional if eight months or seven months are divided in two and part of the session is held before a holiday and part after. I cannot quite see the logic of his argument.

Mr. Chairman, one of our
respected members, the hon. member for Mackenzie River, has suffered serious damage to his health. I am very sorry that this is so. He is a personal friend of mine but he is also a valuable member of the house and I think part of his trouble is related to the inadequate expense allowance for those in outlying constituencies. He is not a member of our party, as hon. members know, but I know him personally. He has given of his time and of his health to the north country in no uncertain fashion. He knows his constituency because at great expense to himself and danger to his health he travels widely throughout the constituency. He could not possibly pay his way on $2,000 a year.
I think it is high time we reviewed the whole subject, particularly so far as our

undeveloped areas are concerned. His railroad pass is absolutely useless to him. There are no railways in his district. We are going to improve that situation somewhat in the near future, but I know personally that at the present time he is unable to meet the expenses involved.
The hon. member's remarks about the mounted police were very timely. I have a letter in my pocket from an ex-commissioner of the mounted police commending the hon. member for Mackenzie River for his very comprehensive remarks in this regard. The long sessions we are having exaggerate the situation. The result is that he only has a very short period, September and October, when he can travel throughout his constituency. He has to fly wherever he goes, and anyone who hires an aircraft for personal reasons in the north country knows that the hon. member could not make more than one short trip down the Mackenzie for $2,000.
I cannot ignore this opportunity to bring before those responsible the urgent necessity of looking into this matter. It affects others besides the hon. member for Mackenzie River, of course, but I have used him as an example because in my opinion he has suffered physical damage in the service of his country. I should like to see serious consideration given to reviewing expenses in general and the expenses of the hon. member for Mackenzie River in particular.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make some detailed references covering a number of votes and perhaps I should do so at this time. I have never been able to understand why the highest officer of parliament, Mr. Speaker, should receive an allowance less than that of even the smallest cabinet minister. When I say "smallest" cabinet minister I mean one who is in charge of a not very onerous department of government. If we had greater respect for parliament I believe we would ensure that the highest officer of parliament received remuneration or compensation, call it what you like, more in line with the dignity of his office.
I should also like to refer to the plea I made a number of years ago on behalf of the deputy chairman of committees. I believe we are doing a wrong to him because in effect the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker and the deputy chairman of committees have year round employment. When the House of Commons is not sitting they are actively engaged in preparation for the next session of parliament involving research work and many other responsibilities of their offices. To pay the deputy chairman of committees only an additional $2,000 a year is in my opinion

most inadequate. I would not be adverse to increasing the remuneration of the Deputy Speaker, but I feel very keenly that the dignity of the office of Mr. Speaker demands that he receive at least as much as a cabinet minister and I believe we are doing a continuing injustice to the deputy chairman of committees.
In addition, I endorse most happily the views expressed by my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West. Over the years, both in the former parliament and in this one, I have been one of the harshest critics of government policy. However, I believe that I take second place to no one in my love for the institution of parliament. I believe it will be a sad day for us when we permit our institution of government to be governed by the experts. In one large area of the world there is a government where in effect the experts or scientists rule the nation. In Hitler's time we had another nation ruled by so-called scientists and experts.
The House of Commons is the place of the people. This is the place where the people speak. After having known many members of parliament it is my belief that they are as good or as bad as most Canadians, and on the whole it is my conviction they are on a higher level than the average Canadian elector. If there is something radically wrong with the institution of parliament or the members who compose parliament, it is my opinion there is something radically wrong with the Canadian electorate because I am convinced that we in this chamber are no more and no less than the people of Canada as a whole.
I do not like politicians and newspapermen making reputations for themselves by attacking fundamentally and basically one of the most sacred human institutions we have. I readily admit that changes and reforms are necessary. We do have a committee to consider our procedure and I am sure that such a committee should continue to work continuously in order to ensure that parliament adequately represents the people, not the government. Parliament was never intended to represent the government, it was intended to allow the people's voice to be heard in the presence of the government. We, I believe, must be continuously on the alert for ways and means for making it a more effective institution of the people. I do not like the inference that those who may be elected to this house do not deserve to be here. I have a tremendous respect for the right of the people to send here whoever they please.

I should like to interject briefly in this debate to comment on the
Supply-Legislation
action taken by Mr. Speaker during the past session as a result of recommendations made at this time last year, and I am sure in years before, particularly with regard to the appointment of extra guides to conduct people around the building and in extending the visiting hours. I have a few suggestions to make, one of which will save some money and the other of which might cost a little money, but I believe both would accomplish something.
First, I should like to refer to the documents that are placed at the seats of members of parliament. I notice behind me I have two French speaking members, and there is hardly room for them to get into their seats because of the pile of documents. Most other desks, at this stage of the session, are fairly full of bulky documents. My seatmate and I decided this year to experiment by eliminating one set of documents. I do not know if we have any other advantages over other members in the house, but at least we have a great deal more leg room and I suspect a more tidy desk. As I say, if all other sets of double desks were furnished with one set of commons bills, Hansard, Senate reports, and so on, I think that would be one way of saving a bit of money.
The other suggestion concerns what goes on in this chamber and in the building after the house prorogues. I have voiced this suggestion to Mr. Speaker earlier this year, but I should like to repeat it publicly now. It concerns something in addition to the information provided by the guides on the workings of the House of Commons. I believe the Speaker of the House of Commons has a copy of the film entitled "The Sceptre and the Mace", which deals with the opening of parliament and contains educational information on how we go about accomplishing things in the House of Commons and the Senate. It is my suggestion that when the house is in recess this film "The Sceptre and the Mace" might be shown at frequent intervals during the day, possibly in the railway committee room or some other appropriate place in the building, so that visitors and tourists, particularly Canadians who are visiting Ottawa in increasing numbers every summer, can get a vivid and clear picture of the working of parliament, even though parliament may not be in session.
Another suggestion which I should like to make at this point is related to a practice followed in Great Britain. I think there might be some fairly obvious point in the main lobby of the building at which some visual indication could be given of what is going on in the house, just what part of the proceedings we are dealing with, and so

Supply-Legislation
on. I do not know whether we would go as far as I am told they do in the United Kingdom, that is to indicate who is speaking at any particular time. However, this would provide some visual indication to the casual or serious visitor to this building concerning what is happening in the house.
I should like to agree with the suggestions that have been made here today, and at other times, concerning the desirability of providing an adequate allowance so that the first commoner could adequately represent us without going broke in the process. It seems to me there has been hardly a week go by when I have been on my way into the chamber that I have not observed our first commoner entertaining visitors on our behalf. I think it is important that he should be given an adequate allowance to cover these fundamental and necessary expenses.
I should like to offer another suggestion which concerns the position in order of precedence which our Speaker occupies. I am given to understand that we are almost unique in that we place our Speaker somewhat farther down the ladder than is the practice in many other legislatures within and without the commonwealth. I feel this is something that might be re-examined, and I would be very much in favour of placing our first commoner as high in the social spectrum as it is possible for him to be.

I had intended to defer my remarks until we reached item 183. However, in view of the fact that I am going to ask for some information perhaps it would be more convenient if I put the question now, thus affording His Honour a little more time to answer it when we reach that particular item. Before I go further, I should like to associate myself with those who have paid tribute to the fine work and the devoted efforts of our staff in this House of Commons. I am sure we all appreciate very much the services that they are giving to us. I quite agree with the hon. member for Kootenay West that, in view of the long hours they are putting in, they are very much underpaid. I agree also with the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that the salary of Mr. Speaker himself is quite inadequate. I have been searching through the estimates to find under what item His Honour gets an allowance for entertainment. I have an impression that in view of present-day costs, that item, too, must be quite insufficient.
The hon. member for Athabasca referred to certain members whose expense allowance did not meet their costs incurred in travelling around their ridings and, therefore,

they had to pay those costs out of their indemnity. I am sure that we would not want Mr. Speaker to be placed in that same position where he would have to finance the expenses incurred by entertaining so many important delegations who are calling here, and who should be entertained on behalf of us all.
The question I wanted to put to His Honour has to do with the salaries of the staffs. The question was touched upon by the hon. member for Kootenay West when he referred to the recent increases in civil service salaries. I should like to know how many of the staff have already received the benefit of that recent increase, and whether the total estimate under item 183 has made provision for the increase.

Mr. Chairman, for two sessions now we have had in this house the experience of simultaneous interpretation, and I think everyone has found it satisfactory. The system has been of great value and has enabled many members to understand speeches made in the other official language.
However, Mr. Chairman, the sessional work is not done exclusively in the House of Commons. I would therefore suggest that the simultaneous interpretation system be extended to the committees, that is to say in two or three rooms where the main committees of the house hold their meetings.
It was said at one point that French speaking members from the province of Quebec did not take an active part in the work of the committees. I do not agree with that statement, but I would say that, even if it were true, there might be a reason for it. When a member who is called upon to put his views before a committee and does as responsible a job as he can only to realize that his audience does not understand him, and that quite often even the chairman of the committee does not understand, it is an unpleasant experience; indeed, it is a bit discouraging for one who has taken the trouble to study a particular subject.
I think if that system were established in a few committee rooms, or perhaps on a trial basis in one of the committee rooms every hon. member would be in a position to make a more efficient contribution to the work which is being done in the committees.

Mr. Chairman, I want to support the suggestion made by the hon. member who just resumed his seat, that the simultaneous interpretation system be extended to the discussions of some of the committees of the house. I have often noticed that French speaking members did not take part in

committee debates just because of the absence of a simultaneous interpretation system. Moreover, as a rule, the chairman of the committee is English speaking and does not understand French. It therefore becomes almost impossible for hon. members from the province of Quebec to take part in committee discussions. That is probably one of the reasons for the absence of French speaking members on some committees because, if they use French, they are not understood. If, on the other hand, they attempt to use English, they often risk expressing their ideas in a form which does not exactly represent what they have in mind.
I also wanted to associate myself with those who complained about the altogether too low salary being paid the Speaker of the house. The Speaker's task is a very difficult one; he has to be present in the house and I would say that it is, in fact, he who directs parliament. In my view, his salary should at least be equal to a minister's.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have found too that there is a certain inequality in the salaries paid to some of the staff.
For instance, I note that in the parliamentary library, the French assistant librarian is paid only $7,500 a year, whereas the salary of the English speaking assistant librarian is $8,580.
On the other hand, I notice that the salary of the editor of the English section of the Debates is $9,060, whereas the editor of the French section gets $8,580.
In the Journals division, I see that the head of the English section gets $9,060 a year, whereas the chief of the French section receives $8,220 only. Moreover, in the same division, the salary of the assistant chief of the English section is $7,500, and that of the assistant chief of the French section is paid only $6,660.
I cannot admit such a difference between the salaries of English speaking and French speaking members of the House of Commons staff.
Mr. Chairman, during three and a half days we dealt with human rights and the elimination of all discrimination with regard to language, religion or race. Yet, there seems to be some discrimination in the House of Commons, as the salaries are not the same for identical work, because, after all, it is probably more difficult for French speaking employees to accomplish the work required of them.
I am therefore of the opinion that it is time that such a situation be corrected.

I shall be brief, Mr. Chairman. I want to make two points only. The first is with reference to the speech made by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet. I would suggest to Mr. Speaker for his consideration that the simultaneous translation system, if it is extended, should first be extended to the seats in this particular chamber for the audience. I give this fact to the house merely by way of illustration. Any time when debate is in English, they might look around the chamber and note how many of the French speaking deputies now need to use the simultaneous translation here in order to understand the words in English. The plain fact is that all our confreres from Quebec are adept, as they always have been, to quickly pick up the use of the English language. I suggest that priority should be first for the spectators in the galleries before extension of the translation system to other parts of the house and then to one or two committee rooms, perhaps as a start.
The other reference I should like to make comes from a remark made by the hon. member for Port Arthur, in dealing with what he called the cultural lag in the institution of parliament. I think that his argument and particularly an article he wrote for a national magazine have been rather effectively met by his confrere, namely the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. But if that be not the case, I certainly want to challenge the remarks of the hon. member for Port Arthur with regard to parliament being in a cultural lag. This, of course, is a term or phrase that has popular usage among the social scientists. It indicates a feeling on the part of those who use this argument that parliament should be as bright and shiny as next year's model car with souped up horsepower, covered with chrome and completely geared for all the vicissitudes of life in the twentieth century.
My own attitude toward parliament is this. May I say that I have been here no longer than has the hon. member for Port Arthur and I certainly would not want to press my young and presumptuous views on the House of Commons. I think any good hard look at our system comes best from members like the hon. member for Greenwood, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate or others who have been here a great deal longer than we have. We are still junior leaguers.
However, my idea is that the people are quite content to have an institution that has about it a faint odour of moth balls, one that does not show signs of becoming a factory with modern and swift assembly lines and the use of automation. I think they prefer parliament to be perhaps a little bit slower than the fast pace of the twentieth century.

I should like to say something on this matter also. It seems to me that we have had probably two extremes and I am not in favour of either one. I think this parliament of ours does not function as well as it might function. I do not think it functions as well as most of the members think it can function. I think we are being silly to stand on tradition and say, "Let us not make a change because it is a change". I think we should consider those changes that are necessary and that all hon. members agree are necessary. This is one place in which there should be no government and no opposition. The members themselves should be free to agree on what changes will make this parliament much more efficient.
I have been satisfied with the operation of this particular department in the past year. We have received courteous consideration. But I should like to make a plea which I am sure Mr. Speaker would also like to make, namely a plea for more money to do the things that should be done particularly in relation to the staff. I am sure the public does not know that the staffs, having regard to their overtime, in the main are not getting paid at all for the work they have to do. That statement applies to the Hansard reporters, the Hansard staff and all the people concerned, not only those in front of the committee but those in the back rooms who never come to the attention of the public. These people are working till one and two o'clock in the morning in order to get the work done so that parliament will function. Their job does not call for them to work until one or two in the morning; they should be finished by 11 or 12. This is a hardship being imposed on them which we have not been able to do anything about because money has not been made available to take into consideration these things.
I should like to ask another question. In the Senate they have an internal economy committee. I did not know who composed it or what its function was because I was not involved and therefore can plead ignorance because it did not affect me personally. But in the Senate they have already made their fourteenth public report and it is reported in Hansard. They have gone into the changes which have been made with regard to the salaries of the people involved and with regard to some of the people who have been promoted. It would seem to me that they
fMr. MeCleave.l
should follow us, because after all we make the arrangements for the money which they spend and they have spent the money before we have spent it on our own people. 1 would like to see this internal economy committee report to the House of Commons in the same way as it reports to the other place.
In their report they state the class of employees concerned. They do not name the people by name but they state how much they get and this keeps them in a pretty open and well understood position so that members of the Senate if they wish, and they did wish in this case, can discuss specific classifications and receive information which is very difficult to receive in the House of Commons.
I think there should be closer liaison between the two internal economy committees so that members of one house do not receive increases before they do in the other and so that increases are kept on a fairly equal basis so that friction does not develop between the two groups of employees.
It would seem to me that some of the changes we could make would bring up to date the advances which are necessary for modern way of living. Many of the members themselves have bought photostat equipment, copying equipment, and some of us have reproduction machines of our own. It seems to me we should give some consideration to the recommendations made a year ago by the consultant from the civil service who recommended quite a number of changes, some of them not acceptable to the House of Commons but some of them very acceptable.
I am pleased to note that Mr. Speaker has given consideration to some of them and that new typewriters are forthcoming next session, because some of the typewriters which we have are museum pieces and I am sure the national museum would be happy to have them. Some of them could never be used economically in a business office because they just are not in good enough shape. The money spent on repairs must be greater than the money the machines originally cost. I would also think that we could put in a number of dictating machines. These are quite costly but they could be attached to a pool where they could be loaned out on a limited basis. They could be kept for only a limited time and one dictating machine would probably do quite a number of members and would be of valuable use, particularly at the end of the session.
I might say I do not need a secretary at this time of year because it is impossible to be in my office and attend committee meetings and the house. I cannot attend all the committee meetings I am supposed to and I

cannot be in the house the length of time I am supposed to, and certainly the place you neglect is your office and your correspondence.
It seems to me that this brings up the major problem with which we are faced. In the first part of the session you have lots of time to decide the things we are going to do during the session, the committees to which you would like to give consideration, time for research, and so on. Then when the session is part way through and the committees are set up you are no longer in a position to do that work because the committees are meeting at an accelerated pace and the house is meeting at the same time. Surely we are adult enough in this country for members to sit down and decide to make better use of our time and facilities.
I met a lawyer the other day and he said to me, "Why is it you people are so stupid? We in the legal profession do not work in the afternoons anymore, it is too hot and you cannot get any work done".
He must have been a C.C.F. lawyer.

No, he was not; he was one of the rankest capitalists I ever talked to. He is not a personal friend of mine but an acquaintance, but even he was of the opinion that this was certainly not an economical way to do business, that we should go home for the summer, come back in the fall and carry on with whatever business is required.
Mr. Chairman, I violently disagree with the argument being used that you have to be old and rich to be a member of parliament. If we have to depend on decaying members of society to run our country just because they have the means whereby they can afford to support themselves, then this will be a fine state of affairs. You will not find businesses which are going ahead and expanding and in competition with other businesses hiring old men who can afford to work for nothing. They hire young men and are willing to pay them, as they sure work them when they get them, and when they get to 40 or 50 years of age they shove them out, and perhaps they run for parliament. This does not seem to me to be a good way of doing things.
Mr. Chairman, I ask you to look around this House of Commons. You will find many young people here who have to buy homes in their own areas, because after all this is a temporary occupation. Nobody can say that he will be here tomorrow or a year from now. This is not the Senate. We have to go back to the people, and all sorts of factors have to be taken into consideration. It seems to me that there is a tendency for young people to take part in politics these days,
Supply-Legislation
which is a good thing; but we have to change our way of doing things. I think you will be surprised to find how many members have children who are even going to public school. If you compare this situation with 25 or even ten years ago, you will find that the number of young people has increased very greatly.
This means that we should as members of parliament sit down and decide what we are going to do about this matter of hours. There is no better place to do that than in a committee under the guidance of Mr. Speaker, who is impartial. I think we should all reach the conclusion that we would come back here and do the work before us as rapidly as possible and then, if it was not possible to complete it at the end of June, agree to come back in the fall to complete that work. Surely it would not be necessary to repeat everything we had said in the spring-
Oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
We could go on with the business in an orderly fashion. If there was an exchange of ideas between members of all parties I am sure we would find that an arrangement of this kind could be arrived at.
Another problem we face is the problem of offices. I am sure this is receiving consideration. A number of members have been asked to move into other accommodation and I would humbly submit that this is not a good idea. Those hon. members should be in the House of Commons close to the seat of business, which is this chamber, and the committee rooms. If anybody has to move-and I think somebody does-I suggest it should be some of the senators who have time and who have no pressure of business. If they have to move to the west block or to the east block or even further down town I shall be happy to make a contribution towards their expenses in travelling up here or going through the underground tunnel which, apparently, is to be constructed.
Another subject I should like to raise concerns radio facilities in the House of Commons. I had the privilege last year of attending the United Nations and I was very surprised and pleased with the facilities which have been installed there. There are four or five studios there and every morning these studios are being used by representatives of the various delegations. There are facilities for making live radio broadcasts or recorded radio broadcasts. These facilities are free and available to all delegates. I think this is something which we should consider. I am one of those members who use the Report from Parliament Hill which is a facility of the press. We are pleased with that. We think it is an asset. But in the

Supply-Legislation
last two or three weeks every time a radio broadcast has to be made 1 have had some important committee to attend or an obligation to be present in the house. It would appear to me we have now reached the stage when radio and television facilities should be supplied in the House of Commons and it should be done on a formal basis. We all know that there is at the present time a small radio station in the House of Commons, but this is a private set-up. I think it is a good thing, and it speaks well for the enterprise of some of the press and some of the radio stations, but it is not under the jurisdiction of the House of Commons.
Another problem I should like to raise- and this seems the time to raise it-is the matter of the committee rooms themselves. I have always been very disturbed by the meetings which are held in the railway committee room. I do not know if members of parliament 30 years ago had better lungs than members who sit here now, but at every meeting I have attended in the railway committee room there is always a continual request by members of that committee for the members who are speaking to speak up because nobody can hear them. I suggest that some consideration be given to improving the acoustics of that room whether by putting drapes over the windows or installing an address system. Some attention should be given to this room because the acoustics are worse there than they are in any other room or section of this building.
In closing I should like to raise one other problem. I think the hon. member for Mackenzie River has been mentioned, and the fact that he has suffered a serious illness. This reminds me that we have a higher mortality rate in the House of Commons than exists even in the Senate where the average age would be 20 or 30 years greater. In the last three years a great number of our colleagues have passed on. It has been suggested that those members who have been here for a long time should be in a position to make provision for their dependents but that is not true with regard to all members of parliament. I believe that when the pension plan for members was put into effect more consideration should have been given to the position of survivors and to placing the widow of a deceased member in a much better position. I highly recommend the method which was adopted-I am not suggesting it was for financial reasons-by the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas who ran for office and came here herself. That certainly is one solution, but I think it would be of more general benefit if we were to put

better protection into the plan which members of the house now have and I would ask that consideration be given to this as soon as possible.
I should like to make one reference to the press gallery. I have always been surprised when I walk into the press gallery to see the number of people who crowd into that small space. I have had the opportunity a number of times of reading the sections of the Ontario factory act which prevent people from being crowded into too small a space. I think we are treating these people in a way which we would not allow people in a factory or some similar place to be treated; we are cramming 50 or 60 people into a space which would supply offices only for three or four members, and when we move the senators into another building, which should be in the near future, the opportunity should be taken of expanding the space available for these members of the fourth estate.

181.	Subscriptions to publications of the commonwealth parliamentary association to be distributed to members of the House of Commons, and to provide for the Canadian share of expenses of the commonwealth parliamentary association, $11,000.

I should like to say a few words on this vote. During the past several months there have been a number of distinguished visitors to our capital city. Perhaps the two most prominent were the prime minister of Australia and the premier of Northern Nigeria. I was most interested in the remarks of those two world statesmen when they addressed the members at the Speaker's luncheon in their honour. Both of them emphasized the importance of the work of the commonwealth parliamentary association, and they both expressed the view that that organization of parliamentarians of the British commonwealth had perhaps a greater potentiality in the furtherance of freedom and democracy and in solving the urgent problem of these days than any other organization. I agree with all the vehemence, energy and understanding that I have with these sentiments. It is because of the work that I have seen the association undertaking in the past few years, but in particular in the past few months, that I am vastly disappointed to find in the estimates this year the sum of only $11,000 for the furtherance of the work of the commonwealth parliamentary association. It may be said that $11,000 is quite a bit of money for the Canada branch; but I am concerned with the fact that $8,000 of that is to go to the headquarters in London for the purchase of publications; only $3,000 is available for the work of the Canadian branch.
There has been a great increase-and I think a great deal of the thanks for the increase in the interest in the work in Canada must go to Mr. Speaker who has been applying himself so thoroughly and intensely to the work of the organization-in the interest in the work of the parliamentary association; but its potentialities are increasing, and Canada is not able to take advantage of the invitations that are issued and is not able itself to issue the invitations in the numbers that I feel the Canada branch should be doing.
There is a regional conference in Malaya this year and Canada has been invited to send an observer. Canada will not have an observer there because we have not any money. Invitations come from other parts 79951-0-451
Supply-Legislation
of the world, and especially from the United Kingdom, to parliamentarians from Canada to go over for certain special studies. We have not got the money. Recently, a regional conference was held in the West Indies at which we were represented. I have heard from all sections of this house and from the West Indies how much they would appreciate the opportunity of attending a conference in Canada, but this Canada branch association has not got the money.
In these days of conflict and misunderstanding I feel certain, as a result of the honour that was given me last year of being able to make a trip to Australia and, of course, to visit Indonesia, Singapore, Pakistan and Israel, that the greatest need of today is for the peoples of the world to know each other better and to know each other's country better. If we only did that we would go a long way toward resolving the difficulties, the problems and the misunderstandings of the present day.
I join with the prime minister of Australia and the premier of Northern Nigeria-and I think I am safe in saying I express the point of view of the Speaker-in saying that great as has been the contribution of the parliamentary association in the past it can be of even greater use and serve a greater purpose in the future, but that means that more money has to be available for the work of the commonwealth parliamentary association.
Instead of having only $3,000 available to the Canadian branch in the next 12 months and only $8,000 as our contribution to the United Kingdom headquarters, we should have $100,000 in this estimate. As an absolute minimum I say there should be not less than $50,000 in this estimate. I sincerely hope that the Speaker can say a few words on the work of the association and on his admiration for it. I hope he can give us some indication of his being able to approach the treasury benches for some more money.
May I also point out it was the unanimous feeling and decision at the biennial conference in Australia last year that the conference should be held every year and not every two years. There is a need for that. Unfortunately under the old system is has to be a host country that can afford all the expenses of putting on the conference. Therefore, the suggestion was made that all the governments be approached with the idea of holding the conference annually but instead of the host country having to put up all the expenses there should be annual grants by the governments to the association so that the association could pay the expenses of the conference. If my memory serves me correctly, the estimate for Canada will be approximately $24,000 annually. On that basis, sir, I think it would

be one of the finest investments that this parliament could possibly make.
I did want to make these few remarks not only in support but in appreciation of the work of the commonwealth parliamentary association, in its regional meetings or in its world meetings to express the hope that we can get more money for this most worthy cause and advance the commonwealth parliamentary association as a still greater instrument for freedom and for peace.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take the time of the committee by repeating what has already been said, but I do want to indicate my support of the remarks just made by the hon. member for Vancouver East. Mr. Chairman, it is not often that I find myself in accord with the principles expounded by my good friend and colleague from Vancouver East, but I should like to take a few moments to reiterate and agree with the remarks he has made, and also my colleague from Burin-Burgeo. I am one of the newer members of the house and it has been an honour and a privilege for me to be an active member of the commonwealth parliamentary association during my tenure here. May I also say it has been a special honour for me to be the executive member of that body for my great province of Saskatchewan. By virtue of this experience, I have worked in close association with the commonwealth parliamentary association and also with the NATO parliamentary association in the house here. I feel they are doing very important work. Because of the fact that Canada has taken such an active part in world affairs, especially since the last world war, we are beginning to realize more than ever that we are not independent but are becoming interdependent and our friendly relationships with other countries are gaining a wide importance in world affairs.
I think our commonwealth parliamentary association is taking an active part in the cementing of good international public relations. It was brought to our attention during the recent annual meeting of the association that our limited resources were cramping the work of the association. I should like to support the suggestion made this afternoon to increase the appropriation for this very worthwhile work. Instead of having to try to get along with an inadequate amount of $11,000, I think the amount should be increased to

$50,000 or $75,000. In my view the money would be well spent and would be one of the best investments that we as Canadians could make.
His Honour the Speaker pointed out the other morning that we had as visitors in the gallery two members of the commonwealth parliamentary association from Australia. Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks in relation to something in which the Speaker had an interest last year. This year we have had translators in several committees of which I have been a member, especially the one that investigated the Jacques Cartier bridge-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As several hon. members
have been good enough to comment on the work of the various parliamentary associations, I want to acknowledge their references very briefly. It is a pity there is not more opportunity in the House of Commons for members of the house who are members of delegations that go abroad to report to the house and to share the benefit of the experiences they have. As hon. members will see from these three items, our principal parliamentary exchanges fall into three groups, the commonwealth parliamentary association, to which several hon. members have referred and which now has a very large and active branch here of 280 members in the two houses, more than ever before; the NATO parliamentary association; and the Canada-United States joint parliamentary group.

These bring many of our members into close touch with countries with whom we are most directly connected and associated in the commonwealth, in the NATO alliance and with our neighbour across the border.
I mention these associations because I am thoroughly convinced that their value cannot be estimated in dollars in a world which has been so drawn together by communication and transportation but is so far apart in many of its thoughts. If more of this kind of exchange between members of parliaments is made possible I feel that it has had a very salutary effect and I have observed that it has had very useful consequences with relation to these three groups.
As hon. members will see when we come to supplementary item 529, we are asking for additional funds in order to join the interparliamentary union, an association dating back 75 years or more and with a membership among countries with whom we now have no parliamentary exchange, Latin American countries, Central American, Asian, African countries which are not in the commonwealth and European countries which are not in NATO. I strongly commend this proposed new application as well as the additional purpose of this supplementary vote. I apologize for anticipating it but I deemed it appropriate to deal with these items together.
The additional purpose of the supplementary vote is to permit the house to reciprocate the hospitality of those who have received Canadian delegations. That becomes rather necessary in the circumstances which have arisen in the last two or three years. I see a number of members here who were on the Canadian delegation to the commonwealth parliamentary association meeting in Australia. Their expenses were paid, of course, by the Australian government as it was their turn to have the conference. But in the course of that journey members of the Canadian delegation were official guests of the state of Israel for one week and of the Indonesian Speaker and parliament for four days. That is only by way of illustration. Last year the Federal Republic of Germany invited a delegation from the House of Commons and five of us went. This year they have invited a delegation from the Canadian Senate. We saw the new German federal state and its democratic processes at the centre as well as in three of the states as a result of their hospitality.
The Speaker there told us that the Bundestag at Bonn had voted one million marks annually, which is over $200,000, for the express purpose of sending delegations from 79951-0-451i

the Bundestag to other parliaments and inviting others to come to Germany. We were the beneficiaries of such an invitation. I think it is important that the Canadian parliament should be in a position to accept these bilateral exchanges, which means that we must be in a position to repay them in kind.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

I should like to ask one or two questions of His Honour, the Speaker, concerning pay increases granted to the staff of the House of Commons, both the staff under this item and under item 184. As I understand the matter, pay increases have been granted to a large number of the staff, but some members of the staff have not yet received any increases. I want to find out and make sure that is merely because the classifications or groups not yet receiving pay increases have not been dealt with, and also to make sure that pay increases, when granted to them, will have the same effective date as those already granted.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: In general, the answer is along the lines suggested by the hon. member. There have been 415 members of our staff who have already received the increase, as part of the series of civil service increases which the house has discussed from time to time, leaving 291 who have not yet had the increase, but who will when their categories are reached in the rest of the civil service. They are in categories which have not yet received the increase in the civil service generally, and we have timed our action with that of the civil service generally, so that the corresponding categories will be increased at the same time. Perhaps that answers the question.

There is one part of the question which perhaps I should develop a bit further. The pay increases in the civil service outside of the house have not been made effective at the same time; that is they have come into effect on different dates, depending on the particular group involved. I would express the hope that the internal economy commission dealing with this matter in so far as the House of Commons is concerned would adopt the principle of having all pay increases effective at the same time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I appreciate the hon. member's concern that that should be done. Actually there are two different dates for those who have already had increases, April 1 and May 1. In so far as those who have not had the increase are concerned, most of them are not temporary employees of the House of Commons but are on the regular establishment of the civil service, and they will receive their increases as a matter of course when those categories are dealt with by the civil service commission and presumably the same commencement dates would be applied to them as to their corresponding employees in other departments.

May I ask one further question? Is the matter of their increase a matter for the civil service commission and the government or is it a matter for the internal economy commission of the House of Commons?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If they are, as most of these people are, permanent civil servants, then it is automatic. The action of the internal economy commission is taken with respect to those who are not under the Civil Service Act, and they were dealt with on a class analogy to the action of the civil service commission.

I should like to raise a question in connection with translations in parliamentary committees. I believe most members of the house have enjoyed the change that has come over the house itself since the translation system was installed. I should like to ask the Speaker whether it would not be possible to make a more consistent arrangement for translation services in the house committees. I should like to know how the service we have had so far has been arrived at. In the broadcasting committee of last year, and in the Jacques Cartier bridge committee this year, there has been someone in attendance to translate, I understand at the request of the French speaking members.
It seems to me that in fairness to both the French speaking members and the English speaking members on the committees, a more thorough and complete job of translations might be available than exists at the present time. I shudder to think of the position I would be in, as well as many of the English speaking members, if we had to express our thoughts or our questions in French. I am sure that cuts both ways. If bilingualism is recognized in the house by the translation system, with the proliferation of committees and the increase in their work, it seems to me we might think more seriously of taking better care of this problem in the house committees. I would be interested in Mr. Speaker's comments on that, and any background information he may be able to give as to how what we had was set up, as well as to any possibility in the future of extension of such facilities.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yes, this is a question which has also been raised earlier by the hon. member for St. Boniface, the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, and the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, and which has been receiving consideration. I, myself, have spent considerable time this session in discussion with the engineers of the organization which services our sound system in the chamber. They are in the course

of preparing quotations for installations which will deal with this problem of simultaneous translation in committees. We are working experimentally. It was my thought that if we had one room properly equipped, where committees which particularly needed the translation could experiment with it, that might be the first step. The cost of equipping all of our committee rooms with facilities, and more particularly with personnel for translation, is quite a sizeable undertaking. We are definitely working on the problem and I hope next session we shall be able to supply translation for at least one committee at a time.
I should like to ask a supplementary question to the one I asked earlier. Of the 415 members of the staff who have received increases, are the sessional stenographers included?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, all of those who are sessional stenographers received the increase which was effective as of April 1, I believe.
My second question is this. Does this figure given here of $2 million plus take into consideration the further increases that have not yet been granted?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: No, it is not in that vote. However, there was a vote of the house to cover the increases as they were brought about and that includes the House of Commons staff as well as other civil servants.

I know that Mr. Speaker will be glad to know that I am not rising on a point of order or a question of privilege at this time. My purpose at the moment is to congratulate him on the wonderful way in which he has presided over the debates of the House of Commons in French and in English. I am sure all members of the committee share my point of view in this respect.
I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would consider my proposal to place on the shoulder band of the protective staff the bilingual designation of their functions, as the House of Commons and Chambre des Communes. I think this would be a fine gesture toward the tourists that come here and would also signify the bilingual characteristics of our country.

I know that anything I might say on the subject which has just been raised is prejudiced because of my long and, for me, highly rewarding friendship with the Speaker. However, notwithstanding that fact, as one whom he keeps in order when the occasion seems to require it may I say that I am sure it has been a long time since this House of Commons has had such a good Speaker.
