General administration-
164. Departmental administration including a grant of $10,000 to Frontier college and the expenses of the international labour conferences, $1,118,255.

In bringing before the house the estimates of the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission, I do so in the knowledge that the efficient functioning of these two departments is of concern to many thousands of Canadians and, of course, to the members of the House of Commons.
As all members are aware, the number of men and women in the working force in Canada has increased considerably in the short period of ten years and the functions and the services of these two departments have been extended to meet the new demands which have been created.
In 1950 the labour force numbered slightly over five million. Today there are some 6,454,000 Canadians in the labour force which shows an increase from 1950 to the present time of some 20 per cent. Hon. members are also aware of the rapidly changing pattern in Canadian industry in a period which has seen a change-over from primary occupation and an increase in the employment in secondary

Supply-Labour
Our women's bureau works closely with other branches of the department, the national employment service, and other departments and with the national women's organizations, tor the promotion of good standards in the fields of women's work and a better understanding of the problems of women in the labour force. I might say at this point that two public spirited bodies-the vocational training advisory council and the apprenticeship training committee-are most helpful to my department in the administration of these agreements.
Having mentioned these bodies, I trust the committee will grant me the indulgence of pausing for a moment to express my appreciation of the valuable work of the loyal and devoted staffs of both the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission. In a period of change they have magnificently met the challenge and have performed a service that is greatly appreciated by myself as minister.
While I am dealing with training I might mention that enrolments in all training programs have continued to increase and that this presents a problem to practically all provinces in finding adequate staffs and accommodation. This is particularly acute in respect of technicians and trades training programs. Eegistered apprentices in training, for example, have increased to some 20,000 persons. Last year training was extended to unemployed persons on a much wider basis than previously. This, as was recently announced, will continue on an expanded basis. Training for disabled persons has increased by about 15 per cent. Apart from apprenticeship training there are some 15,000 persons receiving training under these co-operative federal-provincial agreements. In additions, enrolments in vocational schools across Canada number more than 130,000.
I may say that at the present time vocational training facilities are filled to capacity and there is a need for additional facilities. To meet this need the provinces are being encouraged to establish additional facilities and to take advantage of capital funds which are available under these agreements. More facilities are particularly required to train persons who have left the regular school system either before or after completing it.
In a program of the magnitude we have in Canada caution must be exercised to maintain a proper balance between the long term educational and training needs and the shorter range programs to retrain or refresh those who need such training to adjust to rapidly changing conditions. We also have agreements with the provinces sharing costs of

movement of farm labour, and I shall be pleased to discuss these in greater detail on the individual estimates.
As hon. members know, my department has been active in promoting a program encouraging people to have certain types of construction and repair work done in winter. Following the slogan of "Do it now" this program has had a degree of success over the years. The slogan has become popular and well known and the program was intensified last winter and also in the present fiscal year. My officials inform me that the modest amount spent in advertising by the department has stimulated some $3 million worth of advertising in this field by private industry and has been instrumental in providing a good many jobs during wintertime for persons who otherwise would have been inactive.
The special services branch was responsible for administration of the municipal incentive program which contributed to some $75 million worth of municipal construction during the winter months and provided direct onsite employment for some 50,000 persons. Since this program is dealt with generally by supplementary estimate, and has already been discussed in the house, it does not appear in these estimates.
In the field of civilian rehabilitation, in which my department, together with the Department of National Health and Welfare, also co-operates with the provinces, a simple illustration will serve to show the effect of this program. Of the first 4,689 cases reported as successfully rehabilitated, 3,600 when referred had no earnings whatsoever and with their 3,410 dependents, were being maintained at an annual cost of $3,500,000. After rehabilitation their estimated earnings in the first year will total $8,500,000. I think that this indication in itself justified the program. We have the benefit of the advice of a widely representative national advisory committee in the promotion and operation of this program.
In this respect a great deal of attention has been devoted by my department and the unemployment insurance commission to the problem of the older worker, and we are continuing to pursue this policy among employers.
The information branch of the department also disseminates factual information through press, radio and television, dealing with the various functions and activities of the department.
The annuities branch is of course, concerned with the administration of government annuities, and I will be pleased to answer any questions in this regard at the proper place in the estimates.

In dealing with the unemployment insurance commission one is confronted with a department numbering some 8,500 employees, staffing some 200 offices across Canada. This department deals in a direct and often personal way with many thousands of Canadians across this country and as such its administration is of considerable interest. Costs of administration, including the government's contribution to the fund, in the present estimates come to something over $88 million which as I have said is an increase of some $13,500,000 in the federal government contribution. The commission is charged with administering many millions of dollars annually within the terms of the act and, of course, is concerned to see that proper controls are maintained at all times.
The administration of this department caused me some concern when I first took over my present responsibilities. Over the past two and a half to three years I have endeavoured to help in any way I could to obtain the maximum possible service from this department and to see that the maximum possible service was rendered to all Canadians. To this end I have continuously emphasized the need of courtesy on the part of the commission staffs. I have also made it a point to emphasize the placement side of the operation so that officers whose function it is to find jobs for Canadians were given every facility to do so.
Let me say that it was quite evident from the first that salaries in this organization, particularly on the placement side, were not such as to attract the type of qualified person necessary to perform an efficient job in this regard. At the same time, and perhaps as a result of this, there were acute shortages of staff. Steps have been taken to adjust both of these situations.
The increase in the commission's administration costs this year totals $857,000, which may largely be attributed to salaries. Further salary provisions totalling some $2,794,000 will be provided through the general civil service salaries vote. There is an increase of some $200,000 in the vote relating to transfer of labour, and this covers anticipated removal expenses of workers owing to the decline of the uranium industry in Elliot Lake and Uranium City.
During the fiscal year employers listed some 150,000 more jobs with the placement service than in the previous year, indicating a growing acceptance of this service. The number of placements effected was 987,481, an increase of 120,000.
At the present time, an estimated 70 per cent of urban employers avail themselves of the services of the national 79951-0-452
Supply-Labour
employment service, and the national employment service endeavours to bring to the attention of Canadians this service that we have available to them. The commission during the recent months published a booklet entitled, "N.E.S.-Geared to Canada's Employment Needs" which tells the story of how the national employment service can help employers in recruiting their employees. I know that hon. members would like a copy of this booklet and they may procure it if they ask my office for a copy.
It will, of course, be realized that a national employment service cannot properly operate unless both employers and employees make use of such a service. During the coming months an effort will be made on the part of the commission to contact an increased number of employers in order to obtain a larger number of orders for employment.
The total amount of benefits paid out during the year was $415 million, down somewhat from the $479 million in the previous year. Owing to higher contributions, revenue was up by $40 million to $275 million. Some 190,000 audits were completed and 37,340 investigations were undertaken by the unemployment insurance commission. The enforcement branch carried out 73,547 investigations compared with 67,702 in the previous year.
May I say that the chairman and members of the commission are co-operating fully in the endeavour to constantly improve the administration of this important service. During the coming year the placement service will continue to be strengthened in order that it may fulfil its function of finding jobs for Canadian workers. It is my aim, Mr. Chairman, and I know it is shared by all members of the staff, to provide the best possible service for Canadians. We are making every effort to provide better accommodation, to secure more qualified people for the service and to enlist the co-operation of labour and industry in the general administration.
This government has already announced a number of measures which will help to stimulate employment in the coming months. One of these was announced by my colleague the Minister of Public Works in respect of housing that, commencing on September 1, the ceiling for those who can qualify will be raised to $7,000 and to $7,600 for those with families. These loans will be available to builders of pre-sold homes, with as much money as will be necessary and required to fulfil this need. This most certainly should stimulate a great deal of employment.
Our winter works program, which has been announced by the Prime Minister, has been expanded on the basis of the recommendations of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities. An earlier announcement

Supply-Labour
had been made in this respect and we hope that here, too, there will be a substantial increase in the number of people employed during the coming months.
The training of unemployed workers is a very important thing because at the moment, in my opinion, there should be very few unfilled vacancies, but we have quite a number of unfilled vacancies, and it is probably due to the fact that we have not the properly trained persons to fill those jobs. We hope that because of our incentive to the provinces, the provinces will undertake to train at an increased pace more and more workers in this country and this, too, will help a great deal to stimulate unemployment.
We have been interested in our winter works program in the home improvement field and it has been our thought that the chartered banks of this country would be interested enough to put forward their facilities and make them available to those who want to avail themselves of home improvements in order to help the situation during the coming months. We have taken this further step in this direction to increase domestic construction in the wintertime.
The government has been in communication with the chartered banks through my colleague the Minister of Finance and all the banks have undertaken to co-operate fully in a program of expanded home improvement and home extension construction luring the coming winter. As hon. members know, under the National Housing Act the government guarantees bank loans for purposes of home improvement and home extension. It is hoped, Mr. Chairman, that with this announcement house builders across Canada will take advantage of this program this winter, providing an expanded volume of home construction and improvement in order to provide employment in the building trades during the winter months.
I mentioned earlier that at the request of the hon. member for Vancouver East for a full statement on automation I would be prepared to give it, but before doing so I wish to refer to Hansard of July 23 when the Prime Minister, in announcing the municipal winter works program, said in the last paragraph at page 6817:
I should point out that in addition to this announcement the Minister of Labour has another announcement to make at this time,-
Which I did make.
-and that further projects and plans to meet the unemployment situation will be announced in due course.
Now, as to automation: the Department of Labour, with the assistance and co-operation
[Mr. Starr.l
of management, labour and provincial training authorities, has been examining the employment effects of automation and other kinds of technological changes for several years. Research work began in 1956, and has continued since that time. In 1957 an advisory committee on technological change, with representatives from labour, management, government and the universities, was established to consider and discuss the work undertaken and planned. The findings of the studies conducted so far have been published as the work was completed. Reports have been issued for the electrical and electronics industry, the heavy machinery industry and the household appliance industry. A full report on the automobile and parts industry has been completed and is now being considered by members of the advisory committee on technological change before release.
Studies have been conducted of office automation as well as of technological changes in industry. A case study is being made of a large electronic data processing system recently installed in an insurance company office. A more general survey of all companies with medium and large size computers is now under way and will provide information on the extent, growth and manpower effects of electronic data processing equipment in Canadian offices.
There are a number of significant findings emerging from these studies. One of the most important concerns the effects of technological changes on skills. In the industries studied technological changes have been accompanied by a rise in the employment of engineers, technicians and skilled tradesmen, a decline in the employment of semi-skilled workers and a still more marked decline in the employment of unskilled workers.
Another effect has been a relative decrease in the number of direct production workers and an increase in non-production employment. One reason for this is that most of the semi-skilled and unskilled occupations so far affected by technological changes have been those involved in direct production tasks, while the resulting increasing need for skilled manpower has been in such areas as maintenance and tool room work which are non-production functions. Another reason is that new products, improved production methods, greater quality control and increasing research and development have all resulted in more technical specialists who are not directly involved in production.
Technological changes are not affecting all kinds of semi-skilled and unskilled workers to the same extent. They are resulting in a decreased need for semi-skilled machine operators. Automated transfer equipment and conveyor systems have replaced much

unskilled labour formerly employed in material handling jobs. On the other hand, assembly occupations which are usually semiskilled have been affected to a much lesser extent.
Mechanization is having important effects on office employment, although not to the same extent on the various office occupations. It appears, for example, that middle level supervisory and senior clerical jobs are going to decline. In addition, much routine clerical work will be carried out by machines. On the other hand, evidence suggests that needs for secretaries, stenographers, typists and a growing variety of office machine operators will continue to expand.
Another important result of office automation is an increasing demand for employees to fill the new occupations that are coming into existence-systems analysts, programmers, computer operators and maintenance technicians. On the whole, these new occupations are more complex than the old clerical ones they are replacing and tend to require much more formal education than routine clerical work.
The studies carried out so far suggest that while little difficulty is usually encountered in retraining production workers for the jobs created by technological changes, problems have been encountered in retraining workers for the more skilled and technician jobs which are growing more rapidly. The main difficulty appears to be the insufficient formal education held by many semi-skilled workers today.
The extent to which automation and technological change result in employees being laid off varies a great deal from one industry to another. In growing industries such layoffs rarely occur because the workers affected can usually be transferred to other jobs. In industries where employment is stable or declining, however, lay-offs do take place. In these cases the national employment service tries to find new jobs for those concerned and we are endeavouring to make available more facilities for the retraining of such unemployed. The extension of federal government assistance to the provincial authorities for training programs for the unemployed, announced just a few days ago, had this problem in mind. Our stay in school campaign is also important here because the more education one has the less are the chances of losing one's job or being unemployed for long because of technological change.
We are continuing this research work and will be publishing detailed reports on findings as studies are completed. Our work is discussed regularly with the advisory committee 79951-0-452J
Supply-Labour
on technological change and general reviews of our findings and plans are made to the Canadian vocational training council and the national advisory committee on apprenticeship.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has given us a general account of the work of his department. When we reach the details of his estimates there will be an opportunity to comment on the several items which he covered. I regret that in the statement he has just made he has not highlighted, as I propose to do, the most important single domestic problem in Canada, which is the continuing high level of unemployment in our country. I would have expected the minister to deal forthrightly with this problem, which he knows concerns all of us in this house as well as the people of Canada generally. He referred only at the end prior to his statement on automation, which did not really traverse new ground, to the four prongs of attack devised by the government to mitigate the severity of unemployment.
As I have said on other occasions, notably last Saturday, the government's announced program does not represent the vigorous approach to the solution of this problem which we have a right to expect. It certainly is not a program consistent with the assurances given by hon. gentlemen, when they confronted the Canadian people and indicated that plans which they would devise would remove the spectre of unemployment and the consequential suffering from that economic disease. We have therefore not had, in these the closing days of the session, any demonstration by the government that it has a program capable of resolving or mitigating this serious situation.
All through this session, we in the Liberal opposition have sought to bring home to the government, not with any success, our concern for this problem, and the fact that it requires vigorous action on the part of the government. The government's laissez-faire policy, and its relaxed attitude toward the problem are reflected in the kind of answers we have had to questions. We have had no less than seven questions put to the minister asking him when we might expect, for instance, a report from the interdepartmental committee set up for the purpose of establishing a new measurement for unemployment in our country. We have not yet, in spite of this interval of four and a half months, been given anything that would indicate what progress this interdepartmental committee is making. It may be that the committee has made a decision. It may be that the decision arrived at by the committee simply confirms

Supply-Labour
the pattern pursued in the past, namely a pattern of sampling a number of unemployed, only in the new formula increasing the number of people to be covered by the sampling process.
Then we have had the persistent refusal of the government to treat this House of Commons, composed of the elected representatives of the people, in a manner at least equal to that accorded by the spokeman for the government in the other place. We have asked for the right in this house to examine the problem of unemployment in all its aspects, to examine these proposals that might be embarked upon to relieve this situation, but no recognition of the right of this chamber has been accorded. This has occurred in the face of the fact that the industrial relations committee, set up for the purpose of organization, met only on that one occasion, and still has a motion before it on unemployment, put forward by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River designed to provide corrective action in unemployment.
There is still the refusal of the government to call a conference of labour, management and government to try and resolve this problem in accordance with the recommendations made by the Canadian Labour Congress, and indeed publicly supported in a speech made at Easter by the Minister of Labour when he spoke in the town of Gananoque. Today, following the conference between the federal and provincial governments, where unemployment undoubtedly was discussed-we certainly know from the statements of Mr. Lesage and other provincial premiers that they initiated such a discussion-we have not had from either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Labour any report whatsoever as to the conclusions reached at that conference or as to the nature of the discussions. Yet the Prime Minister, disagreeing with the Minister of Labour the other day, said that the provinces had a responsibility in connection with this matter. Notwithstanding this we reminded the Prime Minister, at that time, that he was repudiating the declared position of the Minister of Labour, who said that this was a federal responsibility.

I am afraid I have to rise on a question of privilege if the hon. member is again trying to distort statements in this house. I made my position abundantly clear, as it has been in the past, on shared responsibility. In the first instance, I have stressed the fact that the federal government does not wish to shirk its part of the responsibility, but there is a responsibility lying with other

bodies. I have said that time and time again, and what the hon. member wishes to convey now is not so.

I have no objection to the Minister of Labour rising and seeking to correct me. I think in debate it is desirable, that he should do so. I can only point out to you, sir, that the time at my disposal is limited. I have no objection to it but I hope he will remember-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He has no right to do it, either.

I have no objection to the minister doing it, because I want now to deal with the correction he has made. I say that the statement the minister has made now, consistent with the statement of the Prime Minister, is not consistent with the position he took as a private member and later as a member of the government. I now propose to establish that fact. On June 29, 1960, the Prime Minister said as reported at page 5535 of Hansard, inter alia:
The Minister ol Labour can speak for himself in that regard, but I am glad to have support for the stand taken by the Minister of Labour in the position taken by the new premier-designate of Quebec, who throughout the campaign, made it absolutely clear that the responsibility for unemployment rested on the provincial administration.

Would the Prime Minister not give some members of the house who did not hear him the opportunity of hearing him confirm the statement he has just made, that the federal government has no responsibility for unemployment?
I said no such thing.

Since my name has been brought into this discussion may I say that, on several occasions, I have said on behalf of the government that we have a responsibility in the matter of unemployment. We do not shirk it. But at the same time I have said, time and time again, that in order to carry out the responsibility and in order to solve the problem of unemployment co-operation is needed from provincial, municipal and, yes, even labour bodies and other interested organizations in this country.
Do you agree with that?

Wait until you have heard the whole story. This was a statement made by the Prime Minister on June 29, 1960. Now, the Minister of Labour spoke in this house on March 3, 1960, and here is what he said as reported on page 1699 of Hansard:
The government as a whole-I have said this on previous occasions and I repeat it-has assumed the responsibility for unemployment. We have said that right from the start, and this is possibly the only time that a federal government in this country within recent years has accepted that responsibility.
On a shared basis.

My hon. friend did not say on a shared basis. I have other

statements that the minister made, and I suggest my hon. friend should not destroy the credibility of his own witness. The fact is my hon. friend, in a statement on March 3, did make a statement that was consistent with the earlier statement that this government, attempting to solve unemployment, was not going to look to another level of government to assist; it was going to solve the problem of unemployment itself. That was the statement made by the Minister of Labour. It was in direct contradiction to the statement made by the head of the government.
I do not deny that Mr. Lesage, recognizing the failure of this government to do anything about unemployment in a fundamental way, has not hesitated as the premier of a province to recognize that he must in the face of this situation seek to do something. I commend him for that kind of initiative. However, I am dealing now with the policy of this government. Here is what the Minister of Labour said as a private member of this house, and it is consistent with his second last reported statement. He said on March 3, 1955, at pages 1693, 1694 and 1695 that unemployment had reached a dangerous and alarming figure. Then he said:
It is not a situation which can be brushed aside nor can the problem be shifted to another level of government. It is a problem which only the senior government of this country can tackle effectively providing they feel, as they should, that the responsibility is theirs.
Then further on he said:
The important thing at the present time is to place the blame and the responsibility for unemployment on the proper government. Delegation after delegation is becoming fed up with the shirking of responsibility on the part of this government. We must place the responsibility with the federal government where it belongs.
Is that statement of March 3 the policy of the government or is it the revised statement the minister has given today, supported on June 29 by the Prime Minister? Is that the way in which this government is now seeking to escape its responsibilities, now that Liberal governments have come into office in two of our provinces, and there will be more?
Where?

Is that the situation? I ask the Minister of Labour not to hesitate to maintain the position he has taken that this was a responsibility of the federal government and one which he did not propose to shirk.
The problem facing us in Canada is a serious one. Unemployment now persists on an increasing scale since hon. gentlemen came into office. The situation month by month
Supply-Labour
reflects the justification for the statement I have made. Here we are on the 28th of July, when on the basis of past experience there should be such an improvement as to indicate that the problem at best is temporary. From the last available figures given to us by the minister and by the Minister of Trade and Commerce-that is the figures on the basis of the bureau of statistics, the lowest figures-on June 18 there were 300,000 people out of jobs and seeking work. That was in June of this year. That means that 4.6 per cent of the labour force in Canada was unemployed.
How does that compare with countries with a like economy? From the minister's own publications we know that in May of this year in the federal German republic out of a population of over 50 million people, with a working force of 30 million, there were only 135,000 unemployed or 0.8 per cent of the German labour force; that in Sweden 2 per cent of the labour force was unemployed; that in Britain, with a labour force of 23 million, 2 per cent of that country's labour force was unemployed. That is a situation that should agitate the minister as nothing else should agitate him. We know that for the first time in May of this year unemployment was higher than it was in the samo period in 1958, and that was a post-war record. To attack the unemployment problem, as the government is doing as if it were merely a question of having more of the year's work done in the wintertime is to indicate a profound lack of knowledge of this problem on the part of the government. We still have distressed or depressed areas such as Sydney, St. John's, Quebec, Levis, Windsor, Winnipeg and Vancouver.
Did the hon. member say Sydney?
Yes; Sydney.
Sydney where?
Sydney, Nova Scotia.
The hon. member had better take another look.

The hon. member for Cape Breton South had better look at the publications put out by the Department of Labour and he will see that is a distressed area.
Not only have we that situation, but we have regional pockets of structural unemployment showing that the problem is more than only seasonal in its character. I have given you minimum figures, Mr. Chairman, but these do not tell the whole story. One form of

Supply-Labour
unemployment which we have in this country and which the government overlooks is underemployment. The figures that my hon. friend quotes do not touch that matter. They refer only to people who are working for more than 33 hours a week. What are the facts taken from my hon. friend's own publications? We know that in June, 1958, 669,000 people were employed for less than 33 hours a week and in the month of June, 1960, 730,000 people worked less than 33 hours a week. In other words, 10 per cent more .people worked short time. That is part of this problem of unemployment.
From the claims for unemployment insurance benefits we know how serious the problem is. We know that on June 30 last claims for unemployment insurance benefits were made in the number of 296,400. This is a rise of 35 per cent over last year's figure. More than 75 per cent of this increase was accounted for by males, normally regarded as a primary earning unit of the family. These claims rose by 25 per cent in Quebec to 91,800. In Ontario as of June 30, 1959 there were 77,600 claims; as of the same day in the same month of this year in that province there were 111,100 claims, or an increase in the province of Ontario of 43 per cent. There was nearly a 50 per cent rise in the number of claimants in British Columbia, from 23,000 to 33,000. Need one spend any more time in indicating how serious this problem is?
The minister mentioned the problem of older workers. That is a problem, it is true, but there is also the problem of the young, the problem of the youth of this nation. Of the expected 780,000 increase in the Canadian labour force during the next five years it is estimated that 300,000 will be in the age category under 25. During the first six months of this year there were on an average 580,000 who were from 14 years to 19 years of age. Of this number approximately 496,000 held jobs. This means that 89,000 were without jobs during the first half of 1960; that is nearly 14.5 per cent of this age group in the labour force or double the rate of unemployment in the total labour force, as 7.5 per cent of the total labour force was without jobs for the first six months of 1960.
How does the government propose to resolve this problem? The minister told us or made an announcement the other day about an acceleration in vocational training. He did not refer to the speeches made two years ago by the hon. member for Trinity, the Leader of the Opposition and others who two years ago urged that this very thing be done. He has made no mention of the complaints of the advisory council last fall. He made no

mention whatsoever of the statements made by the chairman of the unemployment insurance commission last year, namely that only one in ten was trained and that something must be done about the problem. Nevertheless the minister seeks to resolve this problem by the winter works program, a program which, when we had close to 700,000 people out of work, was able to provide jobs in the amount of some 55,000, assuming, of course, that that program was responsible for providing those jobs. Surely the minister does not think that that program represents an effort that would satisfy the Canadian people that this government is seriously tackling this problem?
The Prime Minister announced some modification of that program. He said the federal government would pay 50 per cent of the wages on municipal buildings. But that modification does not represent the demands and the requests of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities. All one needs to do is to look at their brief in order to see their recommendations and to decide whether they are consistent with the minister's statement today that these demands have been met.
If the Prime Minister wanted to give some substance to that program he might have included underground parking garages. He might have mentioned a policy that would guarantee municipal debentures issued in order to raise the municipalities' share of costs for after all the municipalities, many of them in the very areas in which unemployment is greatest, are not able to meet their share of the cost of this program.
Then the government, through the Minister of Public Works two weeks ago, after the prodding of the hon. member for Nipissing, announced that it was going to increase its housing loans in order to meet the problem of unemployment. All I want now to say about that matter is this. No one denies that construction is an important constituent in unemployment. The Minister of Public Works, in the announcement of that program, said that one of the expressed purposes of that program was to create jobs in the wintertime. Since this government is responsible for the low level of starts so far this summer, what they are in effect doing is replacing unemployment in the winter with unemployment in summer. That is the consequence of this program. Instead of embarking upon a real program and instead of taking those steps which were recommended by the Leader of the Opposition and by practically every member in this house who spoke, and which were finally summarized

by the hon. member for Laurier in 25 different suggestions, what did the Minister of Labour do? In the face of this serious problem, more serious in Canada than in any other country in the western world, the Minister of Labour said the problem would be solved by the winter works program, by training more unemployed workers along the lines mentioned by the minister in his announcement, and by the housing program.
What is that going to do for the people in these depressed areas? What is that going to do to provide employment in places like the city of Windsor? Why did the government not recognize at the beginning of this session, let alone the two earlier sessions, the desirability of treating this problem as a government responsibility, not as the responsibility of the Minister of Labour and of that department? Why did they not establish an organism within the government of Canada along the lines now proposed in the province of Quebec, along the lines which have been proposed in the United States, along the lines now proposed by the two candidates for the presidency of that country, and along the lines proposed by the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities, when on May 11 they called upon the federal government to appoint an impartial board of inquiry or royal commission to investigate unemployment in Canada?
Here we are in the dying days of this session, and no further ahead so far as eliciting from this government a policy in keeping with the character of the problem, and certainly a program in keeping with the assurances which were given by the hon. gentlemen when they went before the Canadian people.
This problem this fall and this winter on every available index gives indication of being as severe, if not severer, than in the months which we have just traversed. What is the government doing to meet and to anticipate this situation? Parliament is going to conclude this session very shortly. Will the government call this parliament back into session in the fall to deal with this problem if it becomes serious? Can the government escape the responsibility of calling parliament together to meet the emergency if it should appear, as every indication now establishes? Or are we to prorogue, come back here next year, have a report from the government in the speech from the throne in two or three sentences, meanwhile allowing all these months to intervene, during which the problem of unemployment will stare us in the face as it has now for three years?
That is not what the people of Canada expect this government to do with regard to this matter. I am sure hon. gentlemen are
Supply-Labour
aware that their prestige and their support in the country has very seriously dwindled. The Gallup polls indicate that, and the last Gallup poll was taken, by the way, before the elections in New Brunswick and in the province of Quebec.
But after Nova Scotia.

After Nova Scotia but before Quebec and New Brunswick, which is significant. I venture to suggest that because of the way the government has handled the problem of unemployment in particular the next Gallup poll, later to be published, will show that hon. gentlemen have lost still more support from the Canadian people.
I say that, because there is a growing dissatisfaction with the way in which this government is confronting this problem. We have had no estimate by the government of its plans, not only for next winter but we have had no projection at all for the foreseeable future. This government will have to try to provide in the sixties if it is still in office, and that I believe is a doubtful possibility, for another two million jobs if its promises and assurances are going to be kept. That will be a great task and if two million jobs are provided there will still be 200,000 people out of work.
Are we just to receive from the minister dodging answers, answers which do not in any way convey information? Are we to be again confronted with a refusal to allow this house to examine this problem on the ground that members are going to play politics with this problem? Is that a justification for the contemptuous way in which hon. gentlemen have treated the House of Commons with regard to this matter? We have not had anything from the minister today about the seriousness which will develop as the result of the state of the unemployment insurance fund.
The other day we were given by the minister the figures for four different years showing the extent to which that fund has been reduced, in itself a reflection of the level of unemployment in Canada. What is going to happen next year? Will there be enough money to take care of the unemployed of our country, who have contracted with their employers and with the state for sustenance and maintenance in the event of unemployment? That fund has reached a level way beyond $300 million, in spite of the fact that last year the hon. minister introduced amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, which provided for an increase in the contributions from 25 per cent to 55 per cent, higher without basically changing

Supply-Labour
the pattern of benefits. In spite of that $78 million by way of additional revenue we are to be confronted with a situation which should cause anyone concerned about that fund, based as it is upon contributions from the employers and the employees, to be greatly alarmed.
We have had nothing from the minister today about the actual losses in that fund, actual losses which were reported by the Minister of Finance when he advised us on May 31 that during the fiscal year 1959-60 the fund realized losses totalling $8.4 million, a further $1.5 million in losses realized in April and May of this year. The Minister of Labour did not tell us anything about the loss in the market value of the fund's securities on March 31 of this year, which was approximately $55 million less than their book value, only $5 million less than the book value loss of the fund during the fiscal year 1958-59. The government told us it made advances to the fund, but the Minister of Finance, when this question was put to him first denied it and then corrected himself the next day and said there were advances to the fund from April 1, 1960, to May 6, 1960 totalling $20 million.
I say to the minister, are we not entitled to have from him, and should we not have had it from him at the outset today, not a recital of the valuable and important work of the department, all of which could be given to us when we discuss the estimates in detail, but instead a statistical statement about the problem now? He has figures in his possession, which are later than those in the last release by the Department of Labour and the Department of Trade and Commerce. He should have talked about the problem not only of the old but of the young workers as well. He should have told us what are his prognostications for the next fiscal year. He could or should have told us what the government proposes to do about that problem.
I say to the minister, then, because the minister has not done these things, because he reflects in his statement a complete bankruptcy of policy on the part of this government, I believe he must recognize and be made to see in a friendly but nevertheless in a responsible and vigorous manner, what is the temper of this committee and what is the judgment of the Canadian people. If the minister says this problem is beyond the ability of any government to resolve, if he now takes the position that it is no longer an exclusive federal responsibility, if he takes the position that the assurances given to the Canadian people will no longer be satisfactory, he will win the support and the confidence of this committee to an immeasurable degree. But to sit there day after day and refuse to give

satisfactory answers either on his own part or on the part of other members of the government, notably the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, is not discharging the functions of government in a manner such as the hon. gentleman stated in 1957 and 1958 this government would undertake to do. Every member sitting behind the ministers on the treasury benches who made similar claims in the elections shares the responsibility, along with the government, for not joining with the rest of us in bringing this problem home right where it belongs-right to the treasury benches.

Once again I find I must follow my namesake and once again it seems to me that about the only thing the two of us have in common is our last names. The hon. member for Essex East has once more clearly stated to the committee that apparently, as far as the Liberals are concerned, their sole responsibility is to place the blame for unemployment on the shoulders of the government. I wonder what the hon. gentleman and his supporters would say if the Minister of Labour stood up and said: Yes, we are to blame, and we are to blame because we have done exactly what you people did in the same situation. What would the answer be then from the Liberal benches? This is exactly the same problem as that which the Liberals were unable to meet, and they were unable to meet it because they were incapable or unwilling of facing up to the nature of the problem and the steps necessary to deal with it. This is exactly the present government's failure. It is trying to use the same methods which were used by the Liberal governments of the past, and they have failed dismally. In fact, I would go one step further and say that this government has failed even to follow its own advice. For the last couple of years they have been asking Canadians, in an expensive advertising campaign, to "Do it now". But they have failed even to follow their own advice.
I should like to deal now with an aspect of this problem a little different from those which have been discussed so far, namely to consider some of the effects of the unemployment situation upon our economy. It seems that in this country we have become conditioned to the idea that we must have massive unemployment. It has come to be regarded as a normal state of affairs. In the main, unemployment has ceased to be news, and that seems so strange to me, because let there be a strike in any part of the country and it will fill the newspapers. Articles appear about the loss of man-hours, the loss of purchasing power and the way in which the economy of the country is being upset. We

completely ignore the tact that hundreds of thousands more man-hours are lost every day through unemployment than are lost through strikes during the course of the whole year. But that does not make news.
Another thing we forget when we talk about the cost of strikes and their effect on the economy is that the harm done to local trades people and others is offset by the funds which the strikers very often receive from their local or international union. I know whereof I speak, because in 1953 eight out of the 11 producing mines in the Timmins riding were idle through strikes, some of them lasting eight months or more. Not one business in that town failed during that period or in the year following, because the united steel workers of America spent over $2,500,000 during that strike. I have just been checking the home town news and I find that two businesses have gone under in the last month, just as a result of the slow down in our economy and the resulting unemployment. The people laid off in Elliot Lake coming into Timmins seeking work have been enough to tip the scale with regard to at least two businesses which have been operating for some time. As I say, we make big news headlines out of a comparatively small problem and tend to ignore much greater problems. When are we going to realize that unemployment has effects more serious on the public, on the workers, on the stores and on the whole community than any strike which ever took place in this country?
Little can be said in defence of strikes as such. I forget who said that democracy is the worst form of government in the world except any other, but I would say the same about strikes; they are about the worst possible way of settling a dispute. I wish strikes were unnecessary, and I feel that if both sides played the game they would be unnecessary. In this country we seem to have failed to realize that strikes have to be settled some time and the longer they go on the more disruption they cause. I often wonder why the parties concerned cannot sit down before a strike starts and possibly arrive at the same solution as they reach after perhaps months of idleness and frustration.
Why have we failed to face up to this problem of unemployment in Canada? I say it is because no serious attempt has ever been made to do so. We have always approached it with dribs and drabs and considered it in little pieces. We have never faced up to the fact that we have a serious problem on our hands, and I think the reason is very simple.
All we have ever had in this country are Liberal and Conservative governments and
Supply-Labour
their basic philosophy is that as far as employment is concerned, it is the responsibility of production and industry, and government's should keep their noses out of it. That is the very basis of the principles that the two parties have preferred to believe in. I do not say that the members of the Conservative party or of the Liberal party want unemployment or like it. I think they are just as much opposed to it as I am, and I think many of them have tried very sincerely, within the limits of their philosophy, to find some solution. They take this worn out old tire and put patches on it here and there and finally they get to the stage where they are putting patches on patches, and still they have not found a cure; they still cannot get away from a flat tire. I think it is about time they realized that the best cure is to buy a new tire.
I should like hon. members to think back over the past 50 years and see whether they can find any time in our history, when for any reasonable length of time, where we have solved the problem of unemployment unless the government took a hand in it. The only time we have ever had full employment was when the federal government accepted the responsibility of having all-out production. During wartime we had full employment, full production and jobs for everyone. As soon as the war was over the government stepped out of the picture and free enterprise took over again. What did we have? We had the same thing as we had before the war started. How many times do we have to be taught this lesson before we realize it?
Unemployment is caused by three main problems. One we have always had with us. It is quite true that technical advances have been made in this field, but conditions are such in this country that Canada will always have some degree of seasonal unemployment. Because of climatic conditions in this country certain jobs cannot be done in certain months of the year. As I said, technical advances have been made. We have these new plastic covers which are used to cover buildings and keep the employees working in the winter where formerly they could not work at all. There have been various other technical advances which have assisted us to cut down on this problem to a certain extent, but certainly at least in the foreseeable future it is a problem that is always going to be with us.
A few attacks have been made on this particular problem with some considerable success. The first was the implementation of unemployment insurance. The basic principles of unemployment insurance were carried out at least when the system was started, but I am sorry I cannot say the same for it at the present time. The idea was that over a period of months when you worked

Supply-Labour
you paid a premium, the same as you paid for the insurance on your home, and then during those months when, because of climatic or change-over conditions, or something of that sort, you were unavoidably out of work, from this insurance policy that you had built up you received enough to keep yourself and your dependants going over that short period of time until you went back to work again. That was the basic principle of unemployment insurance.
Another way in which seasonal unemployment has been attacked successfully, although in a very limited way, is by the institution of the guaranteed annual wage. At one time it was very profitable for certain industries to work only six or eight months of the year. They closed down for the other six months or four months to re-tool, to do some repair work or something of that kind, and they did not care about the men who were laid off for those months; it was no responsibility of the company. Since it was more profitable to operate that way, that is the way it should be done. That is the way our free enterprise economy works.
Some trade unions have been strong enough to acquire across the bargaining table what is known as the guaranteed annual wage by which a company, in addition to the individual, accepts some responsibility for year around employment and year around pay cheque. I think it is a very good principle, Mr. Chairman, because surely with all the facilities, all the brains, ingenuity and ability at the disposal of the company, together with the individual, they can arrive at a much better solution than the individual can when he is left to his own devices. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that these two attacks made on this one cause of unemployment can go a long way toward solving that particular problem. Between the guaranteed annual wage and the unemployment insurance fund the problem of seasonal unemployment can, I think, be licked.
If that was the only problem we had it would not be too bad, but unfortunately it is only one of the three major problems we have. As time goes on we find that we have two other major ones as well. The second one is that of automation. Machines are taking over jobs formerly done by 20, 50 or 100 men. There are only two possible solutions to this particular problem. There is a bad solution and a good solution. The bad solution is not to use the machines. We all remember the make work programs we used to have, where a man would pick up a stone here and take it over there and then another man would bring it back again. We had work but we did not accomplish very much. That is the way it would be if we attempted to

hold back the scientific progress that automation is bringing about in our society. But we have to realize that if automation is to bring progress, if it is to benefit mankind, then we have also to take into consideration the problems that automation creates.
That is something that we have not been doing. We have made little dabs here and there. I was very pleased to hear the minister tell us the other day in his announcement to the house that they were increasing the federal contribution to 50 per cent to the provinces which went ahead with some kind of technical training scheme which would retrain workers so that they could fit back into society again. I think that is a very good step and in the right direction, but we have to take a great many steps before we reach our goal sometimes. That is the situation in which we find ourselves today, or else we would not have 300,000, 400,000, 500,000, 600,000, 700,000, 800,000 unemployed every year.
The third major problem of unemployment involves two different fields. I do not know of any better example than the position of the coal mining industry and the uranium mining industry in this country. The end result of both is the same: the eventual shutdown of the industry and a complete shutdown of the employment provided by the industry to many men who have spent their lives in the industry. The uranium industry was much more dramatic because it was much quicker. What took 50 years to happen in the coal mining industry happened in five years in the uranium industry. It was drawn to our attention much more quickly, much more dramatically; it was much more newsworthy, but the end result is the same. Whether it is a uranium miner in Elliot Lake or a coal miner in Alberta, both of them find themselves in exactly the same position. Here again the only solution certainly that we can offer is similar to the one suggested to meet the problems caused by automation.
I say that this problem must be tackled and tackled vigorously because it is not being cured but rather is increasing very rapidly all the time. It is true that bad as things were last winter they were still not quite as bad as they were in 1938 when a Liberal government had been in office for some three years. At that time unemployment reached the highest peak in the history of this country. But if we are to believe the economists, who are almost unanimous in their predictions, unfortunately next winter is going to set a new record in this field.
I was also pleased that after considerable prodding from opposition members, and

I assume and hope from government members as well, the Minister of Public Works announced the other day that as of the beginning of September they are taking the lid off the housing fund. I am glad to see that he is finally following the example of the previous minister who in my opinion almost single-handedly, so far as government action was concerned, was able to turn the tide of recession in 1957. I think that the building program embarked upon by the minister at that time did more than anything else done by this government to prevent what could have been a very much worse recession.
These problems and other related problems are certainly the responsibility of the federal government because they are the only group in the country with the resources at their disposal to meet such problems. Over the past number of years we have had examples of how formerly the Liberal government and now the Conservative government have tried to meet the problems of unemployment. The difficulty has been that they have applied the only remedy they have, unemployment insurance, in an effort to try to cover the waterfront and the result has been disastrous. Unemployment insurance was never designed to cope with the problem raised by automation. It was never designed to meet the problem of closed industries. The result has been twofold. In the first place, in the last three years the fund has been reduced from something over $900 million to approximately $200 million, as I believe I heard the other day, in spite of a substantial increase in premiums.
It is $290 million.

But there is something far more serious which is going to be much harder to cure. While the government has been doing this, while they have been adding weeks to the period of payment of unemployment insurance benefits, they have been building up in the country the old political gimmick involving the idea of something for nothing so that today we are receiving letters from people who say that they have paid into the unemployment insurance fund for ten years and they should get a dividend from it. I have such letters in my office that I can show hon. members, as I am sure many other hon. members have. The people have no idea what the principle of unemployment insurance is at all. They look upon it as something they get from the government not realizing that they are the ones who have paid for it in the first place and the purpose for which they made their payments. I cannot blame people for doing this
Supply-Labour
because certainly there is no insurance principle today in the unemployment insurance fund. All it is today is a sort of glorified welfare fund and everybody in the country from coast to coast is trying to climb on the bandwagon.
There is another very dangerous trend developing in the country, a trend that takes us back to the last time a Conservative government was in power. I refer to the tendency of government members more and more to try to create the impression that the only people who are not working today are those who do not want to work. Many of us can remember all the so-called bums who were wandering across the country from coast to coast in the thirties. I was one of them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Not bums.

I know a number of other hon. members who were in the same boat. They were not able to get work in the places where they were born and because they sought employment elsewhere throughout the country they were chased from town to town by municipal police officers for the sole purpose of getting them out of there before they became a charge on the community and had to be fed, clothed and housed by the community. What happened to all these bums during the forties and fifties? Where did they go?
Apparently the hon. member thinks there are a few of us here.

Very true. Many of them joined the armed forces. Many of them shed their blood for the country, came out of the armed forces, went to work and worked for 15 years, but now things have run their full cycle. I have talked to men who rode the rods during the thirties seeking work from coast to coast and who now find themselves in the same position.
They do not ride the rods today.

No, they do not ride the rods today. We have progressed a little since that time. We have passed social measures so that people do not have to starve today. They can always get enough to keep body and soul together provided they stay in their own community. Possibly that is one of the reasons we have not realized that the situation is almost as bad, if not just as bad, as it was during the thirties. In those days you could starve to death in your home town but today you can always go to the municipal welfare office provided you can establish residence and that you have lived in the community for a year. It may be that in some cases the fact that a man has to

Supply-Labour
remain in the community prevents him from going elsewhere to seek work. Because of this restriction, the social measures we have passed possibly are adding in a small way to the problems today.
We see the same situation raising its ugly head again. Although I hope this is not so, I am afraid that the spreading of the idea that the only people who are out of work are those who do not want to work will increase as time goes on. I have heard hon. members refer to various jobs being available and have seen them produce advertisements to prove it, but what we do not realize is that many of the men who have been thrown out of work are not qualified for the jobs that are available. Furthermore, many of them have the responsibility of a family so that they cannot afford the length of time it would require to take the necessary training in a technical school in order to qualify for these jobs.
That is why I was pleased to see the government take one more little step in the right direction but I think they should take a much bigger step because in view of the facilities the government has at its disposal, whereby it is able to ascertain in the first place what jobs are available and where the surplus of manpower is, the government, if it has the will and desire, should be able to do much more about the problem.
I should like to refer to what happened just after the last war. We had over a million men in uniform, many of whom had never worked a day in their lives as civilians. They had either been out of work from the time they left school until they joined the forces or they joined the forces directly on leaving school. What did we do? We made training available to these men so they would be better qualified to fit into society again. If they were married and had families we made sure that they had enough to keep their families going while they accepted this training, whether it was university, technical or whatever training they took. I would say, Mr. Chairman, that was one of the best things we ever did because we not only helped those individuals but, as a result of this training, they were better qualified when they went back into society and they were more of an asset to this country.
I would say this was the method by which we should approach the unemployment problem today. All we have had in the past from governments in relation to this problem has been a little dab here, a little dab there and a little dab some place else. It has been something like feeding a headache pill to someone suffering from a brain tumour. Sure,

the headache is stopped for a while, but we do not cure the condition; we just postpone the inevitable. That is exactly what we have been doing in regard to unemployment over the years.
I believe it is a fair thing to say, Mr. Chairman, that during the past two years we have never had less than one quarter of a million unemployed. We have had as high as three quarters of a million. As I mentioned before, economists have been predicting that the unemployed could amount to over a million this year. I cannot see any sense in a society which since the war has spent $20 billion on obsolete defence to defeat communism, yet still permits a million unemployed in this country which breeds communism. If the communists ever get a start in this country it will be because of unemployment, and not because they came in from the outside. I should like to back up that statement by asking when communism was at its strongest point in this country? It was back during the thirties and early forties.

I say that this government has a responsibility to all the citizens of this country to ensure that the actions they take are going to be in the interests of all the people of this country and not just in the interests of a few selfish individuals.

On the local level, I vigorously protest the new delay on the part of the unemployment insurance commission in dealing with the dispute between 369 workers of the Dominion Textile of Sherbrooke and the

commission. I shall read a statement published on July 8 last by the workers union of the Dominion Textile of Sherbrooke:
The employees of the Dominion Textile in Sherbrooke heard to their great surprise and dismay that consideration in respect of the right to unemployment insurance benefits of the 369 employees who were dismissed on November 6, 1959, will only be taken up three weeks from now by the arbitration board in Sherbrooke.
Considering that annual leave for workers in that company is to be taken in the last two weeks of July, it is rather difficult to expect the hearing before that board to take place before early in August.
Considering that the case of those 369 employees has been up for hearing since early November 1959, it	is high	time that public opinion	bearoused and informed of the policy and attitude of some officials in the unemployment insurance commission with regard to the claimants who have been unemployed for the greater part of last winter without receiving any benefits (from November 6, 1959 to	February	27, 1960),	and who are	stillwaiting	for a final decision	to be rendered	by
which they would be declared eligible for unemployment insurance benefits.
Having been laid off on November 6, 1959 by the Dominion Textile plant in Sherbrooke, those 369 employees went to the unemployment insurance office, during the following week, to fill out their claim forms. On	November	19, they were	disqualified by the local unemployment insurance official.
The union representing those employees lodged an appeal with the arbitration board in Sherbrooke (of which Mr. Antonio Pinard is chairman). The arbitration board having considered the whole case with much attention and having rendered on December 21, 1959, a unanimous decision which was. in every respect, favourable to the employees concerned, the said local official appealed that unanimous decision before the single arbitrator in Ottawa on January 6, 1960. The arbitrator's hearing was held in Montreal on March 16, and his decision rendered on May 27, 1960.
During the hearing, the attorney of the commission submitted copies of newspapers, claiming this constituted new evidence. All actions or representations by the representative of commission employees only had the effect of beclouding the issue and confusing the arbitrator.
As a result the said arbitrator referred the new evidence to the local board of arbitration for consideration, so that a new hearing might be held on the matter in dispute and a decision rendered on the point at issue before the single arbitrator made a final ruling on the whole matter.
The Sherbrooke board of arbitration has been ready to hear this case since early June, but has been unable to sit because it is still waiting for the file on the investigation conducted by the regional officer, which is not yet ready after over two months' delay.
In view of such useless delays and abusive procedures on the part of certain representatives of the unemployment insurance commission, the executive of the Association des Employes du Textile de Sherbrooke Inc., on behalf of its members, strongly and publicly protests the inconceivable attitude of some officials who seem to be resorting to a method that can only be used by a public authority or by a party without financial responsibility for the costs of a case, and with little regard for the hardship sustained by employees who have been laid off and have been waiting to receive their benefits for over eight (8) long months. The employees are not asking for charity, they are merely demanding their rights, which

Hear, hear.
Again, I thank you-who, as I say, has acquired much experience in the field of labour and I know he means well.

At present, unemployment stands at a dangerous level for this time of year. We can expect an extremely serious situation when the cold season comes around.

Unemployment insurance applicants reached 296,400 on June 30. This is 35 per cent more than the 220,500 registered applicants on June 30, 1959.
A 35 per cent increase. And farther on, the bulletin reads:
More than 75 per cent of the increase over last year applies to male workers, and 70 per cent of them were in Ontario and Quebec.

I recognize that that may be true, I am no expert in the field of textiles; there is no textile industry in this area, and I have not studied the subject. Moreover, in view of the fact that the hon. member has been reading from a report which seems to be genuine, I accept it as I accept his word. I would add, however, that if previous governments did certain things that should have been corrected, that does not absolve the present government from taking its full responsibilities. That, as I say, is my present position, and I can assure the hon. member-

And that of the previous
government.

speechtext: Order. (Translation):

I will say to the hon. member that I try to live in the present, not in the past. I try to look to the future, because, being of a Liberal frame of mind, I cannot live in the past as do the Conservatives.

So far, what action has been taken in that field, Mr. Chairman? Once again, thank you for the applause. But the problem requires very much more than those small remedies. We must look much farther; besides, this is not what our hon. friends opposite were saying or thinking at the time they sat in the opposition. In fact, I would like to indicate with the help of Hansard, what the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) said in 1955 as found at page 2261 of Hansard:
In the midst of abundance, in the midst of surpluses, in the midst of evidences of prosperity this ugly fact of unemployment continues.
Well, Mr. Chairman, this ugly fact of unemployment continues. While government members talk about prosperity, that ugly fact of unemployment not only continues but grows worse. And there are those who claim that the government which had promised to right all wrongs, to improve everything, to change everything, is doing what it should do under the circumstances.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
I accept questions from certain members, but I know the others, and I do not accept anything from them.
Write to Mr. Antonio Barrette.
You cannot answer.
Mr. Chairman, I feel I am entitled to be a bit contemptuous.
Of you?

Then I find at page 3396 of Hansard of May 3, 1955 what the present Minister of Finance said when he sat on this side of the house:
The second problem which has been ignored by the government is the problem of unemployment. This problem has been discussed at length in this session-
