He said:
-or I would seek to go into it at greater length today. But let me content myself, in this limited time, with making this limited observation on the subject, that the government throughout this session has observed a conspiracy of silence in regard to unemployment-
Were we not faced with the very same situation? We have put questions time and again, and the hon. member for Essex East did not let a week go by without asking the minister for information not only on the unemployment situation but also on what the government had in mind to meet the situation. All we got were evasive answers. We were not supplied with the documents which would have enabled us to study the situation. Why? It is precisely because on the other side of this house they realized that nothing substantial had been done to relieve unemployment.
I have another quotation, this one from the Prime Minister. When he was on this side of the house, in 1955, the Prime Minister said, as reported on page 3612 of Hansard:
At the beginning I am just going to say a word in regard to employment. Strangely enough, there has been no serious answer from the government regarding the unemployment problem that still fills the hearts of many Canadians, no answer whatever as to what is to be done now by the government, except a speech by the Prime Minister at the dominion-provincial conference-
How like today.
-as to what is to be expected at a further meeting to take place this coming fall between the federal and provincial authorities.
Again a striking similarity.
Indeed, the great and abiding principles that were to bring about a new millennium in dominion and provincial relations now have been embalmed in the records of history.
Isn't that just like the meeting which took place this year. Provincial premiers wanted to discuss that unemployment matter which is of concern to everybody; but instead of dealing with unemployment, they talked about bringing back the constitution to Canada. Nobody dared tackle that matter. They tried to embalm the whole matter so people would forget about it. Believe me, Mr. Chairman, people are suffering at present and cannot forget this vital matter.
Mr. Chairman, I still have another quotation, but it is the last one. This is a statement made by the Minister of Finance at the time when he was concerned with unemployment. He seems to have forgotten about it since then. He is so busy trying to avoid deficits. As reported on page 2261 of Hansard of 1955, he stated this:
There are people In Canada today who are going hungry as a result of unemployment. There

Supply-Labour
are ruptures in family life that are occurring day by day as a result of unemployment. In the great urban centres where unemployment is acute it is the experience of all those connected with welfare, church or philanthropic work in any capacity, that men are deserting their families deliberately because that is the only way in which their families can qualify for relief assistance.
The same situation exists today, the same which was described by the Minister of Finance when he was on this side of the house. This is exactly what we have today.
I maintain that the government has failed to do its duty, in a fair way, in a way consistent with the seriousness of the situation. It may be still time for the government to take action. Therefore, I ask the minister to urge other cabinet members to look around and realize the seriousness of the situation. The minister if not in this house, at least in his own office, certainly heard, some members of his party complaining of the seriousness of the situation. I do not blame them for not mentioning it in the house because they are "party men", but they are always complaining because they have to admit that the government is making no effort to improve conditions.
Earlier today, a certain member asked me what the government of the province of Quebec did with regard to unemployment. I was just about to mention it.
There are two kinds of unemployment: seasonal unemployment, and almost permanent unemployment, which is caused by automation, by machines replacing man. Well, I am among those who believe that each of the two governments has its part of responsibility. The provincial government has a certain responsibility, and so has the federal government. But the larger part of responsibility is that of the central body. It is up to this government to bring relief to the jobless and to give him work at a time when he is unemployed. The utmost will have to be done in order to prevent those people from suffering hardship; and yet, nothing seems to be done at this time.
On the other hand, I maintain that it is the responsibility of the provincial government to try and increase the setting up within its boundaries of a variety of industries, so as to be able to supply the people with jobs. May I be allowed to suggest that the government consider the proposal made to the Americans in 1920 by the Hon. Mr. Gouin when he told them: "You want to use our forests, etc.; in that case, come and set up your industries in our country." It was at that time that the International Paper emerged which established itself here, as well as the Anglo pulp and paper company. Besides,

those industries gave rise to the magnificent town of Gatineau, in my constituency.
That suggestion came to us from the Gouin government in 1920. We hope the provincial government will find the means of solving the unemployment problem. But while the provincial government is considering the situation, it is the responsibility of the federal government to see to it that people do not suffer from the hardships brought about by unemployment. It must see to it that families have something to feed, house, clothe and warm themselves in winter. That is the immediate responsibility of the federal government, because it is the one that has the greater source of income; its responsibility is the most complete, total and immediate.
Mr. Chairman, I regret that time is flying so fast, because I would have liked to deal perhaps a little longer with the dilapidation of the unemployment insurance fund.
When the Conservative party came into power in 1957, the unemployment insurance fund had accumulated about $900 million to provide for difficult years.
Today, we hear from the minister, according to the latest figures he gave us, that the fund has now gone down to $296 million. If that situation is allowed to continue, the fund will go down substantially, because each month, according to statistics, there is a decrease of $26,800,000. So, if we take off, at one stroke, $26 million from those $296 million, only $270 million are left.
And if this situation should continue, it will become worse next fall and winter and it will mean that the unemployment insurance fund will be totally depleted next winter.
What did the minister provide? What did the government provide to replenish this unemployment insurance fund which is essential to continue to help the unemployed?
This very year, despite the fact that last year, the house raised the payments into the unemployment insurance fund by $78 million through increases in the contributions of workers and employers, the government should have asked the house to vote $300 or $400 million to replenish the fund. But nothing was done. Why? Is it because they fear a deficit?
We have said this in the past, and I repeat it: we think it is quite proper for the government to run up a deficit to alleviate the people's hardship, to bring about social improvement or to prevent human suffering. But when the government does nothing and in spite of that, runs into expenses which might be avoided, I think it is wrong.

Mr. Chairman, this morning I had the visit of a number of my constituents. Never have I had so many calls from heads of families who are in need.
I even had a man crying in my office this morning over the problems he is faced with. That man told me he has been looking for a job for six months, without success. He is reduced to begging. He has no money. As he is reluctant to beg, I had to get in touch with the welfare service in the city of Hull to find out whether they could look after him. That man cried in my office, and you know, Mr. Chairman, how sad it is to see a man cry. Now that is not a unique situation; there are many similar cases, so I should like to close my remarks with this simple quotation-
Mr. Chairman, has my speaking time expired?
(Text):
Will the hon. member permit an interruption? I would appreciate it very much if the hon. member would give me the name and the address of this person. I think I can do something for him.
I certainly will do so and I thank the minister for making that offer.
What is his name?

Mr. Chairman, I feel that was not a question; it was a statement. Before getting into the substance of my remarks this evening-
Give us the time and place.

-I should like to say that this is the tactic that hon. members to my right often employ. Every time we bring in a measure to help the employment situation they say it is nothing and they try to indicate to the people of Canada that this is the only measure with which we are facing the employment situation. Such is never the case. To summarize very briefly, may I say that we have heard speech after speech in the House of Commons by the Minister of Labour indicating that the government has enacted sound measures based on basic Progressive Conservative doctrine; measures which recognize the dignity of the individual, measures which are designed to encourage activity on the local level, measures, I repeat, which in short are in complete accord with the basic doctrines of the party I support. These are the measures, housing-
Oh, oh.

I ask hon. members to my right, will the recent announcement in relation to housing not stimulate employment and the economy? Of course it will. But hon. members laugh. The leader of the C.C.F. party or new party has just laughed, Mr. Chairman. I suggest that he laugh in front of the people who will be employed because of these measures. The Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister announced recently, and earlier this year, an expanded winter works program, a program which, according to the principles of our party, will be enacted on the local level. I remember what the hon.

Supply-Labour
member for Port Arthur said when I spoke last year on a similar occasion and reported the fact that I hoped that in some way I had helped to put this program over in my own area. We all know that the hon. member for Port Arthur has some very funny theories in relation to the functions of a member of parliament. At any rate he accused me of usurping the functions of civil servants. Such was not the case.
I suggest, that the winter works program is a program toward which every member of parliament can take a bipartisan attitude. It is a program designed to stimulate winter employment on the local level and I feel that every member of parliament on both sides of the house has a responsibility to help to put the program over in his or her respective area.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Would he explain where the C.C.F. comes in in a bipartisan program?
You cannot tell the difference between the Liberals and the C.C.F.

I should like to say to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that any problem regarding employment demands bipartisanship, even from the C.C.F. Then we have the measure announced by the Minister of Labour providing increased funds for the education of unemployed people. We also have the increased emphasis that is being put on the national placement service by the Minister of Labour. Every hon. member of the house must recognize the fact that since the government has come to power-
We have had disaster.

-workers from one end of
the country to the other realize the efforts that are being made through the national placement service offices to place men in jobs.
Unfortunately that is true.
Apple polisher.

I could go on to say that these measures are not a cure-all, but in the face of that record, which is not a cure-all, I think opposition members are being most irresponsible, as was the hon. member for Hull, when they say that the present government is not vitally concerned and is not acting in a real way in the face of the present situation.
Hear, hear.
Negative and passive.

I should like to say that the hon. member for Essex East in his usual fashion, with plenty of thunder and fury- in fact I think it was William Shakespeare who said, "Much sound and fury signifying nothing"-made one good suggestion and I will refer to it later. But what in fact did the hon. member for Essex East propose in his speech? In essence the hon. member has demanded a conference to study unemployment.
I demanded action.

In his usual way he tried in his speech to convince the house that the government has attempted in some unknown fashion to stifle debate on the employment situation. Time and time again he said that the house was denied an opportunity to discuss the unemployment situation. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, what are we having now if it is not an opportunity to discuss the unemployment situation?
In the last days of the session.

Just five minutes ago we heard the hon. member for Hull say that the unemployment or employment situation had been discussed often in the House of Commons. Who is right? I suggest that there has been a lot of debate in the house as to who is responsible for unemployment. Frankly, I am not interested in these detailed niceties. I can say one thing-
What about the Prime Minister on January 20, 1958?

-that a man who is out of work is not interested in who is responsible, the municipal, provincial or federal authorities. He is interested in finding a job. I am not going to get into these detailed arguments. I should like to inform the hon. member for Hull that during the last Quebec provincial election campaign the new premier of the province said that unemployment was entirely a provincial responsibility.
Where is the quotation?
I frankly do not agree with this but he said it nevertheless in a burst of political enthusiasm.	.
Would the hon. gentleman tell us where and when he said it? That statement is untrue and the hon. member knows it.
I often wonder, Mr. Chairman-
We know it is untrue because it was made by the premier of the province of Quebec.

I have been asked so many questions that I am only going to answer them very briefly. Before I answer them I should like to say this, and it is a very interesting point. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order; I shall have to ask the hon. member to come back to the subject under discussion.
Supply-Labour

In answer to the question posed to me by the hon. member for Essex East, may I say that I have in my hand a copy of a full page advertisement in Le Devoir, Montreal, dated Tuesday, May 10, 1960, concerning the problem of unemployment. It reads:
(Translation):
The Liberal solution:
1. To consider unemployment as a family problem and a provincial responsibility.
(Text):
Was that statement made by the premier of Quebec?

On May 17, 1960 Le Devoir reports, and I am translating the article:
St. Joseph d'Alma: The leader of the provincial Liberal party, Mr. Jean Lesage, promised Sunday that his government will tackle the problem of unemployment not by "reverting to the system of direct relief"-
Oh, oh.
You are reading the wrong quotation.
Read it all.
Go ahead.

I continue reading:
-not by "reverting to the system of direct relief", founded by the Conservatives in 1931 under Mr. Bennett, as it has just been promised by the leader of the Union Nationale-Mr. Barrette -at Granby, but by a planned economic development of the province and by tactical training of workers at home ...
It is further reported that Mr. Lesage observed that Mr. Barrette had, nevertheless, recognized that the provincial authorities have their responsibility in the solution of the unemployment problem.
Oh, oh.

I want to revert to the original point I tried to make, and that is that the man out of work is not really interested in the niceties of who is responsible for finding him employment. It is for this reason I reiterate time and time again in this house, that I feel the problem of employment or unemployment is a problem that often demands a bipartisan approach from hon. members. It is for this reason, that so many of the utterances of the hon. member for Essex East in this chamber ring hollowly in my ears.
I can say this, as well, that we must recognize the government is taking active measures in the face of the present situation.
Name them.
As I have already mentioned, the hon. member for Essex East had many suggestions to make.

Hear, hear.

Supply-Labour
However, I ask him this one question. Over and above the fact that he demanded that we initiate a grandiose conference to discuss the problem, what concrete measure was proposed-
The hon. member has asked me a question.
I am not interested in what-[DOT]

Order.
The Depuly Chairman: Order; the hon. member for Essex East has the floor.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The hon. gentleman has asked me a question.
No, no.
He has asked me a question.
He knows he would not get an answer.

Are you afraid of the answer?
The Depuly Chairman: Order; once again I must remind hon. members that we cannot have more than one speaker at a time. The hon. member for Essex East was asked a question. I must remind hon. members that they cannot interrupt the hon. member who has the floor unless he permits a question to be asked.
The hon. gentleman for whom I have a deep affection, asked me a question-
No, no.

Unless it was a rhetorical question and not meant to be answered I shall be glad to deal with it if the hon. gentleman wishes me to do so.
The Depuly Chairman: That is not a point of order.
In point of fact, I was asking myself a rhetorical question. I have put on the record this evening some of the active measures, undeniably active measures that have been taken by this government.
What are they?

I am not going to say these are a cure-all; I am not for a minute going to suggest that employment or unemployment, as such, is not a problem, but I am going to suggest that active measures have been taken and more active measures will be taken. I am going to suggest that the people of Canada are not interested in the constitutional niceties relating to the role of the opposition.
Oh, no?

I am going to say that at times it would be nice to hear a constructive suggestion from the opposition in a field as important as this. I believe it is irresponsible partisanship to suggest for one minute that the problem of employment has not been given full discussion in this house since we convened here in January.
Another point with which I feel we must deal is the sort of straw man that deserves to be burned as quickly as possible. Hon. members opposite have suggested that the premier of the province of Quebec made a statement in relation to the unemployment problem, and that it may have been discussed in camera during the recent dominion-provincial meetings. The Prime Minister was attacked for not making a statement with regard to what was discussed in this conference recently. Hon. members opposite well know that no statement, either from provincial premiers or the Prime Minister, could be made in relation to those meetings that were held in camera, so I feel this is just another instance of partisan bickering and hollow hankering over an important issue that merits better attention. Everyone here knows that the Prime Minister or the provincial premiers cannot make statements regarding meetings that supposedly have been held in camera.
This is the type of responsible debate for which I make a plea this evening in relation to the problem of employment. I refer to the type of responsible debate that merits the bipartisan consideration of every hon. member. I may say frankly that I do not think the average working man in Canada, when he finds a job, is interested in knowing whether it is supplied to him by a Liberal administration or a Conservative administration or whether it is supplied by a municipal, provincial or federal government. He wants to find a job. I think that is the attitude that we should all take.
Without carrying on much longer there are just a few more things I have in my mind before terminating my present remarks. Like every other hon. member in this house, I have naturally devoted some serious attention to this problem. I cannot help but think of some possible long term national objectives that we might have in relation to the problem of employment. I am not going to suggest any cure-all; they are not perhaps even suggestions. They are merely thoughts, Mr. Chairman. I often wonder how much immigration, for instance, over the next ten years we should have, and what kind of immigration we should have over the next ten years, taking into consideration the expected natural birth increase, in order best to develop the Canadian economy at an

optimum level. These questions are the sort that I think we should ask ourselves about long term national objectives.
What is the hon. gentleman doing about it?

1 heard another facetious remark by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, Mr. Chairman. I suggest that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate place before us in all sincerity what he believes is the best idea. After all, what is this forum except a place for offering what we hope are constructive ideas. If, when I offer suggestions in a true spirit of trying to be helpful, I wonder why my remarks evoke facetious interjections from some hon. members opposite.
I should like to say that I am a supporter of the government and that it allows its backbenchers to speak frankly. We are not under the dictates of any C. D. Howe. I realize that while I am speaking of long term national objectives, I am expanding this debate in a broad fashion. While the Minister of Labour is often seemingly responsible in the narrow sense for statistics that hon. members opposite throw at him, unemployment statistics depend, as we all know, on the economy at large. I therefore go on with other thoughts. I have heard it suggested that expanded trade will help our economic and thus our employment situation.
I should like to suggest to all the businessmen in Canada that under the aegis of the Department of Trade and Commerce we have trade commissioners who are second to none in the world. I feel we should make even further use of them than we are. While the government can take the lead, I feel that private enterprise can help by availing itself of the real facilities of, I repeat again, one of the finest trade commissions in the world.
Then it has been suggested that under the Department of Trade and Commerce some time in the future we might have a revolving export credit fund which in the initial stages might involve $50 million. These are things that all hon. members must look upon at some time in the future with the hope that they will help our economy and thus in turn our employment situation.
Another thing is this. Many of my confreres realize that I whip this matter a good deal but I feel that both government and private enterprise should strees the simple general notion of what I call "Buy Canadian". I do not think you can hope or feel that the housewife on the retail level in the stores can differentiate or would want to differentiate between Canadian made goods and foreign made goods. Once they
Supply-Labour
have reached the retail level, I think it is too late. But I think both the government and private enterprise should initiate and support what I call a "Buy Canadian" policy.
I know that there seems to be a feeling abroad in Canada that because something is imported it has an aura of perhaps snobbery about it. I think a great many good things are made here in Canada by Canadians for Canadians. I look forward to the day when we can increasingly encourage the situation. The government has already taken a great lead in this matter. I feel that more is going to be done and that more will be done by private enterprise, enterprise that is always stimulated and helped by Progressive Conservative doctrines and principles.
I know that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, as he has done in the past, will perhaps accuse me now of entering into the classical field of high or low tariffs. I am not doing that. I have been one who has always said that we should take a close look at our dumping regulations. I am pleased that the Minister of National Revenue has appointed officers to police more closely the dumping regulations vis-a-vis Canada and outside powers. These are regulations that must be strictly enforced, not only in relation to the textile industry so ably touched upon by the hon. member for Sherbrooke but in relation to many other Canadian goods. Perhaps we shall be obliged to take a more serious look at our position in GATT.
Mr. Chairman, I have been broad in my remarks tonight but these are all things that affect our economy and in turn affect our employment position. They are just a few superficial highlights that I felt might merit attention at this time. I would suggest to some hon. members alongside me that rather than trying day in and day out to make a political football of the employment or the unemployment situation it is time to stop this sort of thing. I know we all like a little bit of infighting now and again but I am sure the people must say at times, "Enough is enough".
The Minister of Labour in these past months during this session and between sessions has posed many problems in relation to the employment situation. He has said time and time again that this government is seriously concerned about it and is taking serious action. I repeat myself. But let us realize one thing and in saying this I hope I am not going to be misunderstood for making these remarks. In my opinion there is such a thing as statistical unemployment. Whether we are taking the unemployment insurance statistics, the national placement service or dominion bureau of statistics statistics or the Martin bureau of statistics;

Supply-Labour
no matter what statistics we are taking, we must take a good look at them.
Especially at the last ones.

I think every Canadian should realize that we have many social welfare measures today, especially since this government has come to power, in that we have extended unemployment insurance benefits. We have social welfare benefits, as well we might, that will never allow anything to happen such as that which happened in the depression days of the thirties. However, Mr. Chairman, I think we must be careful when we are dealing with what I call the problem of statistical unemployment for when statistics are irresponsibly used there is created, not only a lack of confidence on questions of domestic concern but also a lack of confidence among our neighbours to the south and among far away powers. No member of parliament is doing any service to his country or even to his party in the long run when he irresponsibly quotes or reiterates in this house or outside this house statistics that he knows are basically not correct.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Does he think that was equally true between 1953 and 1957?
Who is living in the past?
I know that hon. members in my party whether in power or out of power, have always been most responsible in their use of statistics.
Page the Minister of Labour.

I think perhaps the minister might refer to this matter in his remarks but as I understand it the dominion bureau of statistics samplings are taken from one end of this country to the other. No matter how accurate the samplings are as such in their initial stages I also understand that on these matters the only possible information that can be put down is whether or not the man was in or out of work during the preceding week when he was interviewed.
I might be wrong here, but I think with just those facts alone we realize we are dealing with a very serious problem. In other words, everybody is aware of the fact that we should not for political reasons try and build up what I refer to as statistical unemployment. Certainly there is unemployment and it must be dealt with seriously, but I feel these are statistics which must be dealt

with seriously too. I repeat time and time again that it is not serving our country well when they are irresponsibly used either on the home front or abroad.
In summary, I have felt obliged to refute some of the straw men put up before this House of Commons by members opposite. Second, I have tried my best to outline some of the vigorous measures introduced by the government. They are not cure-alls, not the complete answer; and do not let hon. members alongside ever go to the people of Canada and try and tell them we said any one of them is. The hon. member for Essex East has called our winter works program a mere bagatelle, and this from a member of a government which in 1954 and 1955 told the municipalities that nothing could be done for them. Nevertheless, these measures by themselves are not cure-alls. Taken in toto maybe they are not cure-alls either, but they are certainly a step forward in relation to a problem which must be met and is being met.
I have outlined these measures and made what I hope are at best some helpful suggestions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to inform the hon. member that his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, notwithstanding the fact that the hon. gentleman's time has expired, I wonder if I might be permitted to ask him one question. Can I ask the hon. gentleman if he recalls that in the year 1955 the Liberal government assumed half the cost of unemployment assistance to help the municipalities, notwithstanding the fact that he said we did nothing for them?

Mr. Chairman, members of the committee seem to be in a rather peculiar mood tonight, and one hardly knows what kind of reception one will get. But I do know that we all enjoyed the tour de force of the previous speaker and that his remarks will be a great deal relished when they appear in the press and in Hansard tomorrow.
As a matter of fact, I think there is only one thing wrong with what the hon. member had to say, and that is that it is not going to pay the rent or buy the food or the clothing of the unemployed in Canada today.
The hon. member in his closing remarks said quite a bit about statistics. Good, bad or indifferent, I do not know, but I am afraid that what is happening today as far as the government is concerned is that they are trying to reduce unemployment to a statistic. We hear more talk and more arguments about statistics and whether they are right or wrong than I think we do about the actual question of unemployment itself. That is the

problem, the real fundamental problem, which we have the responsibility of dealing with, not one set of statistics compared to another or whether it is 300,000 or 325,000. It is the problem of unemployment and there is a great deal of it in Canada today.
I feel all of us are concerned with the fact that unemployment in Canada seems to be a perennial and an increasing problem. It is quite all right for hon. members to get up and say that you should not say this, you should not say that, and do not bring that up because it is dangerous to Canada and to countries outside. The real danger is in refusing to face realism, refusing to face facts and refusing to try and work out some plan to handle the problem.
We would be betraying our country if because it may be a little bit unpopular or obnoxious to certain people we were to say the problem does not exist; if we were to close our eyes and say the problem is not there. That may be the attitude of some hon. members but I do not think it is the attitude of the majority. We must be concerned when we pick up our newspapers and read such statements as this, which is taken from the Toronto Star of April 30:
With unemployment figures steadily mounting, many economists and business leaders feel the time has come for a long range look at the problem ...
A cross section of economists and business experts, applying their statistical stethoscopes to Canada's body economic, come up with this general report:
This summer: A substantial boom.
Next fall: A down-turn in the economy.
Next winter: Unemployment worse than this year.
The winter after: A post-war peak of unemployment.
When some of the chief economists and business men of Canada give that general analysis, when we hear from the provinces and our constituencies, and when we get the statistics from the Minister of Labour about this problem, I say we have got to try to face up to the situation and see what can be done now in order to offset any possibility of an increasing tempo of unemployment.
I am not going to go into any long harangue on the details and the broad general picture; that can be done by others. I want to concentrate for a few minutes on the question of the problem of unemployment as it is now being brought to bear through the medium of automation.
I was very grateful to the Minister of Labour this afternoon when he reported on the research studies undertaken in his department on the question of automation. That is something which is inevitable but it is a problem we have got to face up to now if we are going to be able to offset the conditions which new technologies and efficiencies will bring about in this field. If we do not face 79951-11-453
Supply-Labour
up to it, then I say we are being irresponsible as elected members of the people of the country.
I would just like to give a couple of examples as to how automation is operating. Only this week I received a communication from the oil, chemical and atomic workers international union in Vancouver which pointed out that in the 18 months ending May 31 of this year 150 hourly paid jobs had been eliminated through automation in refineries in the Vancouver area. In addition to 150 hourly paid jobs being eliminated through automation, approximately as many staff jobs were also eliminated. So here is a process in the refining industry of my own city of Vancouver which, according to the union affected, has created unemployment for 300 men owing to automation in the industry. I am also informed that the workers who are still employed have been notified that there are going to be more lay-offs yet as they increase efficiency by putting in new automation machines.
That is just one example and I would like to give just one more, because I think it is well known to the Minister of Labour and to the majority of the members of this committee because of the fact that there was a delegation here not so long ago from the united steel workers of America who were representing the employees of English Electric Company at St. Catharines where because of the need for greater efficiency from the company's point of view and because of automation we have the closing of the English Electric plant in St. Catharines.
There have been employed there until recently according to my information approximately 500 employees. As a result of the closing of this plant and the consolidation of the operations in Toronto only 160 of the 500 employees are being invited to sell out at St. Catharines and take employment in Toronto. I understand that the average age of these 500 employees is 53. Nearly one quarter of them are 50 years of age or over and the average length of service of the employees is 16 years. I understand that 80 per cent of the employees are home owners in the St. Catharines area and one third of the homeowners own homes which they value at more than $10,000. In addition, the average number of dependents is 2.26. This means that about 1,000 people are being affected by automation, the need for greater efficiency, the closing down of a plant and its moving to Toronto.
This is not a rare instance. This is happening more and more often and in the new technology it is going to happen more and more often in the future and we have to

Supply-Labour
face up to it. It is inevitable. You cannot hold back styles and new methods. But the people must be taken care of. We cannot take care of the people affected in this way by just expressing pious hopes and saying we are giving continuous study to the matter. Excellent as may be the research work being done in the minister's department and marvellous as undoubtedly are the reports the hon. gentleman receives, we have reached the stage where we should get down to planning; we must get down to something definite with regard to meeting the situation, and I feel that this is where the government has fallen down up to the present time.
The government has failed to demonstrate to me that they are taking a sufficiently serious attitude toward this phase of the unemployment problem or that they recognize that this difficult situation must be met by distinct policies. I feel that if action is not taken we may get into a worse situation still. Though I appreciate what the minister had to say on the studies on automation which are being carried out I should like him to go further and tell us what practical steps the government has in mind.
We are faced with the need to evolve practical plans to handle the situation. If labour and industry do not get together and reach agreement about the way in which this problem is to be met, then it becomes the duty of the government to take a definite stand and bring in definite policies and even special legislation if required. I have heard it said that when this matter was brought to the attention of the government some time ago-the concentration of industry, the closing down of plants in the smaller towns and so on-the government expressed an understanding of the situation but said it had no power to deal with it.
I feel it is necessary for us to get away from this increasing concentration of industry in a few centres. Decentralization of industry is necessary. Plants must be encouraged to continue their operations in centres which depend upon them, and if necessary assistance should be given to these undertakings to stay where they are, to stay where the homes of their employees have been built and where they have earned their livelihood for years and years. I think we need a more satisfactory and a more militant declaration of government policy in this regard. Canada will not reach its real maturity and potential until, by legislation if necessary, we have decentralization of industry, not only within provinces but throughout Canada.
I believe that when there is notice of approaching automation, whether it affects 400

employees, as in the case of the electric company which I have mentioned in some detail or in the case of the refineries in British Columbia where 300 people have been affected in the last three months, the government should take the initiative, if the industry declines to do so, and say: You have got to start planning; if this move is required, then fine, but you have got to plan now, either to bring a new industry in or to take care of these people; if you cannot take these people with you you have got to have a system of portable pensions. This is the sort of thing which has to be planned before the effect of automation comes into being.
I have only one plea, and that is that we do not ask ourselves rhetorical questions as the previous speaker said he was doing but that we face the realities of the situation, that we face up to the inevitability of evolution and recognize that nothing is here forever. The only thing that is constant is change. I say that we have passed the planning stage. We have reached the policy making stage and in the very near future we shall reach the point at which action must be taken with regard to this particular phase of the unemployment problem to which I have confined my remarks this evening. Let us all, irrespective of party, instead of continually looking at the past, start looking at the future.

Mr. Chairman, I should not want to delay the passage of the estimates of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), but I feel it is my duty to speak in order to correct certain misstatements or to disprove some irresponsible statements made in this house.
I listened to the remarks made earlier by the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) and I was greatly surprised to realize that members did not break out in tears on hearing the heart-rending description he gave of the situation. He exerted himself to make us believe that the present situation, and especially in the field of textiles, was an exclusive responsibility of the Conservative party. Mr. Chairman, allow me to refer to the official report and to acquaint the house with the true situation. I have here a report of the Primary Textiles Institute, dated July 5, 1960, in which I read the following:
But during the last decade, serious changes in the situation and in the trend of the industry were noticed.
Needless to say that that industry is the textile industry.
A difficult period set in in 1951 and it is continuing. During that time, 23 spinning mills had to close down, which deprived some 2,000 people of employment opportunities.

On the last page of the same report, we find some statistics according to which, from 1935 to 1939, 120 million linear yards of fabric were imported, while in 1956, under the administration of our friends the Liberals, those imports reached 316 million yards.
During that same period, that is from 1935 to 1939, Canadian industry provided for about 71 per cent of domestic consumption, while it provided for only 55 per cent in 1956.
Mr. Chairman, I should like now to call the attention of the house to a statement made by Mr. Laz Peters, chairman of the Canadian Association of Clothing and Textile Manufacturers. As recorded in the minutes of a meeting of the said association, held in April:
Mr. Peters lauded the efforts made by the Canadian government to put a stop to "the immoderate influx of Japanese clothing and textile" which wrought havoc in the Canadian market and inflicted hardships upon thousands of workers.
He said that imports of clothing and textile from Japan had increased from $5 million in 1954 to $26.5 million in 1958. "If it had not been for the determination of the Canadian government authorities in their negotiations with Japan in the last five months, that torrent would have been still more devastating."
And Mr. Peters concluded:
Only voluntary limitation on the part of Japan can stop Canada from inserting restricting clauses in its trade agreements.
We know, Mr. Chairman, that we are ruled by the general agreement on tariffs and trade, which was negotiated by our predecessors and we necessarily have to face a situation which is of their making.
Mr. Chairman, the unemployment problem is not the sole responsibility of the federal government. That was proved a few months ago. And, as further evidence, if I remember rightly, in 1958 the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) stated that unemployment could not be exclusively attributed to the Conservative party.
The settlement of the unemployment issue demands joint action, which concerns all classes of society. Governments, public bodies, and even individuals, have to do their part and try to create as much employment as possible, for without close co-operation from all classes of society, our efforts will be useless.
During the last few months, and I might even say during the past two years, our Liberal friends have bent over backwards trying to proclaim that there was unemployment, to the point of making every worker believe that he was jobless. As a matter of fact, following such baleful propaganda 79951-0-453J
Supply-Labour
by our Liberal friends who resorted to all available media-radio, television, papers and speeches-several of our workers going to work in the morning had a feeling of being also among the unemployed.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that people now are beginning to realize the situation and are taking Liberal claims with a grain of salt.
The hon. member for Hull paid an unusual tribute to the Conservative members of this house. He paid us a tribute we were not expecting from him. He said that all of us or almost all of us had made representations to our ministers in order that steps be taken to put a stop to unemployment. I can assure the hon. member that it is so, because in the Conservative party it is not only the front line people, the ministers, who express their opinions, but also the backbenchers; and our ministers listen to us, contrary to what used to be the rule in the past.
Everyone recognizes that there are weak points in the Canadian economy. The present Minister of Labour and the other ministers recognize the fact, and all of us are endeavouring to take steps so that there may only be a minimum number of unemployed in Canada. Unfortunately, there are problems that we cannot solve and it has not been possible to this government, in a period of three years, to make up for all the inaction and the lack of foresight that our predecessors have shown during the years they have been in power.
They take pleasure in saying that, in the last war, Canada has experienced an unprecedented period of prosperity, but they hide the fact that in 1936, 1937 and 1938, and even in 1939, the number of unemployed in relation to the population, was much higher than it is now. They hide this information because they believe they can continue to mislead the papulation and that the people will continue to believe them.
Mr. Chairman, before I resume my seat, I would like to emphasize two points from those facts. First, there are more jobs now in Canada than ever before.
And more unemployment.

Second, this Conservative
government has taken the necessary steps, has made huge sums available to the unemployment insurance fund in order to alleviate the difficulties of the workers who, unfortunately, though nobody wants it to be so, are necessarily unemployed for some time.
So, I ask my hon. friends on my right when they make their great statements on the

Supply-Labour
situation, to take those facts into consideration and act accordingly by giving people the information they are entitled to get.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest this afternoon to the minister giving a review of certain studies by his department but I was greatly disappointed that he did not deal with the problem of unemployment as such. 1 think that all of us should be greatly interested in unemployment and should be giving the utmost consideration to putting men back to work. We spent four days on the bill of rights. That bill is very important, but the people in my area are more interested in getting work. The bill of rights has no apparent effect unless they get a job. I think we are getting things a little bit out of focus because, as I said, we spent four days on the bill of rights and we have not spent five minutes in the house on any new government legislation to put one man back to work.
In the Department of Public Works the estimates have been cut by approximately $25 million which is a far cry from the $1| billion which the Prime Minister promised for public works just before the June election in 1958. One man who spoke for the Conservative party in my area thought this was a wonderful thing. He was so entranced by the northern vision that he said he doubted there were enough people in Canada to do the job.
The minister announced that the government would carry on a winter works program on a cost sharing basis with the municipalities. The municipalities are heavily in debt and it is very difficult for many of them to assume more debt at the present high interest rates in order to carry out such projects. The municipalities have had no share in the fiscal policy of the government and I do not think it is fair for the government to call on them to assume more debt at high interest rates in order to help to bail the government out of its mistakes with respect to fiscal policy.
It is true that unemployment was discussed in the house on a motion to go into supply and my leader made some suggestions, as did the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Laurier. I have some 29 suggestions here but I do not think the government has paid much attention to them. At that time they made fun of most of our suggestions and spent their time debating which figures regarding unemployment were right. I have heard much tonight about sta-
[Mr. Ricard.l
tistics but in my area we certainly have unemployed people who are entitled to more consideration than statistics.
I think the time is long overdue for the government to bring measures before members of the house to relieve unemployment. Unemployment is our No. 1 social and economic problem and I think members of parliament should be able to debate some of the proposals which the government must have. I know when the Minister of Labour is asked about anything having to do with unemployment or any measure that might be taken he generally says that this is a matter of government policy and that an announcement will be made in due course. I have heard nothing new. It is true that the government announced a cost sharing winter works program with the municipalities but this is nothing new. They had the same thing last year and it took care of comparatively few of the unemployed.
The hon. member for Essex East referred to a national advisory board and suggested we should have such a board to look into the matter, a board which would keep employment and unemployment under review. I think this is a very good suggestion. For instance, I think it would be very helpful for the government to know how many are out of work because of automation so that they could be able to make proper plans for vocational training. I think it is also necessary to know the number who are registered because of seasonal unemployment and also those who may be unemployed because of shifts of trade and shifts in government policy. We get shifts in government policy because sometimes they are building houses and sometimes they are not. When they are not certainly many men are out of work in my area.
One of the first measures that should be undertaken is a study of our manpower resources. The minister reported in the house some time ago that there was a shortage of certain skilled workers at Elliot Lake. If we had some idea about our manpower resources we would have no difficulty in filling these jobs. I think it is very important that the government should encourage students to stay in school longer than some now do. In my view it is better for our young people to finish their education and to learn different skills before leaving school rather than leaving and adding to the numbers in the unskilled labour market. I think the unemployed could be put to work at this particular time because they are at leisure and not doing anything. I was glad to hear the minister say today that he intended to carry out that program.

Supply-Labour
I heard the hon. member for Essex East say that there was very little unemployment in Australia, western Europe and England. From press reports I have read I know there is a boom in England. I read an article a day or two ago which stated that in western Europe production was up 15 per cent and foreign trade was up 40 per cent. We know that western Germany is importing skilled workers from Italy, Greece, Spain and even from Canada. I understand that in some of the foreign newspapers in Canada there are advertisements for certain skilled workers and I happen to know that two or three German families in my area are returning to Germany. The heads of the households have jobs awaiting them in Germany, and in his particular skill there are more jobs in Germany than there are people to All them. I do not believe it is a very good thing for us in Canada to be losing skilled workers, people who have come to this country and who want to make Canada their home. We are losing them because they cannot get work in this country.
I note that the other place has a committee set up to inquire into unemployment. I heard over the radio this morning that they were sending out a questionnaire. I do not know how much secretarial help the committee of the other place will have, but it seems to me that this is something that should have been pursued by the government itself and not by the other place. It seems to me that also the committee of the other place will not have an adequate staff to deal with all these questionnaires. They might amount to half a million if everyone answers them, but I doubt that everyone will answer them.
I do not believe that a country like Canada can continue year after year with 6 per cent to 8 per cent of its people unemployed in the spring. I am not going to give any figures in connection with the number of unemployed, but I have read that it was as high as 8 per cent, and the year before last it was 6 per cent. I feel that the policy of the government has been one of drift so far as this problem of unemployment is concerned. They have been waiting for something to turn up, and nothing has. The trouble with this government is that they have depended on the unemployment insurance fund. If they did not have that unemployment insurance fund they would be in trouble. If we did not have an unemployment insurance scheme we would have people waiting in breadlines, just as we did in the days of Bennett. Even today, we see people in long lines at the unemployment insurance offices waiting to get their unemployment insurance cheques.
In so far as the unemployment insurance fund is concerned, I was interested in looking at the statement the minister gave which indicated that in the last three years the fund has gone down from $852 million to $296 million. This means it has gone down by $556.5 million, without taking into consideration the depreciation on the bonds in its portfolio. Some people may think this does not amount to very much money, but it amounts to at least $32 for every man, woman and child in Canada and it amounts to $125 for the head of every household in Canada. This represents a cost of running the government. If, as one hon. member suggested earlier, our unemployment is just statistical, why spend so much money out of the unemployment insurance fund? During the years of Liberal administration this fund increased and now it has gone down precipitously, in spite of the increase of nearly 30 per cent in the contributions from employers and employees.
As I have said, this represents a cost of government. When we talk about the operations of the Department of Finance we find that has a lot to do with this particular fund. For instance, in three years the aggregate extra interest we will be obliged to pay will be half a billion dollars, so you can see that the charges on the unemployment insurance fund and the extra interest of the Department of Finance will amount to about $250 for every family in Canada. I believe this is an indictment of a government which said it would not raise taxes and yet, ever since coming into office, it has steadily gone into debt, as well as taking more money from all Canadians in taxes.
One of the difficulties in which the unemployment insurance commission finds itself is that it has taken on long term bonds. We know that in Canada during the last two years it has been better to hold short term bonds. The result of the way our fiscal policy has been handled has been that we have had two markets for bonds, a short term market and a long term market. At the time of the bond conversion the unemployment insurance commission converted its short term victory bonds into long term bonds which went down precipitously. They sold some of these bonds well under the present market price. I believe the price of these bonds went down to 82, and I do know that the unemployment insurance commission sold some at the time the market was around 85. The unfortunate part about the unemployment insurance commission having these bonds is that when they came to sell them in order to get cash to pay these unemployment benefits the market was very thin. The people in the market know the Bank of Canada is offering these bonds, and

Supply-Labour
they immediately withdraw their offers. It is extremely difficult for the Bank of Canada to get a firm price for these particular bonds.
I feel that the basic thing back of much of our unemployment is our own fiscal policy. I believe that the high interest rates we are experiencing tend to stagnate our economy. Certainly in this country it costs more to build houses, and it costs more to go ahead with a project that has to be financed. It costs more for the small businessman or for any industry to expand because of the high cost of money. Certainly this government has found it costs more to operate. The municipalities have to pay more in order to float their debentures; they pay more interest. I know of two or three projects in municipalities right now, one of which is a much needed school, that will not proceed because of the high cost of money. This is certainly contributing to unemployment.
I see unemployed people every week end. I feel heartily sorry for them. I believe when a man is unemployed for a long time he loses his morale. Many of these people have made commitments; they have purchased homes, and their savings are gone. They are just living from day to day. I feel this government should take some action to alleviate the situation. If this government had followed a proper fiscal policy we would not have the number of unemployed we have in Canada today. You cannot blame the Minister of Labour for all of this, but he is a member of the government and since he is a member of the government he will have to share in the responsibility. The people of Canada will be paying out more for unemployment insurance because there are more unemployed. As one hon. member suggested, whether they are statistics or not, the unemployed have needs just as we all have, and the people of Canada will have to go on paying for the mistakes of this government, not only because of its fiscal policy but for unemployment as well and the Canadian people will have to absorb the cost of the depletion of this unemployment insurance fund.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks on the subject under consideration. In the last three sessions, we have been listening to criticism levelled by the opposition at the present employment situation in Canada, but we have heard few constructive suggestions. They have just been passing the buck and saying that when the Conservatives were in office, there was unemployment, and when the Liberals were in office, there was prosperity. There was
CMr. McMillan.]
that phony prosperity in wartime and in the post-war period, and then in 1957, the Liberals did not see fit to consider the recommendations in the confidential report on the economy, no doubt in the hope that the people would go on believing everything was fine. They hoped something would happen to check unemployment, such as the Korean war. The Liberal party kept hoping for a war, which would have checked unemployment. What did the Conservative government do to correct that deplorable situation? It spent over a billion dollars on housing. It initiated a winter works program. Was that enough? While I am not prepared to say yes, I am not prepared to say it was worthless. The winter works program provided employment for over 50,000 people last winter.
In areas such as mine, where the winter starts around late November, and snow banks reach heights of six or seven feet, and the thermometer drops to 30 degrees below zero, it is hard to build water mains, sewers, etc.
Thanks to the representations made to the Minister of Labour by Conservative members, the provisions will be broadened and thus municipalities will be able to share in the winter works program to a greater extent.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few suggestions to the Minister of Labour and also to the government. I hope that our good friends of the opposition will take them into consideration, since they never made any themselves.
In my opinion, the government should assign $1 billion or more to carrying out important works that are needed throughout the country. I am thinking in particular of the famous maritime causeway, the pipe line from Calgary to Montreal, the building of bridges in Montreal and of a tunnel between Levis and Quebec, and many other necessary works that could be done. Where will this billion be found? In wartime, bonds were being issued. Why, then, could the government not issue Canadian bonds that the Canadian public could buy in order to help reduce unemployment and provide jobs for our people.
I feel that the Canadian people would make a point of buying those bonds in order to help the government to solve the unemployment problem.
Could the federal government not also establish a federal-municipal bank in order to help our municipalities? I agree that we do not always have the right to help our municipalities directly, but through such a

bank we could help them carry out certain projects. If we loaned money to them at a reasonable rate, say 3 or 34 per cent, our municipalities could carry out public works programs all year round. And whatever Mr. Lesage may say, we all know that unemployment is a provincial responsibility, we all know that unemployment is the responsibility of all three levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal. However, I think that the federal government could establish a federal-municipal fund in order to help municipalities to carry out public works programs.
I also suggest abolishing unemployment insurance and setting up work insurance instead.
If the government were to follow up my suggestions, our municipalities might employ people who are temporarily out of work. We would not see those jobless filing up at the unemployment offices in the fall, where a qualified worker with experience is told that there is no demand for his specialized services, but that he could obtain some other work. And so he refuses and says: "I have enough insurance stamps, I am a qualified workman, have you anything to offer in my own line?" And he gets as an answer: "No sir, but we have something else for you". And the man replies: "If it is outside my line, I would rather receive my $24, $30 or $34, and stay at home, with my feet near the oven, and be warm." And the worker goes on receiving unemployment insurance benefits.
In replacing unemployment insurance by work insurance, the unemployed would have to accept employment on works done by the federal, provincial or municipal governments.
That work insurance would be contributory, just as unemployment insurance, but the contribution would perhaps be higher. I think my colleague from Chicoutimi (Mr. Brassard! had made that suggestion early last winter.
I believe our trade unions would be in favour of such a project. If we had work to be done the year round, all across Canada, I am sure everyone would be at work and would be adequately paid, and no one would have to depend on unemployment insurance. As I said a moment ago, a great number of people prefer to be idle rather than to be employed at jobs which are not in their line, and it is thus that statistics are hurled at us with the cry: "Murder! It's unemployment!"
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the minister will take note of my suggestions. I admit, they are not very elaborate, but, I believe, they reflect the general ideas stated by my colleagues. They might be considered by economists, who may draw from them, some
Supply-Labour
practical solutions, not in two or three years, from now, but immediately. Let us establish a public works program. I say, once again, let us subscribe $1 billion in government bonds. I am convinced that Canadians will do it gladly in order that major public works be carried out to alleviate unemployment.

Mr. Chairman, when I state we are all worried over the prospective unemployment next winter I believe I am expressing the sentiments of every member of this committee. When I crossed swords in a mild way the other day with the Minister of Labour over the winter works programs plan he mentioned that the cost of labour averaged 34 per cent of the total cost. It had been my idea that the labour on an average did not average more than 22 per cent. However, I take his word.
I have worked out here a table showing how little the municipality gets in the end and how little incentive there is for a municipality to undertake a winter works program. Most of the municipalities in Canada can ill afford to undertake any works programs, whether winter or summer. The financial standing of most municipalities precludes them from making any issue of debentures and borrowing money, especially at 5f per cent. Works programs cost approximately 10 per cent more when executed in the winter plus the interest on the money borrowed. A $100,000 program would cost in winter $110,000. The Minister of Labour said that about 34 per cent of the cost would be represented by labour. That would mean that approximately 66 per cent of the cost, in round figures, would be for materials or $72,600. Labour then would cost $37,400. The government would pay $18,700. The municipality also would pay $18,700. The government's share would then be 17 per cent leaving the municipality to pay 83 per cent or $91,300 as its share of $110,000.
If the municipality had not carried on the works program in the wintertime the cost to the municipality would be $100,000. That would be the real cost of the job if executed at the municipality's pleasure. As it would have cost the municapility $91,300 under the government plan, the municipality, to carry on the work whenever it wanted to do it, would expend only $8,700, so all it would really get from the government would be 8.7 per cent of the total cost of the job. There is not much incentive when only 50 per cent of the cost of labour is to be granted for any municipality to undertake any winter works program because if you deduct from the

Supply-Labour
$8,700 the interest at 5f per cent on the money borrowed it would leave little saving.
However, I should like to make a suggestion to the minister and if he carries out this plan I think it win help very much with regard to unemployment next winter. It would be a great incentive to the municipalities which are ready to undertake winter works programs.
To my mind the cause of a lot of unemployment amongst intellectuals and men in the best paid trades is due in large measure to United States magazines. In the case of the United States magazines printed in Canada, all the preparatory work is executed in the United States and plates ready for printing are sent to Canada. Editors, writers, artists, make-up men, lay-out men, compositors, monotype and linotype operators, stereotypers, electrotypers, all United States labour, depriving our citizens from enjoying these situations and causing a serious slump in the graphic arts industry and adding greatly to the ranks of the unemployed in these highly remunerative situations.
United States magazines that claim to put out Canadian editions are not doing anything of the sort. They are for the most part merely dumping United States magazines into Canada. True there might be a slight change made in the contents by inserting a few pages touching on Canadian matters, but the majority of the text is still American. These United States magazines sell a lot of advertising space to Canadian advertisers and funnel back the profits to the United States. Canadian publications are facing an abnormal and unfair competition from these United States magazines and many of our large Canadian magazines are being forced out of business, adding greatly to the ranks of our unemployed.
In 1951 the total combined circulation of Canadian national periodicals per year was 42 million copies, against a circulation of United States magazines coming to Canada of 86 million copies. In 1957 Canadian magazines combined had reached a circulation per year of 45,600,000 copies against a circulation of United States magazines coming to Canada of 154 million copies.
Now, Mr. Chairman, intellectuals as well as editors, writers and newspapermen contribute greatly to the progress of any country. They stimulate and inculcate in the minds of the citizens that pride of citizenship which stirs them to greater deeds and to the creation of activities which eventually leads to more employment. By depriving our Canadian citizens of the leadership of these intellectual minds we are rendering them a disservice by forcing them to read United States magazines. These magazines in many

cases are a serious threat to our Canadian culture, for they inculcate in the minds of our citizens an American ideology that we do not appreciate. We have a great admiration for our United States friends and we value their friendship. We want to remain on friendly terms with them-
On a point of order, is the hon. member in order in discussing periodicals from the United States under the Minister of Labour's estimates?
They all bear on unemployment.
Well, let the Chairman rule on it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Frankly, I would say that unemployment touches a lot of subjects and I think up until now the hon. member has related his remarks to unemployment to a great extent. He may have been straying a little recently.

Above all, we want to remain Canadians and we want to preserve our Canadian way of life and expression and thought. We prize our Canadian heritage. We are proud to be Canadians. We have two main cultures in Canada and we respect the rights and ideals of one another. We want to preserve these cultures. We meet in harmony and not in conflict and we want to continue to do so; hence our need for magazines with a Canadian mentality so that we may continue to enjoy and cherish the inheritance left to us by our forefathers who were willing to endure the greatest of hardships and even die for the maintenance of the high Canadian principles in which they believed.
In the Gazette of Monday, July 25, 1960 there was an editorial and I would like to comment on it. The editor expresses surprise that in a country like Canada with so many advantages over other countries we should find ourselves with hundreds of thousands of unemployed at a cost to the unemployment insurance commission of approximately $500 million a year. And he asks this question:
-what form of economic activity creates the most jobs for Canadians?
And he answers:
Manufacturing creates more jobs than anything else. And in the last decade manufacturing has tended to decline in relative importance.
He further says:
-about 100,000 more young people every year reach the age when they are seeking jobs... Construction and "service" industries like transportation, communications, trade, finance and so forth offer the most jobs but they can scarcely hope to continue their expansion, unless manufacturing, which is by far the greatest employer of labour, itself maintains its rate of growth.

It is a fact that the most ambitious and highly trained of our citizens are leaving Canada because we do not seem to be able to provide them with the wider opportunities they seek.
Our prospects for an increase in population and in job opportunities depends largely upon the extent to which manufacturing is encouraged. Manufacturing is falling behind at the present time. We import more manufactured goods per capita than any other country in the world.
I am particularly interested in the fate of our unemployed. I believe we should gauge our economy to provide a job for everyone who is able and willing to work. I believe it is an inherent right for a citizen to be able to procure for himself a job of his liking, and I believe it is the duty of the government in power to seek ways and means to provide these jobs, to seek the cause of unemployment, and to do everything in its power to create work for all.
I should like for one moment, to give the committee a little information contained in the Canadian apparel and textile manufacturers association's bulletin of March 25, 1960, which bears on the unemployment situation. This bulletin says:
Value of Japanese exports to Canada of clothing, textile products and fabrics during 1959 showed an increase of 56 per cent from 1958 totals, and in many cases volume outstripped domestic production, reports the Canadian apparel and textile manufacturers association. During 1959 shipments to Canada of clothing and textiles from Japan were valued at $41.5 million, an increase of 56 per cent over the 1958 figure of $26.6 million.
The United States, at least 15 times the size of our market, took only six times as much Japanese textiles in 1959. Imports from Japan of man-made fibre fabrics amounted to 1.4 million square yards in 1958 and 3.4 millions in 1959; imports of cotton fabrics rose from 18 million square yards in 1958 to 25.3 million in 1959. As the committee will realize that is a great cause of unemployment in Canada.
Imports of man-made fibre sports shirts amounted to more than double the Canadian production. I point that fact out to members of the committee and ask them to draw their own conclusions about it. Exports to this country amounted to 370,000 dozen compared with Canadian production in 1958 of 163,000 dozen. We have all worried over the unemployment situation. The prospects for employment next winter are far from bright. Our citizens are most anxious that some plan be formulated to relieve the unemployment situation and I hope that the Minister of Labour will take my remarks in good part and set the necessary machinery in motion to create jobs so that the Canadian people will not suffer next winter and so that their families and particularly their children may be properly fed and clothed.

Jean Lesage, is ready to assume his responsibilities with regard to unemployment in the province of Quebec and to co-operate fully with the federal Minister of Labour in order to enable our fellow citizens to earn a decent living.
Attempts were made to distort statements made in the province of Quebec during the last election campaign. Mr. Chairman, I repeat the present Quebec premier is ready to assume his responsibilities and to work in close co-operation with the federal Minister of Labour and with the present government in order to find an answer to unemployment.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak any longer about unemployment, because other members who rose before me treated that question competently.
During his last election campaign, the present Prime Minister of our country (Mr. Dief-enbaker) solemnly stated that as long as he would be Prime Minister of our country no one would suffer in Canada.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I think that the Canadian people and especially the people of the province of Quebec will agree that never in all the history of this country, have so many of our fellow Canadians suffered as much from unemployment, as since the Conservative party took over.
Mr. Chairman, I am one of those who would like an answer to be found to the

unemployment problem. Certain members on this side of the house offered concrete proposals to the present government in order to solve the unemployment problem, but those suggestions fell on deaf ears.
Mr. Chairman, I should like now to deal with another problem which I have already mentioned since being elected to this house, and I am sure that the Minister of Labour will listen with kindness to the remarks I have to make on that matter.
There exists in this country a social problem which all of us parliamentarians have a duty to solve. I am thinking of those who are 45 or over and who, on account of their age, cannot find work. I have been speaking of this for the last four or five years and tonight I want to mention it again and insist further so that legislation is introduced in our statutes in order to put an end to the kind of discrimination which is practised against our fellow citizens who are 45 or over and who are looking for a job.
I admit that some efforts have been made in that direction during the last few months. The Department of Labour has published a pamphlet to facilitate the hiring of workers 45 years of age and over. I am glad it did, but on the other hand, I believe that this publication of the Department of Labour is not enough. So, I again urge the Minister of Labour to place in our statute books an act which would eliminate this discrimination.
In the last few days, we had, in Ottawa, a federal-provincial conference attended by the representatives of the federal government and of the various provincial governments in this country. At some later conference there should be a proposal to study some way of enforcing legislation which would prevent the discrimination I just mentioned.
The representatives of the federal government should, together with those of the various provincial governments, insert in the statutes of parliament and in the statutes of the various legislatures, some legislation tending to prevent such discrimination. The problem is acute and it is up to us to solve it. Something should be done at all levels to settle the matter.
I trust, Mr. Chairman, that at 40, at 45 or even at 50, a man has acquired enough experience in life to be of use to his country and to his province and to be able to earn his living decently. We who are the legislators have no right to tolerate such discrimination. We have only to read advertisements in the papers, or published by the

federal government to realize that such discrimination exists and that it is useless to ask for employment when one is over 40. It is evident, therefore, as I say, that there is discrimination with regard to those people.
The various American states have passed legislation in this respect in order to help their fellow citizens who are 45 years old and over. Now I shall make a special appeal to the Minister of Labour, asking him to put aside party politics and to accept the request I have been making for a number of years to help our fellow citizens.
Ever since I have taken an interest in the matter I have received correspondence from several parts of Canada, and I should like to quote only a few extracts of letters I have received, in order to show the house that the problem does really exist.
Among others, I received a letter from a fellow citizen of Longueuil saying:
I had a job at the Canadian Pratt & Whitney Engine in Longueuil. I was told that past 45 years of age we were dismissed and I tried to get another job; but I was refused all the time on the grounds I was too old at 40. Mr. Rouleau, we will have to wait until we get our old age pension, or else open a blind pig in order to live.
I received another letter from one Mr. Laforce, in the constituency of Chateauguay, who told me, among other things:
I am 54 years old and I am still able to work very well, I am looking for work, but each time I am told that I am too old.
I received another letter from one Mr. Laurent Blais, of St. Roch, who tells me:
When we go and look for a job, we have to state our age and, each time we say we are more than 40 years old, we are turned down.
