speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, again we have the opportunity of speaking on the problem of unemployment and some of the things that go with it. We have heard many suggestions that in my opinion can be implemented to some satisfactory degree but there seems to be a terrific over-all problem that we have not yet been able to face. I notice that in today's Ottawa Citizen there is an article entitled, "Senate to Send Questionnaire to Unemployed", which reads as follows:
Canada's unemployed are ro be asked to fill out a special Senate-sponsored questionnaire about themselves-who they are, why they can't find jobs, their training, background and vital statistics. This was indicated Wednesday in the Senate by Senator Leon Methot, chairman of the special Senate committee. on manpower.
. "X understand these questionnaires are going to be printed in many languages and sent to every unemployment insurance commission office in Canada", he said in reporting that the manpower committee was launching a research study "in depth" into the unemployment problem.
The questionnaires would be drawn up in such a way as to preserve the anonymity of the applicant. The committee has retained Professor John Deutsch of Queen's University, Professor William Hood of University of Toronto and Warren James, a statistical expert with the defence production department, as the nucleus of its research team.
Very seldom is the Senate ever on the right track, Mr. Chairman, but I hope this is one of the times they are. It seems surprising to me that the House of Commons industrial relations committee has not seen fit to employ people of this calibre to do research work into what is unemployment and what is not unemployment.
It was not allowed to by the government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I realize the government is responsible for whether or not they do it but it seems funny that the Senate should be the ones to do this in-depth study that they appear to be going to do. There is a considerable difference of opinion as to who is unemployed and who is not. I have heard a number of government members say, and I think sincerely, that those people who are registered with the unemployment insurance commission just do not want to work. I do not think that accusation should be made about anybody in Canada until these people are offered the opportunity to work. If they are offered jobs and turn them down then I think it is quite safe to say they do not want that particular employment at least. If we have no jobs to offer, which is the case in most instances, then we cannot very well

say that a person is just lazy and does not want to work. I think that members who use this argument are being unfair to many Canadians who have travelled from one part of the country to another looking for work and have not got it.

Would the hon. member permit a question? Is the hon. member suggesting that any hon. member actually used this argument in the house? I do not think such is the case. There may be a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I do not know whether the hon. member wishes to make it a question of privilege. However, I did not say that anybody had said it in the house. Some members of the government have said this to me and one of them said it today. I do not think it -was said facetiously but rather quite sincerely. I do not think he is in a position to offer employment himself but he mentioned that many of these people do not want to work. It is true that we are having trouble in connection with unemployment insurance. There are people receiving unemployment insurance benefits who do not deserve them in my opinion but I would be much happier to find people receiving unemployment insurance payments who do not deserve them than I would be to find any person being turned down who deserves unemployment insurance benefits.
It is quite true that certain married women are drawing unemployment insurance benefits because of conditions we did not realize when the act was first drafted. It is quite true there are people seasonally employed who are making very close to a yearly income out of such employment and yet are able to draw unemployment insurance which is being paid for by people who are getting less than some of these construction workers earn on a seasonal basis. While this is true, I think we have to be very careful in limiting the provisions so that we will not take away the benefits from those who need them just to stop the very few who are abusing the system, and I think there are some now who do abuse it.
The whole matter of unemployment should be given very serious consideration because it seems to me we are reaching the stage now where we are reaping the effects of automation and yet we have done absolutely nothing to overcome the difficulties. This afternoon the minister mentioned that we are extending training for unemployed people who wish to take technical trade training. I hope this will mean that we will turn out more bricklayers, painters, plumbers and mechanics rather than more clerks, storekeepers and inventory keepers in government offices and

that sort of thing. It seems to me that the problem facing the government is a manifestation of the fact that governments have not yet been able to meet the demand for change in industry.
One problem affecting many Canadian workers has to do with automobiles. In tonight's newspaper there is a letter from an economist who points out that there was an increase of 38,800, or 157 per cent, in the number of new cars imported into Canada from the United Kingdom between 1957-58 and 1959-60, and this was accompanied by a fall-off of $5 million in the value of our wheat exports to the United Kingdom. New car imports from the United Kingdom in the first quarter of 1960 were 26,800, a greater total than our imports for five of the past 10 years. In 1959 Canada imported 73,000 British cars.
I think this illustrates that it is time we took a look at the automobile industry. It is quite true that there is all this ballyhoo about bigger cars, faster cars and so on. However, the Canadian people have decided that they do not agree with the automobile industry. They do not want big cars with powerful motors that use more gasoline. They want the small economy cars. They are not interested in the terrific expanse of tailfin, with the consequent increase in price. They are interested in a small car. I think this is the time for the government to give leadership and say to the industry, you will give the people a number of small cars, and you are going to balance the number of cars against what we need to establish an export-import balance.
You may ask me, Mr. Chairman, why we should tell the automobile industry these things. It is very simple. These automobile companies would rather shut down and lay off their workers than change their system of production. They would rather do this because they do not care a hoot about their workers; they do not care a hoot about the country; they do not even care much about the buyer. What they do care about is making a profit. They can make just the same profit from the cars they manufacture in plants they own in Europe as they can from the cars manufactured in the plants they own in the United States. If it gives them more dollars to import cars they produce in other countries, then they are willing to bring those cars into the country and put them through their own dealerships and make their profit in this way.
It seems to me that the government itself is going to have to take some position in connection with directing industry, especially
Supply-Labour
when an industry continues to produce something that is not going to sell. The only people who are going to be hurt in this situation are the workers. Industry will not be hurt because it will at least break even. However, the workers, the municipalities, the storekeepers and the people who are dependent on the auto workers for a living, these are the people who are going to be very hard hit. In the final analysis, the government which is being asked to support these welfare ventures that are necessary is going to be hard hit because there will be no taxes paid.
In the last few weeks notices have appeared in the local newspapers in my area that there will be two of the major mines in Kirkland Lake closed down. One of these is Sylvanite which has operated for nearly 25 years, and the other one is Kirkland Lake Minerals, which has operated for a long time. At the end of this month Kirkland Lake Minerals will lay off half its working force, and will continue operations with less than 100 employees. Sylvanite, which I think has employed about 100 persons for a number of years, sometimes a great deal more, is going to lay off all its employees.
I think it is interesting to note what they are going to do. This company, like a lot of other companies which close out, is not considering the federal government which has financed the company for a number of years. This company is not concerned with the community or their workmen. The company has done no more than it should have for the community or the workers. It has not even given the worker a decent standard of living or a pension plan. It has paid as little income tax and other taxes as possible to the government, while at the same time obtaining as much from emergency gold mining assistance as it could get. However, when it comes to closing out the company is going to dissolve, according to newspaper reports. It is not going to establish an exploration company to look for another mine in order to employ these workers. The company will close down and hopes to be able to liquidate its assets and repay every stockholder all the money put into that particular operation. They are going to do very well by the people who financed them, but they have not done very well by the people who have worked in this industry. They have not done very well by the government which paid a great deal of money to the company in order to help the community exist during the last 15 years.
I think this highlights what I am saying. If the government does not start directing industry into places like Elliot Lake, then there will be more unemployment. There is no great need for a park at Elliot Lake. What

Business of the House
do the miners want with a park? If they want to go fishing, they can fish in the surrounding lakes. The miner does not need a park with a campsite. He has a $15,000 or $20,000 house in that area, and he does not want it in the middle of a park. He needs a job and industry should be directed there to provide him with a job. I suggest this government should take industry out of Toronto and other municipalities that do not really need it. They have more industry than they have room for now, and some industries should be moved from there to places like Elliot Lake.
Today, with all the technological changes, a worker can produce five or 10 times as much as he could 20 years ago. However, he is going to wear the same amount of clothes, buy the same amount of food and need the same amount of entertainment. I think it must be obvious to everyone that we are not going to solve unemployment problems until we start supplying new jobs to replace those jobs that are no longer there. If our standard of living continues to increase, it will mean more jobs and more purchasing power. People who are unemployed cannot buy anything. They cannot continue to increase their standard of living and they become a burden on those who remain in the productive field.
At the same time this government is not going to solve unemployment, nor is any other government, until it goes into "depth", as the Senate says. However, I do not believe the government will want to wait as long as the Senate has to find the answer because governments do not last as long as senators.
